### Honest negatives

- **A lesson heading is misprinted in the book itself:** Unit 2, Lesson 1 is headed "DO YOU LIKE COMPUTERS?" (printed p. 26, verified on the rendered page) — a carry-over of Unit 1 Lesson 1's title. The contents map (printed p. 8) shows the lesson is really about school life and feelings; anyone citing lesson titles should use the contents title, not the page heading.
- **Dated material:** the appendix still presents Prince Charles as heir who "is going to be king one day" (printed p. 135) — he is now King Charles III. The canteen lesson converts at roughly £1 ≈ €1.60 (p. 28); tourist figures are from 2005 (p. 122), airport figures from 2006 (pp. 125, 150), and several world records are stated as of 1997–2008 (pp. 78–79). Treat all statistics and prices as period content, not current fact.
- **Dated technology and links:** listening is repeatedly cued to "cassette/cd", the net-friends material points to early BBC/CBeebies and Greek portal addresses, and the maps are ©2006 Google/TeleAtlas plates.
- **No single year of publication is printed** in the book (see Identity block); a citation needing a year should cite the Revised Edition (code 10-0233) and note the PDF's mixed 2014–2024 production stamps rather than invent a year.
- **Maps appendix (printed pp. 163–167) is image-only:** the plates carry no extractable text beyond their headers, so nothing in this summary quotes them.
- **The Unit 8 fairy tale is never named in the lesson:** pupils are asked to title it and identify its writer themselves, so this summary describes it by its plot (a prince seeking a real princess) rather than assigning it a title the book does not print there.
- **This file is the Pupil's Book only:** the introduction and several tasks refer to the companion Workbook, which is not included in this PDF.
## Grade 6 — Αγγλικά (Anglika), Student's Book, New Edition (real title as printed)

Real title as printed: **ΑΓΓΛΙΚΑ ΣΤ΄ ΔΗΜΟΤΙΚΟΥ — Βιβλίο μαθητή** (cover, in English: "ΑΓΓΛΙΚΑ / ENGLISH 6th GRADE", "Pupil's Book", "Στ΄ Δημοτικού").

### Identity block

- **Identity verdict: MATCH.** The PDF is exactly the book in the record — the Greek Ministry Grade 6 (Στ΄ Δημοτικού) English pupil's/student book. Cover spread (PDF p. 1, viewed as a render), title page (PDF p. 6) and imprint page (PDF p. 5) all agree.
- **Authors (as printed on cover and title page):** Ελένη Εφραιμίδου, Ελένη Ζώη-Ρέππα, Φιλίτσα Φρουζάκη.
- **Publisher / issuing bodies:** Υπουργείο Παιδείας, Θρησκευμάτων και Αθλητισμού (Ministry of Education, Religions and Sports) and Ινστιτούτο Εκπαιδευτικής Πολιτικής (Institute of Educational Policy); published by Ινστιτούτο Τεχνολογίας Υπολογιστών και Εκδόσεων «Διόφαντος» (ITYE Diophantos). Writing contractor named on the title page: Μιχαήλ Λεβής Α.Ε. (with a Linguaphone mark). The imprint page (PDF p. 5) gives the original-edition credits (Pedagogical Institute project, co-funded 75% European Social Fund / 25% national funds) and a reissue note: the reissue was produced by ITYE Diophantos from a digital layout funded under ESPA / "ΣΤΗΡΙΖΩ", with corrections approved by the Institute of Educational Policy board.
- **Edition / year:** The cover carries the stamp "ΑΝΑΘΕΩΡΗΜΕΝΗ ΕΚΔΟΣΗ" (Revised Edition), book code 10-0235 — i.e. this is the revised/reissued edition, not the first printing. No single publication year is printed on the title or imprint pages read. The PDF is a composite digital file: most page furniture is dated 21 Jan 2014, the front matter 26 Jan 2015 / 28 Jan 2016, some unit files Feb 2015, the Appendix VI map file Oct 2020, and one page (Unit 5, Lesson 3) Nov 2024; PDF creation 21 Jan 2014, modified 31 Jul 2025. So "New Edition" in the record corresponds to this revised Diophantos reissue; a learner-facing citation should say "revised edition (Diophantos reissue)" rather than a single year.
- **ISBN (printed on the back cover, PDF p. 1):** ISBN 978-960-06-2612-4. Book code: 0-10-0235 (barcode element (01) 000000 0 10 0235 5).
- **PDF pages:** 186 (pdfinfo: 186 pages, 40 MB). PDF p. 1 is the full cover spread (back cover + spine + front cover on one sheet) and PDF p. 186 repeats that same cover spread at the end.
- **Printed-page vs PDF-page offset:** For the main body, **printed page = PDF page − 17**. Printed p. 1 is PDF p. 18 (Unit 1 opener) and printed p. 168 is PDF p. 185 (the Greek colophon/distribution notice). This offset was checked against the printed folio in the footer of dozens of pages (e.g. printed 2 = PDF 19, printed 133 = PDF 150, printed 163 = PDF 180). PDF pp. 2–17 are front matter (blank sheets, title/imprint, table of contents on roman-numbered pages, and a Greek introduction to the pupil); all page references below are to **printed** pages unless "PDF p." is stated.

### How the book is built

Ten units, each normally 12 printed pages: a unit opener, three lessons, and a "Check yourself" self-test scored out of 20 with can-do statements. Every unit also carries learning-strategy panels. After Unit 10 come six appendices (printed pp. 121–162) and a sample pupil portfolio (printed pp. 163–167), then the colophon (printed p. 168).

### Unit-by-unit summary (own words, printed page references)

**Unit 1 — Our multicultural class (pp. 1–12).** New pupils from Ukraine, Albania and Georgia introduce their countries in school-newsletter reports — capitals, terrain, weather, work, and problems such as the Chernobyl accident's effect on Ukraine (pp. 1–3). Lesson 2 moves to favourite school subjects and a computer-lab listening (pp. 6–9); Lesson 3 is a guided geography project: read a model report about Britain, then write a five-paragraph report about Greece (p. 10). Grammar arrivals: **Present Simple** with adverbs of frequency (p. 4) and **Present Continuous**, explicitly contrasted with Present Simple (p. 8). Vocabulary: countries, nationalities, landforms, school subjects.

**Unit 2 — Going shopping (pp. 13–24).** A supermarket flyer (bakery, butcher, greengrocer, organic goods), shopping lists, prices in pounds/pence, a department-store dialogue, an early e-shopping project with an online toy order form (pp. 13–15, 18–19, 22). Grammar: **countable vs uncountable nouns**, a/an, some/any, how much / how many, containers and weights (p. 16); verbs of sense + adjective (look / taste / feel / smell / sound) and **few / a few, little / a little** (p. 20). Vocabulary: food, shop departments, clothes, colours and materials.

**Unit 3 — Imaginary creatures (pp. 25–36).** Short texts on Polyphemus the Cyclops, fairies (Oberon, Titania, Puck, Tinkerbell) and Shrek (pp. 26–27); a listening ghost-story play, "The fifty-cent piece" (p. 30); and a classroom-theatre adaptation of *A Midsummer Night's Dream* (p. 34). Grammar is comparison throughout: **comparative and superlative adjectives** (p. 28), **as … as / not as–so … as** (p. 32), and **comparison of adverbs** (p. 33). Vocabulary: appearance, personality, opposite adjectives.

**Unit 4 — The history of the aeroplane (pp. 37–48).** Opens with the Daedalus and Icarus myth (p. 37), then an e-mail from London pen-friends about a Fleet Air (Arm) Museum visit, the Wright brothers and the four forces of flight (p. 38); Lesson 2 is an in-flight "air pocket" dialogue (p. 42); Lesson 3 is a project on Brueghel's *Landscape with the Fall of Icarus* and its poem (p. 46). Grammar: **Past Simple and Past Continuous** introduced side by side (p. 40), then the two combined in one sentence, plus **linking words** (first, then, when, while, as, finally…) (p. 44). Vocabulary: parts of a plane, flight.

**Unit 5 — Travelling through time (pp. 49–60).** A grandmother's 1960s diary pages from Crete (Beatles, mini-skirts, bell-bottoms) drive Lesson 1 (pp. 50–51); Lesson 2 covers the London Transport Museum — recorded information, a guided tour, and asking/giving directions (pp. 54–55); Lesson 3 is a project to make a museum leaflet (p. 58). Grammar arrival: **used to + infinitive** for past states and habits no longer true, distinguished from a single Past Simple event at a specific time (p. 52). Vocabulary: 1960s clothes and hairstyles, transport, museum information, directions.

**Unit 6 — Me, myself and my future job (pp. 61–72).** Career Day job profiles (nurse, ecologist, jewellery designer, air-traffic controller, hairdresser), job advertisements and workplace safety rules (pp. 62–63, 68–69); a listening matching workers to jobs (p. 66); a careers questionnaire and job-interview project (p. 70). Grammar: **modals can / may / should** for ability, possibility, permission and advice (p. 64); **future with will** for offers, promises, warnings, requests, on-the-spot decisions and predictions, contrasted with **be going to** for intentions and pre-arranged plans (pp. 67–68). Vocabulary: jobs, skills, personal traits.

**Unit 7 — Share your experiences (pp. 73–84).** Record holders: newspaper extracts on swimmer Ian Thorpe and on *The Phantom of the Opera* becoming Broadway's longest-running show (p. 74); a radio programme about unusual records — skateboarding, a giant kebab skewer, a champion ferret (p. 78); a project to set a class record and make a records book, with a Paralympics-champion report in the wider unit work (pp. 82, and contents). Grammar arrivals — the book's biggest step up: **Present Perfect Simple** (p. 76), contrasted with Past Simple for a stated past time, and **Present Perfect Continuous** with **for / since** (p. 80). Vocabulary: sports, records, theatre.

**Unit 8 — Blow your own trumpet (pp. 85–96).** Music first: instruments sorted into wind / string / percussion, and a Thessaloniki music-festival leaflet (pp. 85–86); then money — ABBA's money song as listening, pocket money, and what people would spend a windfall on (pp. 90–91); Lesson 3 is a magazine problem page, writing an advice letter (p. 94). Grammar arrivals: **Conditional Type 1** (if + Present Simple, will / can / must / imperative in the result clause) for real present/future possibilities, including a personal-safety scenario about a stranger's car (pp. 88–89); **Conditional Type 2** (if + Past Simple, would + infinitive, preferring *were*) for unlikely or imagined situations and for advice of the "If I were you…" kind (p. 92). Vocabulary: musical instruments, money expressions.

**Unit 9 — Earth Day everyday (pp. 97–108).** An Earth Day story in which a boy who thinks he can do nothing hears the starfish-on-the-beach story and learns that small actions count (pp. 98–99); a visit to the Zakynthos Environmental Centre about endangered species — loggerhead turtles and the Mediterranean monk seal, threatened by tourism, hotels and fishing nets (p. 102); and "The Awful 5", a play about air pollutants (toxins, sulphur dioxide, ozone, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide), printed in full in Appendix II (pp. 106, 142–144). Grammar arrivals: **Past Perfect Simple** for an action before another past action (p. 100), and **clauses of result (so, as a result) and reason (because, because of, as)** (p. 104). Vocabulary: pollution, habitat, endangered / extinct, waste.

**Unit 10 — Time for fun (pp. 109–120).** Films and books: James Bond actors and film lists, and a magazine article about the young-Bond books presenting Bond aged 13 (pp. 110–111); a film-festival lesson built around *E.T.* (pp. 114–115); a project to write and publish a film review (p. 118). Grammar arrivals: **Present Simple Passive** — formed with *be* + past participle, used when the action matters more than the doer, with *by* + agent when the doer is named, and practised on cinema signs and notices (p. 112); and **-ing vs -ed adjectives** for describing a film vs the viewer's feelings (pp. 116–117, per the unit contents and Lesson 2 practice). Vocabulary: film genres, reviews, appearance description.

**Appendices (pp. 121–168).** Appendix I, "It's your choice!" (pp. 121–134): differentiated / alternative activities keyed to each unit (easier reading versions, dietary-habits work for Unit 2, traveller quiz for Unit 5, a beach-clean Past Perfect task for Unit 9, and similar). Appendix II, Resource materials (pp. 135–146): the information-gap sheets, canteen menu, texts and film cards the lessons point to, including the full "Awful 5" play. Appendix III, Grammar File (pp. 147–158): compact form/use tables for Units 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9 and 10 — note there is **no separate Grammar File entry for Unit 5 (used to) or Unit 8 (conditionals)** in this file; those two are taught only inside their units. Appendix IV: irregular verbs table (p. 159). Appendix V: per-unit vocabulary list (pp. 160–161). Appendix VI: a map (p. 162). The book closes with a sample pupil language portfolio — personal pages, reading/speaking/writing activity records, self-evaluation (pp. 163–167) — and the Greek legal notice that Diophantos textbooks are printed and distributed free to public schools (p. 168).

### Honest negatives / primary-series-final verdicts

- **This is the last primary book.** Στ΄ Δημοτικού is the sixth and final grade of Greek primary school (Dimotiko), so this volume closes the primary English series; the next step in the Greek system is Gymnasio (lower secondary), a different series. As a primary-series finale it is deliberately a consolidation-plus-step-up book: it revises Present Simple/Continuous, past tenses and comparisons from earlier grades, then adds the structures a pupil needs at secondary entry.
- **Present Perfect — present, both forms.** Present Perfect Simple arrives in Unit 7 (p. 76) and Present Perfect Continuous with for/since in the same unit (p. 80). There is **no Past Perfect Continuous** anywhere in the book.
- **Conditionals — Types 1 and 2 only.** Type 1 (p. 88) and Type 2 (p. 92) are both taught in Unit 8. There is **no Type 3 conditional** and no mixed conditional.
- **Passive — Present Simple only.** The passive is taught as one system, the Present Simple Passive, in Unit 10 (p. 112) and the Grammar File (p. 158). No Past Simple Passive (or any other passive tense) is presented as a grammar topic.
- **No reported speech.** Neither the units nor the Grammar File contain reported/direct speech as a topic (the words do not occur in the book's text layer).
- **Grammar File gap.** Appendix III has no entries for Unit 5 (used to) or Unit 8 (conditionals), although both are fully taught inside their units — a course built from the Grammar File alone would miss them.
- **Dated cultural surface, current structure.** Some content is visibly of its era (a 2005 young-Bond news article, prices and websites of the 2000s, ABBA and *Phantom* record facts as then reported); the grammar sequence itself is the durable part. The PDF also mixes page files from 2014–2024 (see Identity block), so it should be cited as the revised Diophantos reissue, not as a single-year printing.
## Grade 7 (Advanced) — Αγγλικά, Student's Book — *Think Teen! 1st Grade of Junior High School, Student's Book (Προχωρημένοι)*

### Identity block

- **Real title as printed:** *Think Teen!* — "1st Grade of Junior High School / STUDENT'S BOOK", with the stream word **Προχωρημένοι** (Advanced) printed in red on the title page, in a yellow banner on the front cover, and on the imprint title page. The sources appendix (printed p. 209) names the book in Greek as "Αγγλικά Α΄ Γυμνασίου – Επίπεδο Προχωρημένων – Βιβλίο Μαθητή" (English, 1st Grade of Gymnasio – Advanced Level – Student's Book). A΄ Γυμνασίου is the first year of Greek junior high school, i.e. Grade 7.
- **Stream verdict:** ADVANCED — confirmed. This is **not** the Beginners (αρχαρίων) book. The word Προχωρημένοι appears on the cover, the title page and the imprint page, and the stamp on the cover reads "ΑΝΑΘΕΩΡΗΜΕΝΗ ΕΚΔΟΣΗ 21-0205" (Revised Edition).
- **Authors:** Ευαγγελία Καραγιάννη (Evangelia Karagianni), Βασιλική Κουή (Vasiliki Koui), Αικατερίνη Νικολάκη (Aikaterini Nikolaki). Writing contractor named on the imprint page: Ελληνικά Γράμματα (Ellinika Grammata), under the auspices of the Pedagogical Institute.
- **Publisher:** Ινστιτούτο Τεχνολογίας Υπολογιστών και Εκδόσεων «ΔΙΟΦΑΝΤΟΣ» (Institute of Computer Technology and Publications "Diophantos" — ITYE Diophantos), for the Υπουργείο Παιδείας, Θρησκευμάτων και Αθλητισμού (Ministry of Education, Religions and Sports) / Ινστιτούτο Εκπαιδευτικής Πολιτικής (Institute of Educational Policy). Distributed via ebooks.edu.gr.
- **ISBN:** 978-960-06-2684-1 (printed on the back cover). **Book code:** 0-21-0205 (cover barcode element: (01) 000000 0 21 0205 4).
- **Edition / year:** No calendar year is printed on the title or imprint pages. The book is marked as a revised edition; the imprint page states the reissue was produced by ITYE Diophantos from a digital mockup funded under ESPA / "ΣΤΗΡΙΖΩ", with corrections approved by the Institute of Educational Policy. In-file production stamps are dated 19/2/2015 and 20/1/2016. (No year is asserted beyond what is printed/stamped.)
- **Extent:** 226 PDF pages; 216 printed pages plus unnumbered front matter and cover spreads.
- **Page offset:** **printed page = PDF page − 9** throughout the numbered body and appendices (e.g. printed p. 1 = PDF p. 10; printed p. 141 = PDF p. 150; printed p. 216 = PDF p. 225). PDF pp. 1–4 are the cover spread, title page and imprint pages; PDF p. 5 is blank; PDF pp. 6–9 are the Contents; PDF p. 217 (printed p. 208 position) and PDF pp. 222–224 (printed pp. 213–215 positions) are blank; PDF p. 226 repeats the cover spread.
- **Cast / frame:** A recurring group of teenage "e-friends" (Magda in Nafplio, Jennifer in Cambridge, Petra & Hans in Berlin, Silou in Jakarta, Pedro, Jean Paul, Nadia and others) exchange e-mails across units, anchored on an International Teen Camp in Greece.

### Unit-by-unit summary (own words; printed page references)

**Unit 1 — Welcome! (printed pp. 1–6).** A single opening lesson built around an International Teen Camp. Learners match greetings in several languages to photographs of teenagers, talk about camp leisure photographs, and listen to a camper (Pedro) presenting himself. A "Do you know me well?" guessing game has partners predict each other's likes, habits and abilities and then check by asking. Reading is limited to English words on public signs; a listening task picks English loanwords out of everyday Greek dialogues. Vocabulary is classroom language (asking for meanings, repetition, help). The grammar work is a correct-the-mistakes review of *be*, *have got* and the Present Simple rather than new presentation. Projects: a collage of English signs found locally, and a noticeboard display of English words used in Greek, with a short etymology exercise on loanwords in Greek.

**Unit 2 — Junior High School Life (printed pp. 7–26).** Three lessons. *Lesson 1, "Fancy school?" (p. 8):* a magazine quiz sorts readers into student types ("bookish", "sometime", "struggler"); learners read e-mails and a school timetable, build "school" collocations, and meet the Present Simple (habits and states, third-person *-s*, questions and negatives) and adverbs of frequency; writing is an e-mail about an ideal school. *Lesson 2, "Join our club!" (p. 15):* a Cambridge school poster advertises clubs (reading, choir, drama, cookery, photography, eco team, charity, dance); students read members' e-mails, practise time idioms, and contrast the Present Continuous for actions happening now with the Present Simple, including a self-check on what classmates are wearing/doing. *Lesson 3, "TEEN Best-sellers!" (p. 20):* learners read adapted publisher blurbs of two real teen novels — Jeremy Strong's *Stuff* and Cathy Cassidy's *Indigo Blue* (both Puffin, 2005) — complete library cards for them, hear a radio programme about favourite books, and learn the action-verb vs state-verb distinction (state verbs normally avoid the continuous). Project: presenting books for teens. The unit closes with a two-page self-assessment (pp. 25–26).

**Unit 3 — Teen Matters (printed pp. 27–42).** Three lessons. *Lesson 1, "Food for thought!" (p. 28):* a magazine feature asks what favourite foods (burgers and chips, fizzy drinks, chocolate cake) contain and what harm the fat, salt, sugar and additives do, with healthier alternatives; learners label food labels and the Food Guide Pyramid, discuss festival meals across cultures, and learn countable/uncountable nouns and quantifiers (*many/much, a few/a little, a lot of, any*). *Lesson 2, "Your problem sorted!" (p. 33):* feelings vocabulary through a song about a schoolboy who feels nervous, worried and bored; an agony-aunt reply from "Teen Helpline" advises a shy teenager on making friends; grammar is the modals — *must/mustn't/don't have to* for obligation and its absence, *may/might* for possibility, *should/shouldn't* for advice. Writing: healthy-eating tips, song lyrics, a letter of advice. *Lesson 3, "We're on a shopping spree!" (p. 37):* comparative and superlative adjectives arrive through shopping: Jennifer asks her Indonesian e-friend for gift advice for her 9-year-old brother, and learners read short teen-magazine reviews of four computer games (a *Lord of the Rings* strategy game, *Mario Power Tennis*, *Matrix Online*, *Charlie and the Chocolate Factory*) with prices in pounds, then role-play buying a present. Projects: eating-habits survey and shopping around. Self-assessment pp. 41–42.

**Unit 4 — Looking Back on the Past (printed pp. 43–62).** Three lessons; the narrative-past unit. *Lesson 1, "On a mystery tour!" (p. 44):* a "Homework Helper" webpage profiles five unnamed figures of the past, identified only in the Quiz Key (p. 141) as Alfred Nobel, Jim Henson, Hans Christian Andersen, Mozart and Shakespeare; learners complete a born/died/nationality/profession table and learn the Past Simple, dates and years, and prepositions of time. *Lesson 2, "Tell me a story!" (p. 49):* a prize-winning student story about a burglary after a broken window supplies the model text; weather collocations support scene-setting; grammar contrasts the Past Continuous for background action in progress with the Past Simple for interrupting events; learners write story openings and tell a story about a day they did something wrong. *Lesson 3, "We survived the tsunami!" (p. 54):* a quiz introduces tsunamis, then an eyewitness account by two English children on holiday in Phuket describes the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004; learners read newspaper articles on natural disasters and accidents, consolidate Past Simple vs Past Continuous, and write a newspaper article plus disaster information cards. Project: natural disasters around the world. Self-assessment pp. 61–62.

**Unit 5 — Times Change! (printed pp. 63–82).** Three lessons. *Lesson 1, "Fancy ancient history?" (p. 64):* a Notting Hill class splits into two groups for a museum trip — one reads a guidebook text on Ancient Egypt (the Nile, farming, Rameses II, mummification and the British Museum), the other on the Roman Empire (roads, Latin and Greek, Hadrian and his wall in Britain, gladiators) — then the groups exchange information; grammar is relative clauses with *who/which/where*. *Lesson 2, "A nation in brief!" (p. 70):* a student article profiles the UK — geography, population, the arts, education and sport — and learners compare British and Greek life, hear an embassy official on British superstitions, and learn gerunds (verb + *-ing* as noun). *Lesson 3, "From generation to generation!" (p. 75):* an interview with an older woman in Nafplio contrasts schooling, TV and leisure in the past with today; grammar is *used to* for past habits and states (alongside the Past Simple), supported by a song, "My English is great", in which the singer recalls how he used to learn English; learners write about a partner's past habits and run a three-week "my learning routine" project. Self-assessment pp. 80–82.

**Unit 6 — Teens in Action (printed pp. 83–100).** Three lessons; the Present Perfect unit. *Lesson 1, "Let's go green!" (p. 84):* recycling and school environmental schemes — an e-mail launches an eco-website, a quiz gives environmental facts, and a poster promotes the "three Rs" (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle); learners survey classmates' environmental experience. *Lesson 2, "Many hands make light work!" (p. 89):* voluntary work — learners read a "Volunteers Wanted" advertisement from a zoo in Regent's Park, London, then read a teenager's application letter and CV for the post, learn work vocabulary, and write their own letter of application and CV. *Lesson 3, "Learn by doing!" (p. 93):* a Greek student's e-mail and quiz about Philopappos Hill and ancient Athens (the Pnyx, Demosthenes), a radio news report about a school trip, and an article extract about the Kazantzakis Museum; grammar contrasts the Present Perfect Simple with the Past Simple. Project: devising a treasure-hunt game for a museum or historic area. Self-assessment pp. 98–100.

**Unit 7 — Tomorrow and … Beyond! (printed pp. 101–116).** Three lessons on the future. *Lesson 1, "Travel Plans!" (p. 102):* Greek students from Syros prepare for a one-week summer English course at Royal Holloway in London; from an e-mail and weekly programme learners reconstruct the timetable (placement test, British Museum, theatre trip to *Evita*, Thorpe Park, Cambridge); grammar is the Present Continuous for fixed future arrangements. *Lesson 2, "Good intentions!" (p. 106):* bad habits, advice, and New-Year-style resolutions heard on a teen radio phone-in; grammar is *be going to* for plans and intentions, practised in a diary entry; project: planning the next school trip. *Lesson 3, "In the year 2525!" (p. 111):* learners categorise predictions about future life, read a student article imagining domed and floating cities, interactive video watches, thought-controlled machines and sound-proofing wallpaper, and learn the Future Simple (*will/won't*) for prediction; writing is a horoscope for a famous person, with star-sign vocabulary. Self-assessment pp. 115–116.

**Unit 8 — In the Papers! (printed pp. 117–134).** Three lessons; the passive unit. *Lesson 1, "And the winner is…!" (p. 118):* articles on famous awards — the Oscars (history, the Academy, categories, record-holders) and music awards (Top of the Pops Awards, the Brits, the MTV Europe Music Awards, the American Music Awards) — with fact-table completion; grammar is the Simple Present Passive. *Lesson 2, "Crack the code!" (p. 123):* communication and disability — an interview with a blind 12-year-old introduces Braille; learners work out the six-dot Braille cell, write their names and a secret message in Braille, and meet the Simple Past Passive; discussion covers difficulties faced by people with disabilities. *Lesson 3, "School Reporting!" (p. 127):* Petra and Hans send their school newspaper's spring issue; a how-to article explains roles, content and printing for a school newspaper, learners classify sample newspaper texts, plan their own paper in groups, and hear classmates discussing theirs. Project: the class/school newspaper. Self-assessment pp. 132–134.

**Unit 9 (Review) — Happy Summer Holidays! (printed pp. 135–140).** A single review unit reuniting the e-friends. A webpage advertises the International Teen Camp in Greece (unusual/extreme sports such as rafting, abseiling and canoeing, gentler activities, and eco-holiday options such as grape harvest and beach cleaning); learners sort the activities into word groups, then read the friends' pre-holiday e-mails — first-aid kit, Greek weather and clothing, currency, passports, games (Trivial Pursuit, Scrabble, backgammon/"tavli"), paintings and postcard collections — and answer who-will-do-what questions. Writing: a letter to a friend about travelling in Europe and a short story to accompany a favourite painting (the unit project).

**Appendices (printed pp. 141–216).** Quiz Key (p. 141: answers to the Unit 4 Mystery Person and tsunami quizzes and the Unit 6 quizzes); Speaking Appendix (pp. 142–155: paired Student A/B information-gap pages keyed to lessons); Maps (pp. 156–158: world map and map of the UK, largely pictorial); Grammar Appendix (pp. 159–175: full form/use tables following the course spine in order — *be* and *have got*, plural nouns, Present Simple and frequency adverbs, Present Continuous, action/state verbs, quantifiers, modals, comparatives, Past Simple and Past Continuous, relative clauses, gerunds, *used to*, Present Perfect, the three future forms, Present and Past Passive); Self-Assessment Key (pp. 176–177); "It's Up to You!" (pp. 178–208: optional extra tasks numbered to match the main-book tasks they extend); Sources of texts and photographs (pp. 209–212, in Greek); three blank pages (pp. 213–215); and a legal/distribution notice (p. 216) stating the book is printed by ITYE–Diophantos under Law 3966/2011.

**Grammar spine as it arrives (summary):** *be / have got* + Present Simple review (U1) → Present Simple vs Present Continuous, action vs state verbs (U2) → quantifiers, modals, comparatives/superlatives (U3) → Past Simple, Past Continuous and their contrast (U4) → relative clauses, gerunds, *used to* (U5) → Present Perfect Simple vs Past Simple (U6) → Present Continuous for arrangements, *be going to*, Future Simple (U7) → Present and Past Passive (U8) → whole-course review (U9).

### Honest negatives

- **No publication year is printed** on the cover, title page or imprint pages; only the "revised edition" stamp, the reissue note and in-file production dates (2015/2016) are present. Any catalogue year for this book comes from outside the book itself.
- **Listening content cannot be verified from the PDF alone:** many tasks depend on audio (camp presentation, songs, interviews, radio programmes). Where a listening text is not printed in the book (e.g. the Braille interview's factual answers on printed p. 124 are blank listening gaps), this draft describes the task, not the audio's content.
- **A few pages are image-only or blank in the text layer** (cover spread, the maps on printed pp. 156–158, PDF p. 5, and the blank pages at printed pp. 208 and 213–215 positions); their content is described from the rendered pages and contents listing, not from extracted text.
- The book contains **no separate alphabet/phonics or pronunciation section** in the Student's Book; pronunciation work, where it exists, is embedded in lesson tasks rather than presented as its own strand.
- Dated content is part of the book as printed: several readings are adapted from 2005 teen magazines, game prices are in pounds from that period, and the UK population figure (about 59 million, printed p. 71) reflects its source, not the present day.
## Grade 7 (Advanced) — Teacher's Book

### Identity block

- **Real title as printed:** *Think Teen!* — "1st Grade of Junior High School / TEACHER'S BOOK", with the stream word **Προχωρημένοι** (Advanced, nominative on the cover) / **Προχωρημένων** (genitive on the title and imprint pages). A΄ Γυμνασίου is the first year of Greek junior high school, i.e. Grade 7. This is the teacher's companion to the Advanced Student's Book *Think Teen!* (ISBN 978-960-06-2684-1, book code 0-21-0205); the record title "Agglika A' Gymnasiou (Grade 7) – Vivlio Ekpaideutikou" matches this book.
- **Stream verdict:** ADVANCED — confirmed. The word Προχωρημένοι/Προχωρημένων appears on the cover (PDF p. 1), the title page (PDF p. 2) and the imprint title page (PDF p. 4). This is **not** the Beginners (αρχαρίων) teacher's book.
- **Authors:** Ευαγγελία Καραγιάννη (Evangelia Karagianni), Βασιλική Κουή (Vasiliki Koui), Αικατερίνη Νικολάκη (Aikaterini Nikolaki) — the same team as the Student's Book. Writing contractor (ανάδοχος συγγραφής) named on the imprint page: Ελληνικά Γράμματα (Ellinika Grammata), under the Pedagogical Institute.
- **Publisher:** The book's own imprint (PDF p. 4) is the original one: Υπουργείο Εθνικής Παιδείας και Θρησκευμάτων (Ministry of National Education and Religious Affairs) / Παιδαγωγικό Ινστιτούτο (Pedagogical Institute), published by Οργανισμός Εκδόσεως Διδακτικών Βιβλίων (OEDB), Athens. The PDF itself wears the later reissue cover wrap (PDF pp. 1 and 201): Υπουργείο Παιδείας, Έρευνας και Θρησκευμάτων / Ινστιτούτο Εκπαιδευτικής Πολιτικής, with Ινστιτούτο Τεχνολογίας Υπολογιστών και Εκδόσεων «ΔΙΟΦΑΝΤΟΣ» (ITYE Diophantos) — the ebooks.edu.gr distribution.
- **ISBN:** 978-960-06-2686-5 (printed on the back cover). **Book code:** 0-21-0049 (cover barcode element: (01) 000000 0 21 0049 4). Note this is the Teacher's Book's own ISBN, two digits on from the Student's Book's 978-960-06-2684-1 — a different component of the same package, not a mismatch.
- **Edition / year:** **No calendar year is printed** on the cover, title page or imprint pages. The in-file production slugs are dated 26 November 2008 (main body) and 21 January 2009 (front matter/cover), and the credits page records the book as an EU-co-funded Pedagogical Institute project (Γ΄ ΚΠΣ / ΕΠΕΑΕΚ ΙΙ). The PDF file itself was created in 2012 and modified in 2017 (file metadata only). No year is asserted beyond what is printed/stamped.
- **Extent:** 201 PDF pages; printed pages i–xvi (Introduction) + 1–178, plus unnumbered front matter and the cover wrap.
- **Page offset:** In the numbered body, **printed page = PDF page − 21** (printed p. 1 = PDF p. 22; printed p. 132 = PDF p. 153; printed p. 178 = PDF p. 199). The Introduction is roman-numbered: printed pp. i–xvi = PDF pp. 6–21. PDF p. 1 is the cover wrap (front cover, spine and back cover on one spread); PDF pp. 2–4 are the title page, credits page and imprint title page; PDF p. 5 is blank; PDF p. 200 is the unnumbered legal/distribution page (its production slug reads "Page 180" — no printed p. 179 exists in the file, the last folio is 178); PDF p. 201 repeats the cover wrap.

### What the guide adds (own words; printed page references)

**Method introduction (printed pp. ii–xvi).** A full teaching manual, not a preface. It sets out the series' basis in the Common European Framework of Reference (2001) and the Greek Cross-curricular Unified Framework (2003), and its assumptions: learners arrive with four years of primary-school English, with provision for absolute beginners in the same class (p. ii). It describes the four components (Student's Book, Workbook, Teacher's Book, Audio CD) and states plainly what this book contains: step-by-step lesson plans, linguistic elements, background cultural information, Internet addresses, the keys to the Student's Book and Workbook tasks, the Audio CD tapescripts, extra activities and extra tests (p. iii). Long practical sections follow on teaching vocabulary (vocabulary notebooks, hangman, chain games, bingo, learner-made word-search grids, a join-the-dots listening game, pp. iv–vi), grammar (learners complete tables and work out rules from input texts, p. vi), reading as "text as a vehicle of information" in a pre-/while-/post-reading frame (p. vii), listening with semi-scripted texts containing false starts and hesitations (p. vii), speaking (fluency before accuracy; the teacher monitors and collects errors discreetly, pp. viii–ix), and process writing with multiple drafts, peer feedback and a correction code (p. ix). It also gives a bank of reusable games (Twenty Questions, Tennis, Noughts and Crosses, "Find someone who…" surveys, pp. ix–xi), guidance on cross-curricular discussion themes and large-scale projects (p. xi), the formative assessment scheme — unit self-assessment with can-do statements and learning-strategy tables, plus the three review tests in this book (pp. xi–xii) — the "My Portfolio" idea (p. xiii), a full section on differentiation for mixed-ability classes, including how the colour-coded "It's up to you!" tiered tasks work (green = less demanding, yellow = more demanding, pp. xiii–xiv), a note on the e-yliko educational CD for the advanced level (p. xiv), workbook-use and correction guidance (pp. xiv–xv), a Teacher's Book legend explaining its symbols and cross-reference marks (p. xv), and a reference list (Krashen, Vygotsky, Tomlinson, Nation, Maley, Johns & Davies; p. xvi).

**Per-unit teaching notes (printed pp. 1–130).** Every unit opens with a one-page overview grid: for each lesson it lists language functions, the Vocabulary Link and Grammar Link content, cross-curricular links and themes, a suggested lesson schedule in teaching periods, and an "Aids" list of materials to prepare (e.g. Unit 1, p. 1: students' photos, photos of English signs, Greek dictionaries). The notes proper are keyed task-by-task to Student's Book pages. Each section states its aims and objectives and its target vocabulary and structures, then gives a classroom procedure in bullets — what to elicit, what to play on the CD and how many times, when to allow Greek (L1), how to pair or group learners — with the answers printed inline at the point of use. Recurring extras are flagged in the margins: EXTRA! alternative and extension tasks, pointers to the matching Workbook tasks with page numbers, "Next Lesson" preparation notes, time-limit markers, and cross-references back to the Introduction's method sections. Schedules underline that this is a paced course: most lessons are budgeted at 3–5 teaching periods (Unit 2 Lesson 3 and Unit 3 Lesson 3, for example, get five; Unit 6 Lessons 1–2 and Unit 8 Lessons 1–2 get three).

Unit by unit, the notes cover: **Unit 1 — Welcome!** (pp. 1–7; a single opening lesson, 4 periods: multilingual greetings, camp-activity photographs, Pedro's camp presentation, classroom language, review of *be / have got* / Present Simple); **Unit 2 — Junior High School Life!** (pp. 8–25: student types and school routines; clubs and the Present Continuous; teen best-sellers, action vs state verbs; closes with guidance for the Student's Book self-assessment); **Unit 3 — TEEN Matters!** (pp. 26–42: food and quantifiers with *must/mustn't/don't have to*; feelings, a song, the Teen Helpline advice column, *may/might* and *should*; shopping and comparatives/superlatives); **Unit 4 — Looking back on the past!** (pp. 43–60: mystery personalities and the Past Simple with dates; story-writing with Past Continuous vs Past Simple; the 2004 tsunami and disaster reporting); **Unit 5 — Times change!** (pp. 61–81: the Ancient Egypt / Roman Empire jigsaw reading with relative clauses; a profile of the UK and gerunds; *used to* for past habits across generations); **Unit 6 — Teens in action!** (pp. 82–96: going green, volunteering with a letter of application and CV, and learning-by-doing — the Present Perfect built up in stages and then contrasted with the Past Simple); **Unit 7 — Tomorrow and … beyond!** (pp. 97–112: travel plans and the Present Continuous for arrangements; *be going to* for intentions; the Future Simple for predictions about the year 2525); **Unit 8 — In the papers!** (pp. 113–124: awards and the Present Passive; the Braille lesson and the Past Passive; producing a school newspaper); **Unit 9 (Review) — Happy summer holidays!** (pp. 125–130: extreme sports and eco-holidays, the friends' pre-holiday e-mails, an EU listening, letter writing with peer feedback, and the favourite-painting project — the printed p. 130 notes even supply the painting identifications the Student's Book task needs: Picasso's child with a dove, Degas' dance class, Van Gogh's bedroom, and Lytras' *Ta Kalanta*).

**Audioscripts — the audio layer the Student's Book lacks.** The Student's Book repeatedly sends learners to the CD without printing what is heard; this guide prints it. Boxed "Tapescript" texts appear throughout the lesson notes wherever a listening occurs — the six-language greetings and Pedro's camp talk in Unit 1 (pp. 2–3), the vocabulary-check recordings read off the theme posters in Unit 5 (p. 63), and, most fully, the two-part interview with Tom, the blind 12-year-old, in Unit 8 (pp. 118–119), whose Part B supplies every fact the Student's Book leaves as a listening gap: Louis Braille's birth on 4 January 1809, his blinding accident at age three, Charles Barbier's 1821 twelve-dot code, the first Braille book in 1829, reading speeds of 100–200 words a minute, and the asteroid 9969 Braille. Unit 9's EU dialogue is likewise printed in full (p. 128): Greece as the tenth country to join, in 1981; 27 member countries; 12 in the Eurozone, with the euro introduced in 2002. The three review tests have their own gathered Listening Test Tapescripts (pp. 152–153).

**Tests (printed pp. 131–149).** After an "Appendices / Tests" divider (p. 131) come three photocopiable review tests, each with Name/Class/Date header and per-task point totals, testing all four skills in the same task order (Reading, Vocabulary Link, Grammar Link, Listening as Task 8, Writing as Task 9, Speaking as Task 10): Units 1–3 (pp. 132–136), Units 4–6 (pp. 137–142), Units 7–9 (pp. 143–147). Their full Test Key follows (pp. 148–149), including the marking guidance for the open tasks — writing is awarded in 5-point blocks for content, organisation/spelling/punctuation, style and accuracy; speaking in 5-point blocks for fluency, accuracy and interaction. Two banded sample rating scales for test speaking and writing (bands 0–5 across accuracy/fluency/pronunciation and content/grammar/spelling-punctuation respectively, with instructions for scaling to totals out of 10, 15 or 20) are printed at pp. 150–151.

**Gathered answer keys (printed pp. 148–178).** Besides the inline answers in the lesson notes, the back of the book collects: the Test Key (pp. 148–149); the Listening Test Tapescripts (pp. 152–153); the Key to "It's up to you!" — the Student's Book's tiered optional tasks, keyed by unit, lesson and task number (pp. 154–157); and a complete Workbook Key for all nine units (pp. 158–178), which also flags, in grey boxes, the answers to the Workbook's own "It's up to you!" appendix tasks, and which sometimes answers by pointing back to the Student's Book Grammar Appendix instead of repeating the rule. Open tasks are handled honestly throughout the keys with "Accept all reasonable/possible answers" and sample answers where a model helps (e.g. the passive-voice sample sentences for school, hotel, zoo and restaurant in the "It's up to you!" key, p. 157).

20. Printed p. 178 (PDF p. 199): the book's last key page — Workbook Key Unit 9 Grammar Task 4 answers run "1. visit 2. is lying 3. at the moment 4. mustn't 5. bigger 6. was working 7. used to grow 8. have lost 9. I'll be 10. going to buy".

### Honest negatives

- **No publication year is printed** anywhere on the cover, title or imprint pages — only the 2008/2009 in-file production slugs and the PDF's 2012/2017 file dates. Any catalogue year for this book comes from outside the book itself.
- **There is no gathered Student's Book answer key at the back.** Student's Book answers exist only inline, inside the lesson notes; the gathered keys cover just the tests, the "It's up to you!" tasks and the Workbook. There is likewise no key in this book to the Student's Book's own end-of-unit self-assessment tests — that key is printed in the Student's Book's own appendix.
- **The guide does not reprint the Student's Book.** Apart from the tapescripts and the test papers, reading texts and task wording are not reproduced; the notes are unusable without the Student's Book open beside them at the cited page.
- **No grammar or vocabulary reference of its own:** for rules and tables the guide repeatedly sends the teacher to the Student's Book Grammar Appendix (the Workbook Key does this explicitly), and it contains no wordlist/glossary section.
- **The audio itself is not in the PDF.** The tapescripts fully substitute for the listening texts, but pronunciation models, songs as performed, and the Unit 9 cover-page activity built around a teacher-supplied CD of summer songs cannot be recovered from this file.
- **A stale cross-reference in the original:** the Test Key (printed pp. 148–149) sends teachers to "page 165"/"page 166" for the sample rating scales, but in this book those scales are actually printed on pp. 150–151.
- **Pagination quirk at the end:** the last printed folio is 178 (Workbook Key); the closing legal page carries the production slug "Page 180" and no folio — printed p. 179 does not exist in the file.
- **Dated content is part of the book as printed:** the EU tapescript's figures (27 members, 12 Eurozone countries, euro introduced in 2002, printed p. 128) and the test texts' early-mobile-phone world reflect the book's late-2000s production, not the present day.
- This guide covers the **Advanced stream only** and Unit 1 only as the single opening lesson the Student's Book itself has; it contains nothing for the Beginners stream.
## Grade 7 (Advanced) — Workbook

### Identity block

- **Real title as printed:** *Think Teen!* — "1st Grade of Junior High School / WORKBOOK", with the stream word **Προχωρημένοι** (Advanced) printed in red on the title page, in a yellow banner on the front cover, and on both imprint pages. Α΄ Γυμνασίου is the first year of Greek junior high school, i.e. Grade 7. The catalogue record name "Agglika A' Gymnasiou (Grade 7) – Tetradio Ergasion" is the Greek descriptive name for this workbook (Τετράδιο Εργασιών = Workbook); the book itself carries the English *Think Teen!* title.
- **Stream / type verdict:** ADVANCED WORKBOOK — confirmed, and distinct from the Student's Book. The cover, spine and title page all say WORKBOOK; the book code and ISBN differ from the Student's Book (code 0-21-0205 / ISBN 978-960-06-2684-1 there).
- **Authors:** Ευαγγελία Καραγιάννη (Evangelia Karagianni), Βασιλική Κουή (Vasiliki Koui), Αικατερίνη Νικολάκη (Aikaterini Nikolaki) — the same team as the Student's Book. Writing contractor named on the imprint page: Ελληνικά Γράμματα (Ellinika Grammata), under the auspices of the Pedagogical Institute.
- **Publisher:** Ινστιτούτο Τεχνολογίας Υπολογιστών και Εκδόσεων «ΔΙΟΦΑΝΤΟΣ» (Institute of Computer Technology and Publications "Diophantos" — ITYE Diophantos), for the Υπουργείο Παιδείας, Θρησκευμάτων και Αθλητισμού (Ministry of Education, Religions and Sports) / Ινστιτούτο Εκπαιδευτικής Πολιτικής (Institute of Educational Policy). Distributed via ebooks.edu.gr.
- **ISBN:** 978-960-06-2685-8 (printed on the back cover). **Book code:** 0-21-0048 (cover barcode element: (01) 000000 0 21 0048 7).
- **Edition / year:** No calendar year is printed on the cover, title page or imprint pages. The imprint page states the reissue was produced by ITYE Diophantos from a digital mockup funded under ESPA / "ΣΤΗΡΙΖΩ", with corrections approved by the Institute of Educational Policy. In-file production stamps are dated variously 2015, 2019, 2023 and 2024 across sections (e.g. 24/2/2015 on the original-edition imprint page, 13/10/2023 on the reissue title page). No year is asserted beyond what is printed/stamped.

### How the workbook maps onto the Student's Book

The workbook follows the Student's Book unit-for-unit and lesson-for-lesson: the same nine units, the same lesson titles, the same vocabulary sets and the same grammar spine in the same order. What it adds is a second, written pass over every lesson, built in a fixed four-part pattern:

1. **Reading — usually a NEW text, not the Student's Book text.** Most lessons open with a fresh reading on the lesson's theme (details below). A minority of workbook readings re-use the Student's Book material in a new task shape.
2. **Vocabulary Link** — word searches, crosswords, picture labelling, collocation matching and odd-one-out work on the lesson's vocabulary.
3. **Grammar Link** — the lesson's grammar presented as tables and rules for the learner to *complete* (fill in the missing forms/endings), followed by controlled drills. This completion-table format is the workbook's signature: the Student's Book presents the grammar, the workbook makes the learner reconstruct it.
4. **Writing** — one short, tightly guided writing task per lesson, usually with bullet steps, a model opening and ruled lines.

Two further structural features:

- **Difficulty stars.** Tasks are marked with one, two or three stars (easy → harder); the three-star tasks are almost always the Writing tasks.
- **"It's up to you!" appendix (printed pp. 130–166).** Nearly every main task carries a cross-reference of the form "Task N – p. 1xx". Those numbered appendix tasks (1–67) re-present the *same* texts and items in a scaffolded, easier form — first-letter cues instead of open gaps, choose-the-correct-form instead of production, matching instead of recall. It is a differentiated re-do of the workbook itself, not new content.
- **No self-assessment and no listening strand.** Unlike the Student's Book, the workbook has no per-unit self-assessment pages and no audio tasks of its own; consolidation is instead gathered into the Unit 9 review and the appendix.

### Unit-by-unit summary (own words; printed page references)

**Unit 1 — Welcome! (printed pp. 1–8).** One lesson shadowing the Student's Book opener. Reading is a set of short self-profiles from children who met at the TEEN camp (Tom from Santos, Nadia from Moscow, Jason, Miranda from Bulgaria, and candidate keypals Sarah from Edinburgh, Luigi from Milan, Amanda from Cyprus, Yiannis from Karditsa, Mandy), used for a likes/hobbies matching task and a keypal-pairing task — a workbook-only cast and text, parallel to but different from the Student's Book camp material. Vocabulary: classroom instructions matched to pictures, public signs matched to places, leisure-activity collocations. Grammar Link: completion tables for *be* and *have got* in all forms, true sentences about the learner's family, and question-writing from given answers. Writing: a two-paragraph e-mail presenting yourself to a new keypal, with the content specified paragraph by paragraph.

**Unit 2 — Junior High School Life (printed pp. 9–26).** Three lessons. *Lesson 1, "Fancy school?" (p. 10):* the workbook-only reading is a two-text article on unusual schools — the Santa Claus School in Midland, Michigan (open only six days a year) and Australia's Alice Springs School of the Air (radio/e-mail lessons for Outback children) — sorted statement by statement. Then a 10-subject word search, the learner's own timetable, school collocations, and Present Simple completion tables with third-person *-s/-es/-ies* sorting drills; writing is a paragraph about your student type, explicitly referring back to the Student's Book quiz on its p. 8. *Lesson 2, "Join our club!" (p. 16):* four short club presentations (Mark/Movies, Helena/Photography, Mike/Health, Dorothy/Eco) matched to club names; club vocabulary definitions; idioms with *time*; Present Continuous tables and *-ing* spelling rules; writing is an e-mail to "Christine" describing six family photos in the Present Continuous. *Lesson 3, "TEEN best-sellers!" (p. 22):* reading is Sophie's letter about the film *A Cinderella Story* (Hilary Duff as Sam Montgomery) — where the Student's Book read book blurbs, the workbook works on a film letter; then book/film collocations, word order, action vs state verbs, Present Simple vs Continuous contrast drills, question formation, and writing the blurb of your own favourite book or film.

**Unit 3 — Teen Matters (printed pp. 27–42).** Three lessons. *Lesson 1, "Food for thought!" (p. 28):* workbook-only reading — a 10-item "Healthy Snacking Quiz" with three score bands, followed by a paragraph about a boy called Bob whose answers learners score against the quiz. Food picture vocabulary, food collocations and opposites, adjective formation, a quantifier grid (learners tick which of *a lot of / some / much / many / a few / a little* goes with each food noun), and *must/mustn't/don't have to* applied to diet rules. Writing: a paragraph on your own snacking habits compared with Bob's. *Lesson 2, "Your problem sorted!" (p. 33):* three new Agony Aunt letters (Simona, 12, wants to model against her mother's wishes; Jean Paul, 14, football vs his parents' tennis; Jason, 10, whose little brother takes all his things), each followed by a multiple-choice "what should they do"; feelings adjectives, *must/may/might* for guessing and *should/shouldn't* for advice matched to seven everyday problems; writing is a letter of advice replying to one of the three letters. *Lesson 3, "We're on a shopping spree!" (p. 38):* the comparison lesson is practised not on the Student's Book games but on vocabulary of reviews/fans, adjective opposites, comparative/superlative spelling tables, and — workbook-only reading — three house advertisements written in estate-agent abbreviations (€300,000 detached house, €150,000 flat, €250,000 cottage) that learners decode and compare. Writing: choosing a car for a named family from a three-car data table and justifying the choice with comparatives.

**Unit 4 — Looking Back on the Past (printed pp. 43–60).** Three lessons. *Lesson 1, "On a mystery tour!" (p. 44):* instead of the Student's Book's mystery-person profiles, the workbook reading is a full history text on the Vikings (raids 800–1100, Jorvik captured in 866, Odin) adapted from a British Museum activity book, with note completion; a spidergram vocabulary task then links the Student's Book's five mystery figures by field (Henson/puppets, Mozart/music, Shakespeare/plays and poetry). Grammar: Past Simple of *be*, then regular and irregular Past Simple, each as completion tables plus spelling-sort and dialogue drills. Writing: your biography for the class year book, built from a dates-and-events list. *Lesson 2, "Tell me a story!" (p. 51):* reading is three short jokes whose punchlines are removed and supplied separately in the appendix version; burglary/weather collocations; Past Continuous tables and "what was happening when the teacher came in" picture drills. Writing: notes on what was happening at home at a set time, written up the next day in the Past Continuous. *Lesson 3, "We survived the tsunami!" (p. 56):* the tsunami narrative of the Student's Book is replaced by "World News in brief!" — three dated 2002–2006 news reports (wildfires in Texas/New Mexico/Oklahoma, the Polish roof collapse in snow that killed 66, and the 2002 oil-tanker sinking off Spain) completed into a disaster table; disaster word search and collocations; Past Simple vs Past Continuous joining drills and a long mouse-in-the-house gap-fill story. Writing: a short-story-competition entry about a past event, with a tense-warning checklist.

**Unit 5 — Times Change! (printed pp. 61–76).** Three lessons. *Lesson 1, "Fancy ancient history?" (p. 62):* where the Student's Book split Egypt/Rome texts between groups, the workbook gives a third ancient civilisation — a five-paragraph article on the Indus Valley (Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro, c. 3000–1500 BC, private bathrooms, undeciphered script) with heading matching and note completion. History picture vocabulary and collocations recycled from the Student's Book texts (Rameses II, gladiators); relative clauses *who/which/where* drilled and then used in a paragraph about "my school". Writing is a workbook-only functional task: turning an Attica Zoological Park brochure (€11 adults, €9 children, free under-3s and disabled) into a recorded telephone message. *Lesson 2, "A nation in brief!" (p. 67):* reading is a webpage of superstitions around the world (Japan's unlucky number four, China's lucky red, Thailand's reversible 6/9, Brazil's New-Year lentils, Turkey, Korea) — broader than the Student's Book's British-superstitions listening; UK map labelling, word groups sorted from the Student's Book UK article, numbers written in words, and gerund drills. Writing: an article on Greek superstitions for the school newspaper, researched from family. *Lesson 3, "From generation to generation!" (p. 72):* reading is a full page of a British TV guide (BBC1/BBC2/ITV, Friday 22 January) used to programme-plan for a four-person family with stated tastes across two TV sets; TV-programme vocabulary, including matching Greek programme titles to types; *used to* vs Past Simple for past habits; Internet prepositions. Writing: interview a parent/grandparent on how they learned English and write it up.

**Unit 6 — Volunteers Wanted! (printed pp. 77–92).** The workbook renames this unit: the Student's Book calls it "Teens in Action", the workbook contents and opener head it "Volunteers wanted!". *Lesson 1, "Let's go green!" (p. 78):* reading is an eco-leaflet, "Tips for a Waste-Less School Year" (recycled materials, reusing notebooks, non-toxic products, reusable lunch containers, carpooling), with find-the-items tasks; recycling crossword and choose-the-correct-word environment collocations; Present Perfect Simple built up through a verb table (past simple vs past participle), completion tables and can-collecting sentences. Writing/speaking: mini-dialogues exchanging personal news in the Present Perfect. *Lesson 2, "Many hands make light work!" (p. 83):* reading is a "Student Action Guide" webpage about starting animal/environment clubs, its six links matched to page contents — replacing the Student's Book zoo-advertisement/CV reading, though CV work remains as vocabulary (learners head up a sample CV for a music-club applicant). Present Perfect (2): *just/yet/already/for* in a job-seeker paragraph and chore-list sentences. Writing: a weekend to-do list revisited on Sunday and reported by e-mail in the Present Perfect. *Lesson 3, "Learn by doing!" (p. 88):* reading is verse — a gap-fill poem "Why be a volunteer" and three attributed quotations about volunteering (Anonymous; Winston Churchill; Henry David Thoreau) — instead of the Student's Book Philopappos/Kazantzakis material, whose vocabulary (monument, orator, assembly, compass, inscription) is still drilled. Present Perfect vs Past Simple contrast rules and drills. Writing: an acrostic poem on VOLUNTEER, modelled on a printed example.

**Unit 7 — Tomorrow and … Beyond! (printed pp. 93–108).** Three lessons. *Lesson 1, "Travel plans" (p. 94):* reading is three holiday advertisements (singles' beach holidays, family holidays with childcare, Alpine skiing) matched to two brochure paragraphs, with unanswerable-from-the-text questions to identify; airport/station and summer-course/sightseeing vocabulary sorted into columns; Present Continuous for future arrangements, distinguished from its other uses. Writing: an e-mail inviting a friend's family on a "TEENS Holidays" Greek-island holiday, from note prompts. *Lesson 2, "Good intentions!" (p. 99):* reading is a webpage listing ten New Year's Resolutions for Teens (positive self-image, saying "No", healthy changes, honesty with parents, gratitude) matched to explanatory expansions; behaviour collocations (*bite my nails, fasten your seatbelt, wear a helmet…*); *be going to* contrasted with the Present Continuous (intentions vs fixed plans), including an error-correction set. No separate writing task beyond sentence work in this lesson. *Lesson 3, "In the year 2525!" (p. 103):* reading is a full twelve-sign "Weekly Teenscope" horoscope page mined for *will* predictions; star-sign/date matching; future-life collocations recycled from the Student's Book article (*interactive video watch, floating* cities); Future Simple completion tables and prediction questions about the learner's own future. Writing: a funny horoscope for a friend, entered in a magazine competition.

**Unit 8 — In the Papers! (printed pp. 109–124).** Three lessons. *Lesson 1, "And the winner is…!" (p. 110):* reading is an article on three awards different from the Student's Book's Oscars focus — the Caledonian Junior Award (for young people with learning disabilities), the Hans Christian Andersen Award ("the Little Nobel Prize", gold medal presented by the Queen of Denmark) and the Nobel Prizes (five started under Nobel's 1895 will, first awarded 1901, Economics added 1968, ceremonies on 10 December) — matched paragraph to award. Awards collocations, then an Oscars gap-fill recycled from the Student's Book. Grammar: Present Simple Passive, introduced by active/passive judgement tasks, then active-to-passive conversion. Writing: passive-voice quiz cards made from facts in learners' Greek schoolbooks. *Lesson 2, "Crack the code!" (p. 115):* the Student's Book's Braille lesson is re-angled: reading is a magazine article on emoticons (built from "emotions" + "icons", made of keyboard letters/numbers/punctuation) with a 13-item emoticon-matching task whose answers are printed on the page; Braille survives in the vocabulary/collocation work (*invent a code, thanks to Braille, blind in her right eye*) and as the model example for the Past Simple Passive. Grammar: sorting Present vs Past Passive, conversions, and an MP3-player gap-fill text. Writing: a survey and opinion paragraph on text-message abbreviations (examples given: *b4, w8, g2g, idk*). *Lesson 3, "School reporting!" (p. 119):* reading is "High School News in brief" — four short school-news items (national dancing competition, football tournament, inventions exhibition, a new break-time meeting place) matched to headlines; newspaper-jobs word search; a long collocation review built around Petra and Hans's school-newspaper e-mail exchange with Magda; then an explicit whole-course grammar review (tense identification, keyword-to-tense sorting, mixed multiple choice, personal questions). This lesson is the workbook's grammar round-up.

**Unit 9 (Review) — Happy Summer Holidays! (printed pp. 125–129).** A short review unit with no new grammar. Its reading task recycles seven extracts from the workbook's *own* texts (Vikings, superstitions, School of the Air, waste-less tips, Polish snow news, family-holiday brochure, Indus) to be matched back to their headings, followed by learners naming their favourite and least favourite workbook text. Then word-group recall grids (subjects, food, weather, disasters, TV, environment, sports, holidays), mixed vocabulary choice items, a ten-item grammar choose-the-form review, and a closing writing-genre audit: learners list which unit/lesson taught each of the year's ten writing genres (letter of advice, story, superstitions article, holiday e-mail, photo e-mail, snacking-habits description, opinion piece, quiz cards, blurb, biography) and collect useful phrases for each.

**Appendix — "It's up to you!" (printed pp. 130–166).** Divider at printed p. 130; tasks 1–67 on pp. 131–166, grouped by unit. As described above, these are scaffolded re-workings of the main tasks: the same keypal profiles, Santa/School-of-the-Air article, club texts, Agony Aunt letters, Vikings text, news reports, Indus article, TV guide, eco-leaflet, Student Action Guide, horoscope, awards article, emoticons text and school news all reappear with lighter task types (first-letter cues, binary choice, matching). It adds no new reading texts. Followed by Sources of texts and photographs (printed pp. 167 and 169; printed p. 168 is blank) and the legal/distribution notice under Law 3966/2011 (printed p. 170).

**Grammar spine as practised (summary):** *be / have got* completion tables (U1) → Present Simple, Present Continuous, action/state verbs (U2) → quantifiers, modals, comparatives (U3) → Past Simple, Past Continuous and their contrast (U4) → relative clauses, gerunds, *used to* (U5) → Present Perfect Simple, then vs Past Simple (U6) → Present Continuous for arrangements, *be going to*, Future Simple (U7) → Present and Past Passive, plus whole-course review (U8) → mixed review (U9). Identical in order and content to the Student's Book spine; the workbook's contribution is the completion-table presentation and the drill volume, not new grammar.
