### Unit-by-unit summary (own words; printed page references)

**Unit 1 — Unity in Diversity (printed pp. 9–26).** *Lesson 1, "People and Places" (p. 10):* children from different climates (Nuru, Tikki and others) introduce appearance and place; a school-newspaper interview with anthropologist Ms Susan Franz explains human characteristics — skin colour and melanin, facial features, body build — as long adaptation to terrain, sun, cold and altitude. Grammar is a contrast, not a first presentation: Simple Present (habits, general truths, timetables) against Present Continuous (now, changing situations, future arrangements), plus adverbs of frequency. Listening follows Imani, a child near Lake Malawi, through her daily routine; writing is a description of a person, modelled by Eva's letter about her new Ukrainian friend Olga. *Lesson 2, "Joined in our Differences" (p. 15):* culture as a shared spider-diagram (food, history, customs, celebrations); Yoko (Japan) and Pierre (France) present greetings, body language, food and arts in their countries, a listening student presents Spain, and stative verbs arrive — states not normally used in continuous forms, with meaning changes when some are (*have / be having, think / be thinking, taste / be tasting*). Projects: "Cultures on my street" interview and a class song for unity in diversity. *Lesson 3, "Different Places – Different Buildings" (p. 19):* landmarks (Taj Mahal, Colosseum, Erectheion, Sydney Opera House and others) lead into full readings on Agia Sophia in Istanbul, the Leaning Tower of Pisa and the Sydney Opera House; comparatives and superlatives, irregular forms, and *(not) as … as* are presented from those texts, then used to compare two stadiums. Projects: a famous landmark, a building-story competition, and a Multicultural Fair on houses, food and clothes. Self-assessment pp. 25–26.

**Unit 2 — Echoes of the Past (printed pp. 27–46).** *Lesson 4, "Mysteries of Our World" (p. 28):* Atlantis — a BBC radio programme fills in notes (Plato, Solon, Egypt), then an interview with Greek archaeologist Alexandros Demetriou weighs the Atlantic, Mediterranean and Thera/Akrotiri theories and concedes there is no proof; Simple Past is contrasted with Present Perfect (finished time vs past-with-present link / unfinished time). Writing is an archaeologist's discovery e-mail and interview; projects are a natural-disaster study and an "Unsolved Mysteries" presentation (Stonehenge, Easter Island, the Pyramids and others). *Lesson 5, "Across the Ages" (p. 33):* Pompeii — a geologist interview, then a four-part reading on daily life, the AD 79 Vesuvius eruption, and the plaster-cast excavations begun in 1748; Past Continuous arrives (action in progress, interrupted action, parallel past actions) alongside *used to* for past habits. A mediation task relays a Greek article about the lakeside settlement of Dispilio to a Swedish penfriend. *Lesson 6, "Life on the Water" (p. 39):* ancient Egypt — a jumbled-paragraph article on the Nile floods, "black land" (Kemet), mummification, hieroglyphics and pyramid building; Past Perfect arrives as the tense for the earlier of two past actions, practised in short accounts of Egyptian farming and Theran wall painting. A guided Nile tour listening and a first-person story of a boy in Malia, Crete, hit by the Thera eruption model story writing. Self-assessment pp. 45–46.

**Unit 3 — Time Out (printed pp. 47–64).** *Lesson 7, "Get on Board!" (p. 48):* adventure holidays — a "World Tour" advertisement (in print since 2000, offering Great Wall walks, safaris, rafting, ghost towns and more) supports work on gerunds and on verbs of preference: verbs followed by *-ing* for general preference against *would like / would prefer / fancy / would rather* patterns for specific choices. Project: a leaflet about the learners' own town for exchange students, modelled on Skiathos. *Lesson 8, "What an Experience!" (p. 52):* a Thorpe Park theme-park leaflet and a friends' planning dialogue; the future system is sorted — *be going to* for plans and evidence-based predictions, Simple Future (*will*) for instant decisions, offers, warnings and opinion-based predictions, Simple Present for timetabled future events and in time clauses, and Present Continuous for arrangements. Writing is an informal personal letter; a mediation task explains a Greek municipal summer-camp leaflet. *Lesson 9, "…Let the Games Begin!" (p. 57):* sport through an interview with curling champion Raphael Duke — a granite-stone ice sport, described in the interview as demanding strategy, with teams, brooms and no referees — plus listening on ancient Greek Olympic athletes and a sports quiz. Grammar is *so / such … that* for result, *too / enough*, and question tags for checking and confirmation. Self-assessment pp. 63–64.

**Unit 4 — Let's Change Our Schools (printed pp. 65–82).** The opener mediates a Greek extract from Nikos Kazantzakis on his late-19th-century schooling. *Lesson 10, "Looking at Other Schools" (p. 66):* an adapted extract from Joan Benoit's school journal contrasts a crowded, rule-bound junior high with a choice-rich high school; a video-conference listening presents the Strömberg school in Finland (first names for teachers, learning by doing, student responsibilities). Modals of obligation arrive as a set: *must / have to* (past *had to*), *mustn't* (prohibition) against *don't have to* (no necessity), and *should / ought to / had better* for advice. Writing: school rules and a journal entry. *Lesson 11, "Change through Time" (p. 70):* technology enters school — a 2006 *New York Times* extract on laptops replacing pencils and lunchboxes, interviews on technology in education, and an interactive-whiteboard advertisement debated by a student committee; modals *could / may / might* for possibility, *can / could / may* for permission, and *can / could* for requests. Writing is a formal report suggesting after-school clubs / equipment. *Lesson 12, "Change: An Ongoing Process" (p. 76):* the history of writing and printing — Mesopotamian marks, cuneiform, hieroglyphics, Linear A and B, Byblos, and Gutenberg's movable metal type and converted wine press — with a side lesson on texting acronyms and emoticons; relative clauses arrive in full (*who / which / that*, omission when object, *whose, when, where*). The project is a structured debate, "Teachers cannot be replaced by computers". Self-assessment pp. 81–82.

**Unit 5 — The Arts! (printed pp. 83–100).** The passive-voice unit, opened by famous quotations about art (Van Gogh, Miró, Plato, Picasso, Wilde, Degas, Hugo and others). *Lesson 13, "Quite an Art!" (p. 84):* spring as a shared theme across painting, poem and music (Millet, Vivaldi, Stravinsky); learners assemble a puzzle of Picasso's *Guernica*, hear a museum guide on the 26 April bombing of Guernica, and read a leaflet interpreting the mural's figures as a statement on war's suffering. Present Simple Passive arrives here (form, process description, rules), applied to art-centre regulations; a gallery listening teaches painting styles (Cubism, Realism, Impressionism, Pop Art, Surrealism) and Greek painters are matched to titles. *Lesson 14, "It's Music to My Ears" (p. 90):* music types, and a radio programme on the Voyager golden disc as a way to communicate with aliens — the frame for Past Simple Passive and the *by*-agent, with Present Perfect and Future passive forms also tabled. A classical-music listening matches Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Tchaikovsky and Debussy to works and periods. *Lesson 15, "Acting Up!…" (p. 94):* drama from ancient Greek theatre (Dionysus, chorus, masks, men playing women) through Shakespeare — a *Romeo and Juliet* plot summary is read and its ending heard — to a biography of the poet Odysseas Elytis; grammar work is converting active sentences into passive ones, and writing is a biography. Project: staging scenes from Homer's *Iliad* for visiting South African students. Self-assessment pp. 99–100.

**Unit 6 — Healthy Living (printed pp. 101–120).** *Lesson 16, "You are What You Eat" (p. 102):* a Greek INKA survey of what school canteens actually sell against what they are allowed to sell, a BBC listening on school lunches in other countries, and a reading on Jamie Oliver's 2005 "Feed Me Better" campaign (working with dinner ladies at Kidsgrove, initial resistance, a large Downing Street petition, government action). Conditionals Type 0 (general truths) and Type 1 (possible future) arrive here from the health claims in the lesson; learners sort food "myths" from "facts", run a health-and-fitness questionnaire with charts, and write a reply e-mail of advice to a friend who eats junk food. *Lesson 17, "The 'Greenest' Way to School" (p. 109):* transport surveys and a Bike-to-School Week leaflet arguing fitness, independence, safety and environmental benefits; Conditional Type 2 arrives (imaginary present/future, *If I were you…* for advice), and a mediation e-mail answers German students' questions using a Greek newspaper survey on cycling in Karditsa. *Lesson 18, "Going 'Green'" (p. 113):* an Eco-Schools energy-saving project by students in Komotini, worked through identify–research–act–inform steps, supplies *unless* (= *if … not*), clauses of purpose (*to / in order to*) and clauses of result (*as a result, therefore*); writing is a 5–7–5 haiku celebrating nature. Project: making the learners' own school healthier, fitter and greener. Self-assessment pp. 119–120.

**Unit 7 — Embracing Our World (printed pp. 121–138).** The reported-speech unit, on friendship. *Lesson 19, "Against the Odds" (p. 122):* qualities of a friend (a jumbled poem to reassemble), then a news story from Orlando, Florida (18 August 2001): Amanda Valance tows her friend Edna Wilks to shore on a surf board after an alligator attack. Reported statements arrive from the story's quotations — backshift of Simple Present, Present Continuous, Simple Past, *can* and *must*, pronoun/time changes, *say / tell* — and reporting orders and requests. *Lesson 20, "Seeing Through a Friend's Eyes" (p. 127):* a blind boy's friendship with Abram, an ice-cream seller, in a story heard and read in extracts — perception through sound and touch — extends reported speech to Present Perfect, *will* and *may*, lists further introductory verbs (*add, warn, advise, explain* and others) and the standard word changes (*this–that, now–then, tomorrow–the next day* and so on); John Godfrey Saxe's poem of the blind men and the elephant, each partly right, closes the lesson. *Lesson 21, "Friends Without Frontiers" (p. 131):* penfriend e-mails from classes in Singapore and in Fortaleza, Brazil, and an interview about the eTwinning school-partnership programme; reported Yes/No and Wh- questions arrive (asked *if / whether*, question word retained, statement word order, no *do*). Writing is a partnership e-mail; internet-safety advice is given in the project. Self-assessment pp. 137–138.

**Unit 8 — Welcome to the World (printed pp. 139–150).** A revision unit with **no new Language Focus section** — the Contents list all three lessons as "Revision of tenses and forms". The opener retells Marco Polo's journey from Venice to Kublai Khan's China and its effect on Columbus. *Lesson 22, "Breaking the Boundaries" (p. 140):* Stefanos's letter traces an eTwinning prize trip — Thessaloniki, Madrid, France and Paris, the Chunnel to London, on to Germany and Helsinki — followed by recorded travel impressions and a negotiation speaking task planning a free afternoon in Hastings from real attraction leaflets. *Lesson 23, "It's a Small World After All" (p. 144):* the travelling class's postcards home from Russia, China (the Great Wall), Japan and Australia, organised by what they saw, heard, tasted and felt; learners send a virtual postcard. *Lesson 24, "A World Without End" (p. 147):* a guess-the-country quiz (the clues point to Brazil, Egypt and Greece), a final e-mail concluding that people everywhere share the same needs, fears and hopes — explicitly linked back to Unit 1's "Unity in Diversity" — and C. P. Cavafy's "Ithaca" in the Keeley and Sherrard translation, discussed as a poem in which the journey matters more than the destination. The book's only self-assessment here is the speaking/learning reflection on printed p. 150.

**Appendices (printed pp. 151–184).** "It's Up to You!" (pp. 151–159: optional extra and extension tasks keyed by unit, lesson and main-book page, including extra readings — e.g. Spartan boys and girls, a showjumping news item, alternative-fuel vehicles, a walking school bus); Supplementary Material (pp. 160–162: debate tips and judging, diagram types — star, chain, spider, fact/opinion, pie chart, vocabulary map, 5 Ws — peer feedback, and the cut-out Picasso puzzle pieces and timeline/diagram sheets the lessons refer to); Key to Self-Assessment (pp. 163–166); Grammar Reference (pp. 167–176: form/use/time-expression tables in course order — present tenses, comparatives, Present Perfect, past tenses and *used to*, preference verbs and the future forms, *so/such/too/enough* and question tags, modals, relative clauses, passive voice, conditionals with *unless* and result/purpose clauses, and reported speech); Word Lists (pp. 177–178: unit-by-unit vocabulary, plus a British and American English spelling/word list); Irregular Verbs (p. 179); Maps (pp. 180–182: the Americas, a world/Europe–Asia map, and Greece); Sources of photographs (p. 183, in Greek); and a legal/distribution notice (p. 184) stating the book is printed by ITYE–Diophantos under Law 3966/2011 and distributed free to public schools.

**Grammar spine as it arrives (summary):** Simple Present vs Present Continuous + frequency adverbs, stative verbs, comparatives/superlatives and *(not) as…as* (U1) → Simple Past vs Present Perfect, Past Continuous, *used to*, Past Perfect (U2) → gerunds and preference verbs, the future forms (*going to / will* / timetabled Present Simple / arrangements), *so/such*, *too/enough*, question tags (U3) → modals of obligation, advice, possibility, permission and request, relative clauses (U4) → **Passive voice: Present (p. 87) → Past and *by*-agent (p. 91) → turning active into passive (p. 96)** (U5) → **Conditionals Type 0 and Type 1 (p. 106) → Type 2 (p. 111) → *unless*, purpose and result clauses (p. 116)** (U6) → **Reported speech: statements, orders and requests (pp. 125–126) → further backshifts and introductory verbs (p. 129) → reported questions (pp. 132–133)** (U7) → whole-course tense revision in use, with no new presentation (U8).

### Honest negatives

- **No publication year is printed** on the cover, title pages or imprint pages; only the reissue note and in-file production dates (2013–2015 on most signatures, 2020 on the last maps page, 2023 on the cover signature) are present. Any catalogue year for this book comes from outside the book itself.
- **The ISBN is a Set ISBN only.** Both cover appearances read "ISBN Set 978-960-06-2739-8"; no ISBN belonging to the Student's Book alone was found in the file.
- **Listening content cannot be verified from the PDF alone:** many core texts exist only as audio (the Atlantis programme, the Pompeii geologist, the Finnish video conference, the Voyager programme, the Shakespeare facts, the blind boy's story, the eTwinning interview). Where the script is not printed, this draft describes the task and its printed frame, not the audio's content.
- **The maps (printed pp. 180–182) are image pages whose text layer is garbled** (letter-spaced/reversed glyphs); they are described from the contents listing and rendered pages, not from extracted text. The cover title is likewise image-set and was read from the render.
- **Unit 8 contains no new grammar presentation** despite being a full three-lesson unit: the Contents list each of its lessons only as revision of tenses and forms, and no Language Focus box appears on printed pp. 140–149.
- The book contains **no separate alphabet/phonics or pronunciation section**; pronunciation, where it appears, is embedded in lesson tasks.
- Dated content is part of the book as printed: readings are adapted from sources of 2002–2008 (a 2002 holiday brochure, a September 2005 Greek cycling survey, an August 2006 *New York Times* school-technology article, International Friendship Day 2007, a spring 2008 art show), and several "current" facts — Thorpe Park arrangements, websites named for postcards and country research, and the Great Wall figures quoted in the postcard — reflect those sources, not the present day.

### What the guide adds (own words; printed page references)

**Method introduction (printed pp. 5–16).** A twelve-page teaching manual. It places this course at **Threshold B1** level and grounds its design in the Greek Cross-thematic Curriculum Framework (ΔΕΠΠΣ) and English Curriculum (ΑΠΣ) for junior high school and in the Common European Framework of Reference, around three principles — literacy, plurilingual/multilingual competence and pluricultural/multicultural competence (p. 5). Its stated aims are communicative competence, cultural awareness, lifelong learning strategies (memory, cognitive, compensation, metacognitive, affective and social), and integrating English with other school subjects, delivered as a topic-based course in which every unit has three lessons built on one theme (pp. 5–6). Skill-by-skill sections follow: reading in pre-/while-/post- stages with graphic organisers (pp. 7–8), listening in the same three stages — with the explicit statement that **all the listening texts are transcribed and the transcripts are in this Teacher's Book** (p. 8) — speaking as "speaking to learn" versus "learning to speak", with group-management guidance (pp. 8–10), writing and error treatment (pp. 10–12), language focus and pronunciation (pp. 12–13), alternative assessment — self-, peer- and portfolio assessment, the European Language Portfolio, and the end-of-unit Review pages that learners self-correct from a key printed in the *Student's Book's* appendices (pp. 13–14) — differentiated learning through the "It's up to you!" tiered tasks, in which closed tasks are rewritten at different difficulty levels for learners to choose from (p. 14), and project work: a mini-project/extended-project system with a full supervision checklist for the teacher, from assigning roles and research strategies to weekly meetings, display and presentation (pp. 14–16). It closes with a short reference and website list (CEF, European Language Portfolio, Council of Europe, eTwinning; p. 16).

**Per-unit teaching notes — Student's Book (printed pp. 17–102).** The course is numbered by **lessons, not just units**: 8 units × 3 lessons = Lessons 1–24, and the notes follow that numbering throughout. Each unit opens with an overview (some overviews begin at the foot of the preceding unit's last page) stating the theme, what each lesson does, and how to work the Student's Book cover page; each lesson then gets an objectives box (reading/listening/speaking/writing aims), its Language focus and Vocabulary lists, and task-by-task procedure notes keyed to Student's Book pages, with answers printed inline at the point of use, background information the teacher needs (history, geography, art and music notes), project staging, and useful websites. In order: **Unit 1 — Unity in diversity** (pp. 17–25: Lesson 1 People and Places — describing people, Present Simple/Continuous revision; Lesson 2 Joined in our Differences — cultures and countries; Lesson 3 Different Places — comparatives/superlatives through famous buildings); **Unit 2 — Echoes of the past** (pp. 26–38: Lesson 4 Mysteries of our World — Atlantis and the destruction of Helike; Lesson 5 Across the Ages — Pompeii; Lesson 6 Life on the Water — ancient Egypt and the Nile, closing with story-writing and a taught peer-feedback lesson); **Unit 3 — Time out** (pp. 38–46: holidays, entertainment and sport — Lesson 7 Get on Board, adventure holidays and gerunds; Lesson 8 What an Experience!, a theme park; Lesson 9 …Let the Games Begin!, curling and the Olympic spirit); **Unit 4 — Let's change our schools** (pp. 47–59: Lesson 10 Looking at Other Schools, opening with a Kazantzakis extract; Lesson 11 Change through Time, schools of the future and modal verbs; Lesson 12 Change: An Ongoing Process, the history of writing from Linear A to e-books, closing with a fully briefed teachers-versus-computers debate, arguments supplied for both sides); **Unit 5 — The arts** (pp. 59–73: Lesson 13 Quite an Art!, Picasso's *Guernica*; Lesson 14 It's Music to my Ears; Lesson 15 Acting Up!, theatre history closing with the large-scale project of rewriting and staging scenes from the *Iliad*, budgeted at 3–4 weeks' preparation over up to two months); **Unit 6 — Healthy living** (pp. 73–86: Lesson 16 You are What you Eat; Lesson 17 The 'Greenest' Way to School; Lesson 18 Going 'Green', closing with an Eco-Schools-style action project with a photographic before/after record); **Unit 7 — Embracing our world** (pp. 86–97: friendship and caring — Lesson 19 Against the Odds; Lesson 20 Seeing through a Friend's Eyes, reported speech; Lesson 21 Friends Without Frontiers, closing with step-by-step eTwinning partnership instructions); **Unit 8 — Welcome to the world** (pp. 98–102: a short revision unit on travel — Lesson 22 Breaking the Boundaries; Lesson 23 It's a Small World After All; Lesson 24 A World without End, which deliberately closes the circle back to Unit 1 through Melina's e-mail and Kavafis's *Ithaca*).

**Workbook teaching notes and answers (printed pp. 103–138).** A second, parallel set of notes covers the Workbook unit by unit (Units 1–8, Lessons 1–24 in the same numbering). It mixes short teaching suggestions with dense answer keys — vocabulary, language-focus, pronunciation, listening and everyday-English answers lesson by lesson — and prints the Workbook's own listening transcripts where the Workbook task is a listening. It ends with the Unit 8 general-knowledge quiz answers (printed p. 138: Helsinki, Atlantis, Vesuvius, Elytis, Australia, Gutenberg … Eiffel Tower, Rio de Janeiro) and the hidden phrase "HAVE A GREAT SUMMER!".

**Transcripts — the audio layer the Student's Book lacks.** There is no separate tapescript appendix: transcripts are printed **inline, headed TRANSCRIPT, inside the lesson notes** (and inside the Workbook notes) at exactly the point where the class hears the recording — far more of them than in the Grade 7 book, dozens across the book. Examples in full: Imani of Malawi's daily routine in Unit 1 (printed p. 19: up at 4 a.m., dishes carried to the lake, school, chores, bed at 8:45); the Pompeii interview with its plaster casts of people, a dog with its collar, bread and eggs (p. 31); Tom's unannounced adventure cruise around Paros, Naxos, Tinos, Mykonos and Santorini in Unit 3 (p. 39); the ancient-Olympics text in Unit 3 (p. 45: Protesilaus's discus and Chionis's long jump, both records set in 656 BC and unbroken until 1900/1928); and the *Guernica* bombing account in Unit 5 (p. 61: 26 April 1937, a market day, three quarters of the town destroyed, the government figure of 1,600 dead as a minimum). The Introduction states the principle once, for the whole book: every listening text is transcribed here (p. 8).

**Tests (printed pp. 147–168).** Seven photocopiable tests, one per three lessons — Test 1 (Lessons 1–3), Test 2 (Lessons 4–6), Test 3 (Lessons 7–9), Test 4 (Lessons 10–12), Test 5 (Lessons 13–15), Test 6 (Lessons 16–18), Test 7 (Lessons 19–21) — each headed "Score: …… / 50" and built to the same five-part pattern: Reading, Vocabulary, Language focus, Everyday English, and a Writing task of about 100–120 words for 10 points. Test 1's reading is Tipi's account of life in ancient Egypt (p. 147); Test 7's language-focus section is a ten-item reported-speech rewrite of a forest-fire escape story (pp. 167–168) and its writing task is an e-project piece on a best friendship (p. 168). Unlike the Grade 7 tests, these tests have **no listening and no speaking section**.

**Gathered answer keys (printed pp. 139–146 and 169–172).** Two gathered key blocks supplement the inline answers. Before the tests come the keys to the differentiated "It's up to you!" tasks: first the Student's Book set, keyed by unit, lesson and activity with Student's Book page numbers (pp. 139–141 — e.g. Unit 1 Lesson 3's Spartan-school answers, p. 139), then the Workbook set in the same format (pp. 142–146). After the tests, under the heading "ΑNSWERS", come the Keys to Tests 1–7 (pp. 169–172), scored section by section with point values, giving suggested answers for the open Everyday English items. The keys end on printed p. 172 with Key to Test 7; printed pp. 173–175 are blank.

### Honest negatives

- **No publication year is printed** anywhere on the cover, title or imprint pages — only the 2012 in-file production slugs and the PDF's 2012/2017 file dates. Any catalogue year for this book comes from outside the book itself.
- **There is no contents page and no gathered Student's Book answer key.** Student's Book answers exist only inline inside the lesson notes; the gathered keys cover only the "It's up to you!" tasks (Student's Book and Workbook) and the seven tests. The key to the Student's Book's own end-of-unit Review pages is not here at all — the Introduction (p. 13) points to the Student's Book's own appendices, pp. 163–166 of that book.
- **There is no Test 8.** The seven tests cover Lessons 1–21 only; Unit 8 (Lessons 22–24), the revision unit, has no test and no test key in this book.
- **The tests test no listening or speaking** — five written sections only, 50 points each — and there are therefore no listening-test tapescripts or speaking/writing rating scales, unlike the Grade 7 Advanced Teacher's Book.
- **Running-head errors in the original tests:** Test 4's title page says "Lessons 10-12" but its inner running heads say "LESSONS 9-12" (printed pp. 157–158); Test 5's title page says "Lessons 13-15" but its running heads say "LESSONS 12-15" (pp. 160–162); Test 7's last page is headed "TEST 1 (LESSONS 19-21)" (p. 168). The title-page lesson ranges are the correct ones.
- **No separate tapescript appendix and no audio in the PDF.** Transcripts are complete but scattered inline through the notes under the heading TRANSCRIPT; pronunciation models and performed songs cannot be recovered from this file.
- **The guide does not reprint the Student's Book or the Workbook.** Reading texts and task wording are generally not reproduced (transcripts and test papers excepted); the notes are unusable without the Student's Book — and, for printed pp. 103–146, the Workbook — open beside them at the cited page.
- **Three blank printed pages at the end:** printed pp. 173–175 carry only printer's crop/registration marks before the legal page; printed p. 4 at the front is likewise blank.
- **Unit 8's notes are much thinner than the rest** (printed pp. 98–102, five pages for three lessons, against 9–13 pages per earlier unit) — it is a revision unit, and the guide treats it as one.
- **Dated content is part of the book as printed:** the Unit 1 overview's population figures are explicitly 2008 figures (China "just over 1.3 billion people in 2008", the Vatican at 911 inhabitants, printed p. 17), and the websites and eTwinning instructions reflect the book's 2012 production.
- This guide covers the **Advanced stream only**; it contains nothing for the Beginners stream.
## Grade 8 (Advanced) — Workbook

Β΄ Γυμνασίου is the second year of Greek junior high school, i.e. Grade 8. ### How the workbook maps onto the Student's Book

The workbook follows the Student's Book unit-for-unit and lesson-for-lesson: the same eight units and the same 24 lessons, numbered continuously across the year (Lesson 1 "People and Places" to Lesson 24 "A World without End"), with the same lesson titles, the same vocabulary sets and the same grammar spine in the same order. Its internal pattern differs from the Grade 7 workbook's: there is no fixed Reading / Vocabulary Link / Grammar Link / Writing cycle and no per-lesson Writing section. Instead each lesson is built in numbered sections:

1. **Section 1 — Vocabulary, usually mined from the Student's Book text.** Most lessons open by sending the learner back into the Student's Book reading (the task cites the Student's Book page, often down to the paragraph) to find words matching definitions, opposites, derivatives or puzzle answers, followed by word-formation, collocation, phrasal-verb and word-group work on the same set. The workbook therefore cannot be used on its own for these tasks — the Student's Book must be open beside it.
2. **Section 2 — Language Focus.** The lesson's grammar, practised through gap-fills set in short workbook-only texts, error correction, sentence transformation and controlled production. Unlike the Grade 7 workbook, the grammar is not re-presented as completion tables; the presentation stays in the Student's Book and the workbook drills it.
3. **Later sections — functions, listening, pronunciation and short new readings.** Most lessons add one or more of: a functional speaking strand with a boxed phrase table (greetings and introductions, directions, suggestions, permission, opinions, advice, thanking); a listening task; a pronunciation listen-and-repeat set; and/or a genuinely new reading text printed only in the workbook (details below). Extended writing is rare and short — picture descriptions, interview questions, sentences from notes, one sensory poem — rather than a guided composition per lesson.

Two further structural features:

- **Listening is present throughout** (unlike the Grade 7 workbook): travel-agent information, a summer-school programme, a celebrity-chef interview, a song, film music, a rescue story and classroom presentations are all heard, not read, and five lessons carry pronunciation sections. No tapescripts are printed in the workbook.
- **"It's up to you" appendix (printed pp. 132–142).** Selected main tasks carry a cross-reference of the form "It's up to you p. 13x". The appendix tasks are headed "Extra – Vocabulary / Language focus, activity N, p. X" and are keyed to a specific main-book activity; each carries one, two or three stars. They are *additional* practice on the same point — extra drills plus a handful of short new texts — not a scaffolded re-do of the main task, and they are not grouped as numbered tasks as in Grade 7. No legend explaining the stars was found in the book.

**Grammar spine as practised (summary):** Present Simple / Present Continuous and stative verbs, comparatives (Unit 1) → Past Simple / Present Perfect, Past Continuous and *used to*, Past Perfect (Unit 2) → gerunds and preference verbs, *going to* / Future Simple, *so / such*, *too / enough*, question tags (Unit 3) → modals of obligation, modals of possibility / permission / request, relative clauses (Unit 4) → Present passive, Past passive, active-to-passive transformation (Unit 5) → Conditionals Type 0 / 1, Type 2, *unless* and purpose / result clauses (Unit 6) → reported statements and imperatives, reporting verbs, reported questions (Unit 7) → whole-course tense revision (Unit 8). Identical in order and content to the Student's Book spine; the workbook's contribution is drill volume and the extra texts, not new grammar.

### Unit-by-unit summary (own words; printed page references)

**Unit 1 — Unity in Diversity (printed pp. 6–21).** *Lesson 1, "People and Places" (p. 6):* vocabulary is mined from the Student's Book anthropologist interview (p. 11 there), then a full appearance/character adjective bank is built up and used to describe pictured people from Greece, Mexico, Egypt and England. Grammar is drilled inside a workbook-only gap-fill about Omar, a twelve-year-old nomad boy in the Sahara whose family is striking its tents and loading camels to move to an oasis. A listening check-off task follows Anna, a UNICEF volunteer, talking with Ndube, a twelve-year-old in Zimbabwe, about his school, chores and family; the lesson ends with /ŋ/ and /s/–/z/–/ɪz/ pronunciation work. *Lesson 2, "Joined in our Differences" (p. 12):* definitions and a word search drawn from the Student's Book speeches (p. 16 there); the phrasal verb *make up / make for / make out* in its senses; Present Simple vs Continuous drilled in cultural generalisations and in a workbook-only gap-fill text, "Time for games!", on hopscatch, marbles, tangrams and chess around the world. A functions strand teaches greetings and introductions through two short dialogues, and the lesson closes with a timed ten-question Europe quiz (loch, clock tower, Barcelona 1992, tulips, Brussels, the Rhine and Danube, the Alps, and the English names of two countries given in Greek). *Lesson 3, "Different Places – Different Buildings" (p. 17):* three workbook-only gap-fill paragraphs supply the building vocabulary — Greek/Roman pillars and domes, the Colosseum (completed AD 80, four storeys, 50,000 spectators) and Stonehenge — followed by eleven dwelling types matched to definitions, building materials matched to dwellings, and a building-parts word search. Comparatives are drilled on world landmarks and then on six pictured statues (the Great Sphinx, the Corcovado Christ, the Statue of Liberty, the Bamiyan and Dafo Buddhas, the Colossi of Memnon, the Motherland Calls).

**Unit 2 — Echoes of the Past (printed pp. 22–35).** *Lesson 4, "Mysteries of Our World" (p. 22):* the workbook-only reading is a full article on the Maya — Chichén Itzá, pyramid burials, picture writing, nature and jaguar gods, and the unsolved abandonment of their cities, adapted from a Time-Life "Lost Civilisations" publication — worked through question formation. Opposites and derivatives are mined from the Student's Book archaeologist interview (p. 29 there); *-ed* pronunciation and the *lie / lay* confusion are separated out. Past/Perfect tenses are then drilled in a second workbook-only text, "The Enigmatic Incas" (empire from AD 1438, the Spaniards in 1532, mummies found beneath Lima's streets), with time expressions sorted into past-only vs past-to-present bridge, and the lesson ends by having learners write the questions for a ready-made interview with a Machu Picchu archaeologist (Hiram Bingham, 1911, 2,000 feet up in the Andes) and a word puzzle on what the Incas called gold and silver. *Lesson 5, "Across the Ages" (p. 26):* compound words and *break* phrasal verbs from the Student's Book Pompeii material, a natural-disasters spider diagram (volcano, earthquake, fire, flood), then Past Simple / Past Continuous drilled through both parts of Aesop's fable "The Wind and the Sun" (moral printed: persuasion over force), a Greeks-vs-Romans *used to* comparison from notes (Spartan girls at school, the Agora vs the Forum, gladiators), true/false correction on Pompeii (Vesuvius, AD 79), and a Santorini potter's first-person eruption account with the correct tense form to be circled. A functions strand covers reacting to good and bad news. *Lesson 6, "Life on the Water" (p. 31):* a crossword and same-word-different-meaning pairs mined from the Student's Book Egypt text (p. 40 there), a tense-sequencing exercise that makes learners label which action came first, then two workbook-only gap-fill texts — women's work in ancient Egypt (household, weaving, market selling, Herodotus surprised by men weaving) and how papyrus was made, the second set as find-and-correct-the-tense-errors — and the lesson's writing is a short text built from telegraphic notes on how the Great Pyramid was built (Khufu, from 2606 BC, up to 30,000 workers, blocks dragged up earthen ramps).

**Unit 3 — Time Out (printed pp. 36–53).** *Lesson 7, "Get on Board" (p. 36):* opens with a workbook-only holiday-maker questionnaire whose five answers sort the learner into adventurous, intellectual or cosmopolitan types (Samaria gorge and museum vs shopping in Iraklio among the cues). Travel vocabulary, airport vocabulary and *turn* phrasal verbs follow; gerunds and preference verbs are drilled in an Emily-and-Joan dialogue about travelling abroad and going to Rome by boat rather than plane; compound activity words (scuba diving, hang gliding, kite surfing…) are assembled. There is a listening form-completion from a travel agent's details of a "Mountain Trail Hiking Holiday", a directions functions strand, and a two-page workbook-only London leaflet: short entries for nine sights (Buckingham Palace's 600 rooms, Big Ben at 106 m, the London Eye at 135 m with 32 capsules) are labelled on a map by following written directions, and a further listening numbers the sights in tour order. *Lesson 8, "What an Experience!" (p. 43):* a rollercoaster-shaped definition hunt in the Student's Book leaflet (p. 53 there), vocabulary sorted across party / theatre-cinema / restaurant / PC settings, and scrambled collocations (*book a ticket, wait in a queue, pay the bill…*) to unscramble and use. Future forms are drilled in six short Eurodisney dialogues (Indiana Jones rollercoaster, Peter Pan show at 5:30, parade finishing at 7:00) plus error correction on future time clauses. The functions strand teaches asking for, making, accepting and refusing suggestions, ending in a paired role-card negotiation over how to spend a last day together. *Lesson 9, "…Let the Games Begin!" (p. 49):* sports sorted under *do / go / play*, venues, equipment and true/false sports facts; a listening in which four teenagers' talk is matched to cautious / ambitious / confident / enthusiastic; question tags taught with rising vs falling intonation and then applied to ten sports-trivia statements (nine baseball players, Bob Beamon's long-jump record); and *so / such* and *too / enough* drilled and combined, closing with three short workbook-only texts on adventure sports in Greece (bungee jumping into the Corinth Canal and at Aradaina in Chania, kite-surfing on Paros and Naxos, wakeboarding at Poros).

**Unit 4 — Let's Change Our Schools (printed pp. 54–69).** *Lesson 10, "Looking at Other Schools" (p. 54):* vocabulary and *over-/under-* prefixes from the Student's Book text (p. 66 there), seven *break* idioms deliberately misused for correction, and school-system word choice. A workbook-only cloze paragraph profiles Hillhead High School in Glasgow — pupils from 35 countries speaking 30 languages, more than 80 Friday-afternoon activities, over £50,000 raised for Children in Need in ten years. Modals are practised by writing Nick's questions for Eric's answers about an English school day (registration at 8:55, lessons 9:20–3:15) and completing Eric's account of uniforms, state vs "public" schools and A-levels, with a Great Britain school-types table. A workbook-only "DOs and DON'Ts in England" list (queueing, saying sorry, not staring, not asking personal questions) is converted into a must/should list for the learner's own country, and a listening completes a summer-school week's programme from the director's announcements. *Lesson 11, "Schools Change through Time" (p. 60):* vocabulary from the Student's Book advertisement (p. 72 there), opposite pairs, *make* vs *do*, *take* phrasal verbs in all their senses, jobs matched to personal qualities, and an interview to reconstruct. Modals are rewritten, labelled by use (request, permission, possibility, prohibition, obligation, ability, advice) and produced from situations. The workbook-only reading is a job advertisement for a Summer Camp Group Leader at Halkidiki's International Summer Camp (children aged 9–13, 20 children per leader, a printed contact number), checked true/false and then role-played as an interview; a functions strand covers asking, giving and refusing permission, ending in a charity-bazaar role play. *Lesson 12, "Change: An Ongoing Process" (p. 66):* a definition crossword mined from the Student's Book writing text (p. 77 there), synonym replacement from the same text, and adjective formation with *-able / -al / -ive*. Relative clauses are introduced by matching seven achievers to their deeds (Spielberg and *Jurassic Park*, Mozart's three symphonies by age 11, Braille's 1829 printing for blind people, Seferis and Elytis and the Nobel Prize in Literature, Magellan, Roald Dahl, da Vinci's flying machine), then drilled through pronoun completion, error correction (including *the man which…* type errors) and sentence joining.

**Unit 5 — The Arts (printed pp. 70–87).** *Lesson 13, "Quite an Art!" (p. 70):* war-art vocabulary mined from the Student's Book text (pp. 85–86 there), then a workbook-only three-part gap-fill survey of ancient art — Greek amphoras and paint colours (soot black, seashell purple, chalk white), Japanese calligraphy scrolls and gilded wood carving, Chinese nature painting. Present passive is drilled on art processes and museum sentences. The second workbook-only reading is a set of three short artist biographies with gaps — Dalí (born 1904, expelled from art school in Madrid, melting clocks, died 1989 aged 85), Leonardo da Vinci (born in Vinci in 1452, *The Baptism of Christ* at twenty, Milan at thirty) and El Greco (1541–1614, born in Crete, signed with his full Greek name) — checked true/false, and the functions strand teaches asking for and giving opinions. *Lesson 14, "It's Music to my Ears" (p. 75):* a gap-fill on making music from bins, bottles and tins; instruments sorted into wind / stringed / percussion and players named; a music word-web; and a true/false music quiz (two Strausses, Wagner and Verdi born the same year, Beethoven composing while almost deaf). Passive is drilled through a Music Awards ceremony text in the present, the same ceremony retold from prompts in the past, and a workbook-only "United by Music" gap-fill on Live 8 (2 July 2005, more than a million people, Bob Geldof, "No More Excuses", Live Aid's 100 million dollars for Ethiopian famine victims, two billion viewers). The lesson ends with a gap-fill song to complete and then check by listening, and a listening that orders ten well-known film scores. *Lesson 15, "Acting Up!…" (p. 80):* the main reading is workbook-only — real London West End listings (from the July 2000 *London Planner*) for *The Mousetrap*, *The Phantom of the Opera*, *Cats* and *Singin' in the Rain*, with prices of admission given as times and running lengths, theatregoer tips (disabled access, backstage tours, shows suitable if English is not your first language), and seven named would-be theatregoers to match to a show. Theatre vocabulary, *come* phrasal verbs and a schwa-pronunciation set follow. The passive strand converts an Epidaurus Festival advertisement (Euripides' *Orestes* and *Bacchae*, Aristophanes' *Peace*, August dates, 50% discount for children and students) into a continuous passive text, judges active vs passive sentences, and rewrites active sentences as passive. The lesson closes with a mediation task: three Greek film summaries from a February 2006 listings magazine (*Pride and Prejudice*, *Zathura*, *The Chronicles of Narnia*) are explained in English to a friend in a scripted dialogue.

**Unit 6 — Healthy Living (printed pp. 88–103).** *Lesson 16, "You are What you Eat" (p. 88):* definitions mined from the Student's Book text (p. 104 there), food-taste adjectives, the Mediterranean Diet Food Pyramid to complete with some thirty foods, a pyramid-messages gap-fill (thirty minutes of daily exercise as the minimum), a labelled restaurant-kitchen picture for fifteen cooking verbs, a workbook-only Spanish rice recipe (serves 4; bake at 180°C for about 15 minutes) with the correct cooking verb to be circled — the book invites learners to make the dish — a menu to design for one vegetarian and one non-vegetarian guest, and eight *put* phrasal verbs. Conditionals Type 0 / 1 are drilled as food riddles (what melts, what keeps you awake, what makes you sneeze) and error correction, including a stated 500-calories-a-day / half-a-kilo-in-7-days claim to be judged as printed. A listening interview has Jamie Oliver looking back on filming *School Dinners*; the functions strand teaches asking about a problem and giving advice, applied to a workbook-only herbal-remedies leaflet (chamomile, oregano, rosemary, mastic, saffron, ginseng) matched to five sufferers (toothache, sleeplessness, poor concentration, cough, lost appetite). *Lesson 17, "The 'Greenest' Way to School" (p. 95):* definitions and a derivative table from the Student's Book text (pp. 109–110 there), then two workbook-only readings: "Active Students Fit for Better Grades", a gap-fill report of a study of 33 Ontario schools where daily activity and no junk food accompanied an 18-percent rise in test scores over two years, with named teacher and pupil quotations; and a safe-cycling leaflet whose six rules must be given their headings (helmets, bike checks, standing out, watching, road rules, special care for under-tens). Type 2 conditionals are drilled on cycling, walking and junk food, converted from statements, and spoken in "If you could…" pair questions; the lesson ends with an /æ/–/ɑː/–/eə/ pronunciation set. *Lesson 18, "Going 'Green'" (p. 100):* vocabulary from the Student's Book text (p. 114 there), then the workbook-only jigsaw reading "The Heat is On" — five paragraphs on the greenhouse effect with five sentences (plus one extra) to restore, stating that man releases 400 thousand million tons of carbon dioxide a year and predicting a 15–30 cm sea-level rise. Conditionals are written from the text and assembled from clause fragments; purpose and result linkers (*in order to, therefore, as a result…*) are completed; two "green gadget" advertisements (a Danish digital flower that dies if energy is wasted, a Japanese umbrella-stand watering can) are turned into conditional sentences; and the lesson ends with an environment crossword.

**Unit 7 — Embracing Our World (printed pp. 104–117).** *Lesson 19, "Against the Odds" (p. 104):* opens with a workbook-only jumbled story to reorder — Partner, a twelve-year-old Golden Retriever, seizing a rattlesnake that fell from a tree in front of two eight-year-olds and winning an award — followed by synonym work on the Student's Book alligator text (p. 124 there) and a second workbook-only gap-fill rescue story, Priscilla the three-month-old pig swimming a drowning eleven-year-old, Anthony Melton, to shore in a Texas lake. Noun/verb homographs and *look* phrasal verbs follow. Reported speech is introduced on news-style statements, *say* vs *tell* is sorted with its collocations, and a first-person shark-survival extract attributed to Krishna is rewritten in reported speech. A listening completes notes on David Hurst, a blind man who rescued a drowning swimmer from the sea off a beach in Wales and is also credited with marathons, high-mountain climbs and judo and water-skiing medals; the reverse task then turns a reported newspaper interview with his wife back into her exact words. *Lesson 20, "Seeing through a Friend's Eyes" (p. 110):* sound words (*sneeze, whistle, yell, sigh…*), sound-effect words (*rustle, crash, splash, slam…*), touch adjectives and touch verbs — the senses vocabulary for the Student's Book poem (p. 130 there), whose definitions also form a puzzle. Learners then write their own six-line sensory poem to a printed model ("Summer is blue…"). Reported speech continues with sentences from Helen Keller's *Story of My Life* (deaf and blind from nineteen months; Anne Sullivan teaching her to speak by touch) and her teacher's "love is like the clouds" speech, both to be reported with varied reporting verbs, two Keller quotations to discuss, and a closing note on Braille. *Lesson 21, "Friends without Frontiers" (p. 114):* definitions from the Student's Book texts (p. 131 there), *multi-* prefix words, and *touch* idioms (*get / keep / lose touch*). Reported questions are practised by reporting a complete workbook-only e-mail from Eric in Sweden about an inter-school environment e-Project, and reporting-verb choice is drilled on the class's first-e-mail mistakes. The functions strand teaches thanking and responding to thanks in seven paired scenarios, and the lesson ends with silent-letter pronunciation work.

**Unit 8 — Welcome to the World (printed pp. 118–131).** A revision unit: the Student's Book sets no new grammar for Lessons 22–24, and the workbook follows suit. *Lesson 22, "Breaking the Boundaries" (p. 118):* travel expressions mined from the Student's Book letter (p. 140 there), pastime definitions, a phrasal-verb dialogue between Dana, who wants to take up rock climbing, and John, who prefers adventure games on the Net, and a travel word search. Workbook-only cultural material follows: greetings around the world to match to Japan, France, Thailand, Africa, Italy, New Zealand and England; Japanese noodle-slurping and Canadian burping as compliments, with a European table-manners DOs-and-DON'Ts list to turn into advice; a true/false "Check your memory" quiz on famous buildings whose answers are to be checked in the Student's Book, Unit 1, Lesson 3; and British coins matched to their emblems (rose, thistle, lion, Britannia, portcullis, Prince of Wales' feathers) with flag symbolism explained for South Africa and the United Kingdom. *Lesson 23, "It's a Small World After All" (p. 123):* comparatives written from a printed six-city weather panel (Tokyo mostly cloudy 20°C, Sydney light showers 10°C, Delhi partly cloudy 30°C, Moscow clear 12°C, and Beijing and Helsinki), a workbook-only gap-fill text on world climates (deserts under 25 cm of rain a year, Antarctica to −60°C), citizens' views to write in speech bubbles for a town-improvement plan (ramps, buses, footpaths, cycle lanes, by-passes), a listening in which five international students present traditional dishes, an error hunt for ten verb-form mistakes in a workbook-only e-mail about eating in China (chopstick practice, tea houses, Beijing Night Food Market), and eight souvenirs (boomerang, tatami mats, nesting doll, Beijing tea cups, samovar, eucalyptus soap, kimono, brass dragon) matched to cultural notes. *Lesson 24, "A World without End" (p. 128):* no new input at all — a sixteen-question "global bingo" game with its bingo card, and a two-page acrostic-style puzzle whose sixteen answers must all be retrieved from earlier lessons of the book (the Corcovado Christ's city, Plato's mythical land, the volcano that destroyed Pompeii, the composer of *The Magic Flute*, the inventor of the phonograph, and the like), the first letters forming a message.

**Appendix — "It's up to you" (printed pp. 132–142).** Eleven pages of Extra tasks, grouped by unit and lesson and each headed with the main-book activity it extends and a one-to-three-star mark. Most are further drills of the same vocabulary or grammar point; a minority carry short new material, including gap-fill texts on the Sahara and on homes in extreme places (Unit 1), a "Sizing Up: Towers" comparison table and a fatal-voyage text built around the curse-of-the-Pharaohs mummy story (Unit 2), a Palaeolithic cave-painting text and a Japanese Noh/Kabuki theatre text (Unit 5), a Stradivari-violins text (Unit 5), a tuna-sandwich recipe (Unit 6), energy-saving and environment-definition work (Unit 6), and a complete thank-you e-mail from Carla in Italy to be reported in reported speech (Unit 7). Unit 8 has no appendix section. Followed by the origin-of-photographs list (printed p. 143, a single page, in Greek) and the legal/distribution notice under Law 3966/2011 (printed p. 144).

### Honest negatives

- **No publication year is printed** on the cover, title pages or imprint pages; only the reissue note and in-file production stamps (2013–2023, varying by section) are present. Any catalogue year for this book comes from outside the book itself.
- **The workbook is not self-contained.** A large share of its Section 1 tasks consist of finding words in the Student's Book text (Student's Book page — often paragraph — cited in the task), so those pages yield no reading text of their own; the workbook-only readings listed above are the exception, concentrated in Sections 2–5. Counts of "texts in the workbook" must not treat the Student's Book-mining tasks as workbook texts.
- **The workbook has listening tasks but no tapescripts and no answer key,** and **no self-assessment pages** (the Student's Book's self-assessment key has no workbook counterpart). The only answers printed anywhere are the worked examples inside tasks and the sports-trivia example in Lesson 9.
- **No legend for the appendix star marks was found** in the contents, the main body or the appendix pages checked; the stars are reported as printed, without an asserted meaning.
- **Back matter is thinner than in Grade 7:** there is no sources-of-texts list — printed p. 143 lists only the origin of photographs (in Greek), and the Contents (printed p. 5) does not list pp. 143–144 at all.
- **A few pages are blank or near-blank in the text layer** (PDF p. 5, blank apart from its production stamp); picture-only tasks (word searches, crosswords, photo labelling, the bingo card on printed p. 129) are described from the rendered pages and task instructions, not from extracted text. The Mrs Hurst interview on printed p. 109 is set in a two-column layout whose text layer interleaves; its content is reported from the task framing and the legible reported-speech text.
- Dated content is part of the book as printed: the West End listings are from July 2000, the Greek film summaries from February 2006, Live 8 is reported as a 2005 event, the summer-camp salary in the appendix interview is given as "500 D" (drachmas-era wording carried into the appendix), and prices, phone numbers and web addresses in the texts are period details, not verified as live.

### What "Beginners" means here — and what the book assumes

This is the second year of the lower stream, and it is **not a beginner book in the absolute-zero sense**. There is no alphabet, phonics or handwriting work, and no recurring cast of characters to carry a learner along: the Grade 7 Beginners e-friends frame is gone, replaced by ten stand-alone thematic units. What the stream label buys the learner is pace and scaffolding, not a lower starting point:

- Unit 1 opens by **revising** the Present Simple and Present Continuous contrast — including state verbs and the infinitive of purpose — as already-met material to be sorted into uses, not as a first encounter. The first full reading text (printed p. 4) is a dense ~300-word article, and learners are immediately asked to find reference words and to separate general-truth verbs from change verbs inside it.
- The grammar ceiling rises steeply across the year and goes well beyond the Grade 7 Beginners ceiling: Past Simple (U2), comparatives/superlatives and relative clauses (U3), modals and the Simple Future (U4), the **Present Perfect** contrasted with the Past Simple (U5), **zero and first conditionals with *unless*** (U6), **Past Continuous and *used to*** (U7), question tags (U8), the **second conditional and *wish* + Past Simple** (U9), and the **Passive Voice** in present and past (U10). By Grade 8 the two streams cover much of the same grammar territory; the Beginners differentiation is in how each point is staged.
- The scaffolding is systematic and is the stream's real signature: every unit opens with a one-page map of its grammar, functions, vocabulary and "learning strategies"; every unit is exactly 12 printed pages (three lessons plus a two-page scored self-evaluation ending in can-do tick boxes); Greek is used openly as a support — mediation tasks translate Greek texts into English in almost every unit, idioms are matched to Greek equivalents, and one full reading text in Appendix II is in Greek; Appendix IV (printed pp. 168–184) then re-teaches the whole grammar course in short form-and-use tables, followed by a unit-by-unit vocabulary list and an irregular-verb table.
- Cross-curricular load is assumed throughout: learners are repeatedly sent to their Geography, History, Physics and Ancient Greek lessons, and to the internet, as part of the English task itself — the book assumes a pupil inside the Greek school system, not a general learner.

### Unit-by-unit summary (own words; printed page references)

**Unit 1 — I'm only human (printed pp. 1–12).** *Lesson 1, "Tribes of the forest" (p. 2):* Amazon rainforest lead-in — foods that come from the forest, −ed/−ing feeling adjectives, and a mini-project on forest loss — then a picture-labelling task on tribal life (huts, spears, necklaces, vegetation) that introduces the infinitive of purpose, and a full article on the Yanomami and neighbouring tribes: what the forest gives them, the "slash and burn" way of clearing a small garden plot, and why logging companies are driving the tribes out. Grammar work separates Present Simple (general truths, habits) from Present Continuous (change in progress). *Lesson 2, "Way of Life" (p. 6):* a radio interview with a travel writer, heard for sequence and attitude only; a spidergram of how the forest is used; a gapped dialogue between two schoolgirls, Lina and Eleni, full of spoken phrases for disbelief and teasing; and a reply-letter task modelled on a letter from Naraneti, a Zulu girl in South Africa who does not go to school. *Lesson 3, "Save the tribes" (p. 10):* a jigsaw project comparing Yanomami, Aborigines and Zulu on location, food, transport, problems and tools, ending in a poster for a European project. Self-evaluation pp. 11–12.

**Unit 2 — Making a difference (printed pp. 13–24).** The Past Simple unit. *Lesson 1 (p. 14):* famous-people cards (Venizelos, Pyrros Dimas, Marie Curie, Mozart, Shakespeare, Leonardo, Madonna) matched to deeds and ages, jobs vocabulary and verb+noun phrases, then a biography of Mother Teresa printed as nine numbered paragraphs **out of order** — born in Skopje in 1910, a nun at eighteen, sent to Calcutta, founder of a charity there in 1950, Nobel Prize in 1979 — which learners sequence, mine for past verbs and turn into a timeline; a role-play on charities uses the resource pages. *Lesson 2, "Same or Different" (p. 18):* listening on the film *Spartacus* (both scripts are printed in Appendix II), attitude phrases sorted positive/negative, a short play on Justinian, Theodora and the Nika Revolt, and a class film survey written up as a graph and a report to the school council. *Lesson 3, "A Show" (p. 22):* a group project — an end-of-term show on a famous person's life, researched with a fact file. Self-evaluation pp. 23–24, including a gapped Gandhi text.

**Unit 3 — Technology in our lives (printed pp. 25–36).** *Lesson 1 (p. 26):* three portable media players compared on memory, weight, battery and price to build comparatives and superlatives (with *good/better/best*, *bad/worse/worst*), shopping and fault vocabulary (discount, queue, guarantee, refund, faulty), and a two-part "What kind of shopper are you?" quiz (Part 1 is pictorial, printed p. 28). *Lesson 2, "Gadgets" (p. 30):* a technology-skills checklist, five heard advertisements matched to their persuasive phrases, present-choosing inside a €350 budget, and a model formal complaint letter about a faulty DVD player, reworked as an e-mail; a pen-friend letter from Yuri asks for phone-buying advice. *Lesson 3 (p. 34):* a project to redesign an advertisement for young buyers, surveying persuasion techniques (music, humour, fame, jingles, science). Self-evaluation pp. 35–36, including computer troubleshooting matches. Relative clauses are listed for this unit in the Contents and the grammar appendix tradition, but the lessons themselves foreground comparison; relatives are worked properly in Unit 8.

**Unit 4 — Communication (printed pp. 37–48).** *Lesson 1 (p. 38):* first impressions and body language; *will/won't* sorted by function (promise, threat, offer, prediction, fact), *have to / don't have to* and *should / shouldn't*; then the "BODY TALK" leaflet text for a body-language seminar, built on the claim that communication is mostly body and tone rather than words, with a large verb-collocation set (nod, shrug, clench, gaze, stare, squint, peep, glare) and −ed/−ing adjectives after *sound, look, feel, seem, appear*. *Lesson 2, "Expressing Attitude" (p. 42):* intonation and politeness in a heard dialogue between Andy and Clark; gestures in other cultures; a short Freud-and-dreams text with a traditional dream-symbol matching task; and three problem-page letters about dreams matched to advice replies, leading to writing about one's own dream. *Lesson 3, "Clothes and communication" (p. 46):* what dress and ornaments signal, centred on Turkana women's dress in Kenya, and a life-size design-your-own-outfit project. Self-evaluation pp. 47–48.

**Unit 5 — Change and experience (printed pp. 49–60).** The Present Perfect unit. *Lesson 1, "Everyday experiences" (p. 50):* a spot-the-difference pair of pictures (Rose, ready to travel) generates *already / yet* sentences; *have been to* vs *have gone to* is stated explicitly; museum vocabulary (artifacts, exhibits, fossils, coins, souvenirs) feeds two museum leaflets — a Bristol museum that has exhibited El Greco, and a Tower of London exhibition of Kremlin treasures for the 300th anniversary of Peter the Great's visit — and two postcards that recycle the same material. *Lesson 2, "A Change" (p. 54):* *for / since* with the Present Perfect against *ago* with the Past Simple; a London-sights map task with a heard phone call about places already visited or not yet visited; a find-someone-who survey that forces a Present Perfect question followed by a Past Simple follow-up; and postcard writing, including correcting a deliberately faulty postcard from Athens. *Lesson 3, "Famous people" (p. 58):* a Greek-to-English mediation task on a newspaper report about filming *El Greco*, the six wives of Henry VIII in order, and a group biography of a famous woman in history (Irene the Athenian, Bouboulina, Theodora, Joan of Arc, Marie Curie, Mother Teresa). Self-evaluation pp. 59–60, including a Crete/Knossos text mixing both tenses.

**Unit 6 — What a waste! (printed pp. 61–72).** *Lesson 1, "Rubbish and pollution" (p. 62):* household rubbish lexis, then zero conditional for facts (what happens if paper is recycled, if glass is not broken up, if cans are thrown away), first conditional for future results, and *unless* as "if not"; the reading is three children's letters — Agnieska on car smog in Tirana, Marios on a rubbish-strewn camp at Aspropyrgos outside Athens, and Deng on litter fines in Beijing before the 2008 Olympics — each with three candidate solutions to judge. *Lesson 2, "Eco-art" (p. 66):* container words (a bar of soap, a tube of toothpaste, a packet of crisps, a carton of milk), a heard radio programme on reusing household junk, and heard instructions for making a kite from an old plastic bag, followed in order. *Lesson 3, "Recycling as art" (p. 68):* headline-to-response matching, consequence sentences for a man with bottles, tomatoes and boxes in his yard, sorting waste into glass/plastic/paper/metal, recycling facts, an opinion letter about starting a recycling club, and a project to make a piece of eco-art and an awareness campaign. Self-evaluation pp. 71–72.

**Unit 7 — Magnetism and the world we live in (printed pp. 73–84).** *Lesson 1 (p. 74):* migrating birds open the unit — a heard cartoon conversation (script in Appendix II) in which the old explanation, instinct, is set against magnetism — giving Past Continuous forms and *used to*; a fact-or-myth game on famous scientists (Einstein, Planck, Newton, Maxwell, Galileo) with one-line life sketches; and short texts on the Philadelphia Experiment story and on animals navigating by magnetite in their brains. *Lesson 2, "Magnetic fields" (p. 78):* word origins, including Greek-derived scientific words and Xenophon Zolotas's 1957 speech made almost entirely of Greek-origin words (printed in Appendix II); definitions of *magnetism, compass needle, attract, repel*; labelling a magnet diagram; building a compass; a heard lecture on static electricity and the northern lights; a Sherlock Holmes role-play about stolen turtle eggs, retold in the Past Continuous. Writing compares two newspaper versions of the *Mary Celeste* story against the sailors' own statements. *Lesson 3, "Save the turtle" (p. 82):* a poster-and-sponsorship project for the sea-turtle charity ARCHELON — beach parties, sun beds, tourists and fishermen as threats; a sponsor form is printed in Appendix II. Self-evaluation pp. 83–84.

**Unit 8 — Getting around (printed pp. 85–96).** *Lesson 1 (p. 86):* matching travellers to suitable transport, unusual world transport, travel idioms built on horses, the history of the wheel in a timeline (invention, the Penny-farthing, the modern bicycle), and three short adapted articles — a sideways bicycle invented by a Dublin engineer, skateboarding, and a bicycle that floats on water — each salted with travel idioms and question tags. *Lesson 2, "Signs and travel" (p. 90):* relative pronouns (*who, which, whose, where, when, how*) inside sentences that also carry tags; tag-question and intonation rules; a travel-idiom set matched to Greek equivalents (*hit the road, rock the boat, miss the boat, hold your horses*, and others); a heard description of the Maglev train; street-noise decibel listening; road-sign shapes and colours; and writing a semi-formal letter recommending a day trip. *Lesson 3, "Bikes for the world" (p. 94):* the Bikes for the World scheme applied to Namibia — a scattered population of two million, for whom a bicycle means access to health care, education and work — planned through a neighbourhood questionnaire and a class report. Self-evaluation pp. 95–96.

**Unit 9 — 'Keeping up appearances' (printed pp. 97–108).** *Lesson 1, "'I wish I were…'" (p. 98):* the unit opens with "The Unreal Image", a short article warning that model photographs are retouched fantasy and that genuine friends do not judge by clothes; character adjectives, an in/out fashion list, a spidergram of what influences fashion (history, climate, religion), and the *I wish I were / didn't have…* pattern practised on appearance worries, with a music-and-personality quiz text (pop, rock, folk and hip-hop fans) judged for how much truth it holds. *Lesson 2, "History of fashion" (p. 102):* school-uniform debate, clothing idioms (*dressed to kill, pull up your socks, wear your heart on your sleeve, in someone else's shoes, talk through your hat*), the second conditional and *wish* rules stated from examples, a fashion-history quiz reaching back to tunics, cloaks and the chlamys, a heard Byzantine Museum guide talk, a clothes-shop role-play, and problem-page "Teen worries" letters answered with *If I were you…* advice. *Lesson 3, "Byzantine and the Present" (p. 106):* a mediation task — a Greek Benaki Museum leaflet turned into a note for an Australian visitor — and a project to design modern outfits from historical motifs for a museum competition. Self-evaluation pp. 107–108.

**Unit 10 — A Material World (printed pp. 109–120).** The Passive unit. *Lesson 1, "A Plastic World" (p. 110):* materials past and present (a soldier's kit sorted into wool, metal, leather, stone and the materials that did not yet exist), then the reading text "A Plastic World", which states where oil was first found, what plastic is made from, and which countries make bags, toys, phones, ships and sports shoes — every key sentence in the passive; *made of / used for* and the passive rule (be + past participle; the agent only when it matters) follow, with future materials from plants (hemp, bamboo, pine, soybeans, nettles, corn). *Lesson 2, "Silk" (p. 114):* a heard lesson on the history of silk sequenced and put on a timeline running from 3000 BC to 2008, silk's uses and its link to social rank, passive questions with the agent (*by*), and an e-mail-writing task explaining a delayed CD order from an order form covered in staff notes (out of stock, courier strike, wrong address, a discount). *Lesson 3, "Ancient constructions" (p. 118):* a project on how the Pyramids, Stonehenge, the Easter Island statues and the Lighthouse of Alexandria were built, a short text questioning whether Charles Babbage really invented the computer, and a group lecture to prepare on the Antikythera Mechanism, found in 1901 and at least 2,000 years old. Self-evaluation pp. 119–120.

**Appendices (printed pp. 121–194).** Appendix I, "It's your choice!" (pp. 121–153): optional extra work keyed unit by unit — Karen hill tribes and Pygmies and children in ancient Athens and Sparta for Unit 1; a two-student Bouboulina biography gap-fill for Unit 2; computer-game and TV-addiction material for Unit 3; a Japan quiz and text for Unit 4; museum and Greek World Heritage material for Unit 5; world children's environmental problems for Unit 6; a Bermuda Triangle text and a class-newspaper project for Unit 7; Athens transport and city/country travel texts for Unit 8; more "Teen worries" and a songwriting competition for Unit 9; and a repeat of the plastic text and CD-order task for Unit 10. Appendix II, "Resources" (pp. 154–161): the material other lessons point to — the Justinian/Theodora play cards, the two *Spartacus* listening scripts in full, charity information sheets, the Greek Spartacus history text, the Nefeli party-outfit text, the migration cartoon script, the Zolotas speech, the ARCHELON sponsor form, Namibia background, a Maglev text, and a purely pictorial clothing page for Unit 9 (p. 161). Appendix III (pp. 162–167): the self-evaluation answer key for all ten units. Appendix IV (pp. 168–184): an extensive grammar presentation in course order — Present Simple and Continuous, Past Simple, comparisons and adverbs, modals and the Simple Future, Present Perfect, conditionals (presented there as Type 1 and Type 2), Past Continuous and *used to* with a directions section, tag questions and relative pronouns, *wish*, and the Passive — followed by the unit-by-unit vocabulary list (pp. 183–184). Appendix V (p. 185): irregular verbs in three columns. Appendix VI (pp. 186–189): maps — a two-page world map, England, and Europe. Sources and relevant internet sites (p. 190, partly in Greek); three blank pages (pp. 191–193); legal notice (p. 194).

**Grammar spine as it arrives (summary):** Present Simple vs Present Continuous, state verbs, infinitive of purpose (U1) → Past Simple, regular and irregular (U2) → comparatives and superlatives, relative clauses named (U3) → *will/won't, have to / don't have to, should / shouldn't* (U4) → Present Perfect vs Past Simple, *for / since / ago, been* vs *gone* (U5) → zero and first conditionals, *unless* (U6) → Past Continuous vs Past Simple, *used to* (U7) → question tags, relative pronouns in full (U8) → second conditional, *wish* + Past Simple / *would* (U9) → Passive Voice, present and past, with *by*-agent (U10).

### Honest negatives

- **No publication year is printed** on the cover, title page or imprint pages; only the revised-edition stamp, the reissue note and in-file production dates (2013/2016, with 2023 stamps on the front and legal pages) are present. Any catalogue year for this book comes from outside the book itself.

The Beginners verdict rests on book code 0-21-0206, its catalogue entry, and the "ARX" production filenames on the body pages. A reader who identifies streams by the cover word alone would miss it.
- **Listening content cannot be verified from the PDF alone, except where a script is printed:** Appendix II prints the Unit 2 *Spartacus* monologue and dialogue and the Unit 7 migration cartoon in full, and those are described from the scripts. The other recordings — the Unit 1 radio interview, the Unit 3 advertisements, the Unit 5 London phone call, the Unit 6 radio programme and kite instructions, the Unit 7 planetarium guide, static-electricity lecture, Holmes story and song, the Unit 8 Maglev dialogue and street sounds, the Unit 9 Byzantine Museum guide, and the Unit 10 silk lesson — are **not** printed in this book; this draft describes those tasks, not the audio's content.

Printed pp. 191–193 are blank. On a few heavily illustrated pages the text layer interleaves columns, so those summaries rest on headings, tasks and the Contents as well as the readable text.

Three statements are reproduced above exactly as printed and should not be reused as fact without checking: oil "first discovered in Pennsylvania in 1839" (p. 111), the Beijing fine given as 50 Yuan in the pre-reading task on p. 65 but as "500 Yaun" in the letter itself on the same page, and the Babbage text's statement that his computer "was driven by petrol because there was no electricity at the time" (p. 118).
