### What the guide adds (own words; printed page references)

This is the teacher's companion to the Beginners *Think Teen!* Student's Book, Workbook and Audio CD for Grade 8. It does not reprint the pupil book; it tells the teacher how to run each lesson, what the answers are, what the recordings say, and what the revision tests' answers are. Its added value falls into four blocks — and its organisation is different from the Grade 7 teacher's books in the same project: there are no unit planning tables with teaching periods or aids lists, no gathered keys at the back, and no test papers or rating scales; everything is interleaved unit by unit.

**1. A method introduction (printed pp. iii–xvii).** The opening first states the aim and level: the course furthers pupils' existing language awareness to a competence roughly corresponding to A2 of the Council of Europe Framework within a year's study, on a timetable of only 2 hours of tuition per week, so a holistic approach is adopted instead of isolated language patterns (p. iii). Long sections then explain, in turn, the course's four innovations — the cross-curricular methodology (learning English through other school subjects, with a fully worked example project on stereotypes and prejudice, pp. iv–vii), the project method, self-assessment built on the CEFR (the A2 self-assessment grid is reproduced, p. viii) and the European Language Portfolio with its Passport / Biography / Dossier parts (p. ix), and differentiated instruction through open-ended tasks and the tiered "It's Your Choice" appendices (pp. ix–xi). Page xi states plainly what this book itself contains: step-by-step procedural notes for each lesson, linguistic information and explanations, cross-cultural information, Internet addresses where possible, a key to the Student's Book tasks, the key to the Workbook activities, and transcripts of the Audio CD listening tasks and songs. The rest is a skills handbook: how the cover page of each unit works as an advance organiser (pp. xi–xii); vocabulary taught lexically — in themes, collocations and chunks, recycled in different contexts, with guessing from context taught as a cumulative skill (pp. xii–xiii); grammar taught inductively, one main structure per unit, with pupils completing rules in grammar boxes and checking them against the Student's Book Grammar Appendix (pp. xiii–xiv); reading in a pre- / while- / post-reading frame, from authentic texts lightly adapted (p. xiv); listening from semi-scripted texts with pauses, false starts and rephrasing (pp. xiv–xv); speaking organised so stronger and weaker pupils work together, with the teacher monitoring and saving error correction for the end of the task (p. xv); writing staged as a process, with the main task done in class, not set as homework, and peer comment built in (p. xvi); projects with a specific role assigned to every group member (p. xvi); and self-evaluation, can-do statements and portfolios, with the explicit instruction that the self-assessment tests are success-orientated, with no pass or fail (pp. xvi–xvii). It closes with notes on the Workbook's use — its activities may best be set as homework, so pupils go back to the coursebook to find the answers (p. xvii).

**2. Step-by-step per-unit notes (printed pp. 1–214).** Each of the ten units opens with a one-page header the pupil book does not present in this form — topic, the unit's grammar, the reading / listening / writing skills targeted, the vocabulary field and an aim — and then walks through the Student's Book in order: cover page, Lesson 1, Lesson 2, Lesson 3 with its project, and the unit self-evaluation, task by task. The procedure is written as direct teacher instructions (what to write on the board, what to elicit, when to allow Greek, how to pair pupils), with the answers printed at the point of use under "ANSWERS" / "SUGGESTED ANSWERS", the script of each listening printed where it is taught, background briefings and web addresses added, and cross-references to the differentiated "It's Your Choice" tasks. After the lesson notes of every unit come two gathered answer sections for that unit alone: a "Workbook" section keying the unit's Workbook activities, and "It's Your Choice" sections keying first the Student's Book's and then the Workbook's tiered appendix tasks. The ten units, with the grammar the guide actually teaches in each, are:

- **Unit 1 — I'm only human (pp. 1–20).** Tribal life contrasted with the modern world (the Amazon rain forests introduced as "the lungs of the world", p. 1); Present Simple and Present Continuous, state verbs, and the infinitive of purpose. The notes add a full extra reading text on schooling in ancient Sparta and Athens (p. 19) and a class website for Greek education in antiquity.
- **Unit 2 — Making a difference (pp. 21–36).** People who changed others' lives; the Past Simple (affirmative, negative, interrogative; regular and irregular verbs). The lead-in itself supplies the identifications the cover sketches need — Neil Armstrong, Alexander Graham Bell, Constantine Karamanlis, Leonardo da Vinci, Homer, Tomas Edison and Leonidas of Thermopylae (p. 21) — and Lesson 3 turns a class film survey into a questionnaire, a graph and a written report (p. 29).
- **Unit 3 — Technology in our lives (pp. 37–49).** Gadgets, shopping and making an advertisement; comparative and superlative adjectives, fact versus opinion. The notes include a complete shop dialogue, a computer-troubleshooting key (Activity D, p. 45), and the unit's Workbook answers on the same spread.
- **Unit 4 — Communication (pp. 50–73).** Body language, gestures, intonation and dreams; the modal verbs *will / won't, have to / don't have to, should / shouldn't*. Teacher-only extras include the lyrics of Selena's "Body Talk" printed in full to set the reading scene, with the reading's answer that communication is 55% body language, 38% tone of voice and 7% words (p. 58), and a listening script about a charity adventure-playground project, with a pointer to a differentiated-pedagogy activity on OXFAM (p. 62).
- **Unit 5 — Change and Experience (pp. 74–96).** The Present Perfect introduced and contrasted with the Past Simple. The centrepiece is a complete tapescript of a London-sights phone call (Greenwich, the Tower of London, HMS Belfast, Madame Tussaud's, the London Eye) with its ordering answers (p. 84); Lesson 3 is a mediation lesson, and the project notes print a Greek newspaper text about the filming of *El Greco* in Heraklion, Crete (p. 89).
- **Unit 6 — What a waste! (pp. 97–119).** Rubbish, pollution and eco-art; the zero and first conditional and *unless*. The listening notes script a radio programme on re-using household waste (glass jars, cardboard boxes, cereal packets, margarine tubs, p. 107), and the project pages add junk-art background and museum web addresses, including the National Museum of Contemporary Art in Athens (p. 115).
- **Unit 7 — Magnetism and the world we live in (pp. 120–145).** The most cross-curricular unit: Past Continuous against Past Simple, and *used to*. A full background page explains where magnetism sits in everyday life — VHS and cassette tape, floppy and hard disks, card magnetic strips, cathode-ray screens, loudspeakers and microphones (p. 121) — and the scientist biographies supplied for the listening include Planck and Einstein, the latter placed as a technical assistant examiner at the Swiss Patent Office in 1902 (p. 129). Static-electricity and balloon experiments are scripted for the classroom.
- **Unit 8 — Getting Around (pp. 146–167).** Transport; question tags and relative pronouns (*who, whose, which, where, when*). Extras include travel idioms glossed into Greek (p. 155), the full listening script of a trip on Shanghai's Maglev train — "it was a flight… we never left the ground" (pp. 155–156) — and a Culture Corner text on train-spotting, read out by the teacher to check the self-evaluation answers (p. 161).
- **Unit 9 — Keeping up appearances (pp. 168–192).** Dress, status and stereotypes; the second conditional and *I wish* + Past Simple. The museum listening is scripted in full — late Roman and Byzantine dress, the Chora Church (Kahriye-Cami) mosaic in Constantinople, and how hem length rose with status (p. 181) — and the writing strand is a "Teen worries" advice lesson.
- **Unit 10 — A Material World (pp. 193–214).** Materials and how products are made; the passive voice in Present and Past tenses. The notes script a whole classroom dialogue on silk — the legend of Justinian sending two Persian monks to China around 500 A.D., silkworm eggs hidden in hollow bamboo staffs, and a cocoon thread 600–900 metres long (p. 201) — and a world-products map key (Pennsylvania oil, Finland mobile phones, toys and games from China, athletic shoes from India, plastic bags from Indonesia, p. 213) before a mail-order complaint e-mail writing task.

**3. Answer keys.** There is no single key at the back of this book. Answers are given in three places, all verified above: inline in the lesson notes, task by task, including suggested and open answers; in the per-unit "Workbook" sections that follow each unit's self-evaluation (e.g. Unit 3's Workbook Activity 1a/1b keys, p. 45); and in the per-unit "It's Your Choice" sections keying the tiered appendix tasks of both the Student's Book and the Workbook (twenty such sections in all, two per unit). Self-evaluation keys are likewise printed unit by unit (e.g. Unit 8's, p. 161; Unit 7's, p. 140).

**4. Audioscripts.** There is no audioscript appendix. The script of each listening — and of the songs — is printed in the lesson notes at the point where it is taught, under varying headings ("Tapescript", "Listening script", "Recording script", "Listening Script"). They are complete enough to teach from without the CD in hand: for example the Unit 1 phone dialogue in which a girl is teased about a boy who "likes Olympiakos" and "sits behind you in the Geography lesson" (p. 7), the Unit 4 charity dialogue (p. 62), the Unit 5 London tapescript (p. 84) and the Unit 9 Byzantine-dress museum talk (p. 181).

**5. Revision-test keys (printed pp. 215–221).** The book closes with a "REVISION TESTS" section that is **keys only** — no test papers, no marks, no rating scales. It gives the answers, activity by activity (Activities 1–8), for the five pair-of-units revision tests that are themselves printed in the Workbook: Units 1 & 2 (pp. 215–216), Units 3 & 4 (pp. 216–217), Units 5 & 6 (pp. 217–218), Units 7 & 8 (pp. 218–219) and Units 9 & 10 (pp. 220–221). Open activities are handled with "Open answer(s)" plus a model (e.g. the Hobbit film example, p. 216), and the last key page works the passive both ways — "Oranges are grown in many parts of Greece", "Australia was discovered by Cook in 1770" (p. 221).

### Honest negatives

- **The Beginners stream is nowhere named in this book.** Unlike the Grade 7 Beginners Teacher's Book (which prints Αρχάριοι on its cover, title and imprint pages) and unlike this grade's Advanced Teacher's Book (which prints Προχωρημένοι on its cover), this file carries no stream word at all. The Beginners verdict above is an identification from author, design, ISBN sequence, unit sequence and the paired Workbook — solid, but it is an inference from the package, not a label the book gives itself, and it should be recorded that way.
- **No publication year is printed** anywhere on the cover, title or imprint pages; only the September 2012 production slugs and the PDF creation date date the file. Any catalogue year for this edition comes from outside the book.
- **The production slugs are misleading if read as evidence:** every page carries the slug "210046 AGGLIKA A GIMN KATHIGITI" — the production file name of the Grade 7 (Α΄ Γυμνασίου) Beginners Teacher's Book, code 21-0046 — even though the printed content is Β΄ Γυμνασίου throughout. The slugs also change date and file name at printed p. 1 (13/9/2012 "a meros" file for the front matter, 16/9/2012 file for the body), showing the PDF was assembled from two production files.
- **There are no test papers, rating scales or mark schemes in this book,** and no lesson schedules in teaching periods or aids lists of the kind the Grade 7 teacher's books print. The "Revision Tests" section (pp. 215–221) is a key only; the tests themselves are in the Workbook (checked there: the Units 1 & 2 Revision opens with the same Activity 1 the key answers, scored "___/5 points" per activity).
- **There is no gathered key or audioscript appendix:** Student's Book, Workbook and "It's Your Choice" answers and all listening scripts exist only interleaved, unit by unit, at the point of use, under inconsistent headings (Tapescript / Listening script / Recording script).
- **The audio itself cannot be verified from this PDF.** Scripts and one song's lyrics are printed, but no CD is included in the file, so nothing here proves what the recordings sound like or that every Student's Book listening has a script in the notes.
- **This guide cannot be quoted for the pupil texts themselves.** It paraphrases, answers and scripts the Student's Book tasks; the readings, dialogues and artwork the pupils see are in the Student's Book, not reproduced here, except where a script, a song lyric (p. 58) or a teacher background text (e.g. the Sparta / Athens reading, p. 19; the *El Greco* newspaper text, p. 89) is printed in full.
- **The book's own errors are preserved, not corrected, in this draft's quotations:** the Unit 10 header repeats a stray "Topic Making a difference" line (p. 193); the Introduction once calls the level "2nd Grade of High School" (p. x); the Revision Tests key prints "playright" for playwright (p. 215); and the Unit 6 header spells "Introdcuing" (p. 97).
- The web addresses the guide recommends are printed as of the book's production (2012-era addresses, e.g. the crystalinks.com Greek-education page on p. 19); this draft records that they are in the book and does not claim any of them is still live.
## Grade 8 (Beginners) — Workbook

### Identity block

- **Real title as printed:** *Think Teen!* — "2nd Grade of Junior High School / WORKBOOK". Β΄ Γυμνασίου is the second year of Greek junior high school, i.e. Grade 8. The Greek catalogue title is "Αγγλικά Β΄ Γυμνασίου – Επίπεδο Αρχαρίων – Τετράδιο Εργασιών" (English, 2nd Grade of Gymnasio – Beginners Level – Workbook).
- **Stream verdict:** BEGINNERS — confirmed, but by identification, not by a stream word on the page. Unlike the Grade 7 Beginners workbook, this file prints **no** Αρχάριοι (Beginners) word on its cover, title page or imprint pages (checked on the renders of PDF pp. 1–4 and in the text layer). The Beginners identification rests on four converging identifiers, all verified in this file: (1) book code **0-21-0110**, which is the manifest record 21-0110-02, "Agglika B-Gymnasiou-Arch_Tetradio-Ergasion" (Beginners workbook); (2) the in-file production slug on nearly every page, "21-0110_AGGLIKA_ARX_TETR_B GYM.indb" — ARX = Αρχαρίων; (3) the author, Patrick Mc Gavigan, who is also the author of the Beginners Student's Book, and (4) the unit list, which matches the Beginners Student's Book unit for unit (Unit 1 "I'm only human", Unit 7 "Magnetism and the world we live in", etc.). The Advanced workbook is a demonstrably different book: different authors, book code 0-21-0113, ISBN 978-960-06-2740-4, the word ΠΡΟΧΩΡΗΜΕΝΟΙ printed on its title page, and a completely different unit list ("People and Places", "Mysteries", …). This is **not** that book.
- **Author:** Patrick Mc Gavigan. Writing contractor named on the imprint title page (PDF p. 4): Μιχαήλ Λεβής Α.Ε. / Linguaphone, under the auspices of the Pedagogical Institute. Illustrator: Θεόδωρος Πιακής (Theodoros Piakis).
- **Publisher:** Ινστιτούτο Τεχνολογίας Υπολογιστών και Εκδόσεων «ΔΙΟΦΑΝΤΟΣ» (Institute of Computer Technology and Publications "Diophantos" — ITYE Diophantos), for the Υπουργείο Παιδείας, Έρευνας και Θρησκευμάτων (Ministry of Education, Research and Religious Affairs) / Ινστιτούτο Εκπαιδευτικής Πολιτικής (Institute of Educational Policy). Distributed via ebooks.edu.gr.
- **ISBN:** 978-960-06-2737-4 (printed on the back cover). **Book code:** 0-21-0110 (back cover barcode element: (01) 000000 0 21 0110 1). This matches the manifest record for this file (21-0110-02, Tetradio Ergasion, Beginners).
- **Edition / year:** No calendar year is printed on the cover, title or imprint pages. The imprint page (PDF p. 3) states the reissue was produced by ITYE Diophantos from a digital mockup funded under ESPA / "ΣΤΗΡΙΖΩ", with corrections approved by the Institute of Educational Policy. In-file production stamps read 1/9/13 on the main signatures and 1/21/16 on the front-matter signatures. No year is asserted beyond what is printed/stamped.
- **Extent:** 142 PDF pages; 134 printed pages plus unnumbered front matter and cover spreads. Printed pp. 1–98 are the ten units and their review/test blocks, printed pp. 99–129 are the closing section "It's Your Choice", printed p. 130 is the Irregular Verbs table, printed p. 131 is the sources page, printed pp. 132–133 are blank and printed p. 134 is the legal notice.
- **Page offset:** **printed page = PDF page − 7** throughout the numbered body and back matter (e.g. printed p. 1 = PDF p. 8; printed p. 88 = PDF p. 95; printed p. 130 = PDF p. 137; printed p. 131 = PDF p. 138). PDF p. 1 is the cover spread, PDF pp. 2–4 are the title and imprint pages, PDF p. 5 is blank, PDF pp. 6–7 are the Contents, and PDF p. 142 repeats the cover spread.
- **How the workbook is built (read this first):** The workbook mirrors the Beginners Student's Book unit for unit — the Contents (PDF pp. 6–7) reprint the Student's Book unit/grammar/vocabulary/skills map — but it is not a lesson-by-lesson copy: each unit is a single numbered run of activities (restarting at Activity 1) that constantly sends the learner back to the Student's Book ("Look at the reading text … in your student's book p. 4"; "Look at Task 3 in your Student's Book, p. 57"). After every two units comes a scored Revision + Test block (Activities in two alternating strands, each item marked out of points, each block ending "TOTAL ___/40 points"). The closing third of the book, "It's Your Choice" (printed pp. 99–129), is a second, optional pass over all ten units in which the same readings and tasks return in more heavily scaffolded, mostly multiple-choice form. There is no answer key anywhere in the book.

### Unit-by-unit summary (own words; printed page references)

**Unit 1 — I'm only human (printed pp. 1–9).** The opener is picture-only (p. 1). Reading (pp. 2–3) is five short face descriptions of tribal people — a Bushman in the Kalahari, an Aborigine chief with a boomerang, a Zulu girl, Kayapo men before a dance, a Bedouin — matched to photographs, then questioned on feelings and detail, with a story-line task built on the Student's Book page 5 pictures. The rest of the unit works the Present Simple / Present Continuous contrast and question forms: a guessing game about a classmate's clothes, home and likes (p. 4), matching peoples to dwellings, regions and transport (Eskimos, Maasai, Indians, city people, Bedouin; p. 5), an error-correction letter from a 14-year-old in an African village whose mistakes are the exercise (p. 6), a multiple-choice cloze on tribal life and a tribes-to-continents matching (p. 7), and vocabulary drawn from the Student's Book "Tribes of the Forest" text, with a title-writing extension (pp. 8–9).

**Unit 2 — Making a difference (printed pp. 10–19).** The Past Simple unit, built on famous lives. Vocabulary opens with sentence completion on the Athens Olympics opening ceremony and an earthquake-ruined city (p. 11); a History Quiz (p. 12) matches seven pictured figures (among them Alexander Graham Bell, Neil Armstrong, Thomas Edison) to their fame and dates, with an internet check and a write-your-own-quiz follow-up (p. 16). The main reading (pp. 13–14) is the story of Pocahontas (born 1595, father Powhatan) retold as a verb-gap puzzle that spells out where she lived, followed by a second life — Agnes, who fed the poor and founded a charity — whose italic phrases learners paraphrase. Later activities cover irregular verbs, expressions of attitude, a word-box hunt for six famous names (Mandela among them), a multiple-choice general-knowledge quiz (what Metaxas said to Mussolini; the first man on the moon), film/theatre question-writing under the headings "Helping humanity / History / Pop music and films" (p. 17), and a 30-word film or play review as the unit's writing (p. 21 is the test page; the review task itself sits in the review block).

**Review of Units One and Two (printed pp. 20–21).** A two-page scored Revision + Test: first-letter vocabulary completion recycling the rainforest/tribes material, sentence-half matching on the famous lives, suitable-question writing for given answers, and the short film/play review — closing at "TOTAL ___/40 points" (p. 21).

**Unit 3 — Technology in our lives (printed pp. 22–29).** Comparatives and superlatives, relative clauses, and a review of present and past tenses, all through gadgets. Learners sort relative-clause sentence halves (the place *where*…, the phone *which*…; p. 23), play a true/false guessing game about group members (p. 24), and pool information in threes from three gadget advertisements to complete a comparison chart — a €565 laptop with a two-year guarantee and 12% discount, a €97 CD player holding 10 CDs, and a third item (p. 25). A class competition finds "the most" (most brothers or sisters, etc.; p. 26), shop-dialogue questions and answers are matched (p. 27), synonyms and phrases with *as* are practised (p. 28), and the unit ends with odd-one-out vocabulary groups (credit card / cheque / cash / SMS; p. 29) and a persuasion/advertisement strand named in the Contents.

**Unit 4 — Communication (printed pp. 30–35).** Modals — *will/won't, have to/don't have to, should/shouldn't* — through body language and dreams. Definitions are matched to communication words (p. 30); a grammar activity builds modal responses to everyday situations, with a time-clause activity and look/stare/glare/gaze vocabulary (pp. 31–32). Learners say which body phrases fit given situations (p. 33, first half), complete a newspaper piece on facial expressions, and do the book's one activity actually labelled "Listening" (p. 33) — in fact a word-form gap-fill (disappointment/disappointed, boredom/bored…) inside a story about two sisters, Marina and Nicoletta. The unit closes with phrasal-verb sentence completion, dream-interpretation matching, and a wordsearch for ten articles of clothing (pp. 34–35).

**Review of Units Three and Four (printed pp. 36–39).** Scored Revision + Test: open opinion questions (best football team in Greece; laptop or PC; MP3 or iPod), correct-word choices on comparatives and superlatives, sentence-writing with product vocabulary (product, manufacturer, model, battery, price, advantages), and body-verb matching (shrug / fold / bite / point to throat, teeth, finger, arms). Total /40 (p. 39).

**Unit 5 — Change and Experience (printed pp. 40–48).** The Present Perfect unit, set around travel. It opens with a holiday note whose water-smudged words must be reconstructed ("Dear Smaragtha…", p. 40), headline-writing for news pictures (p. 41), dialogues matched to notices using travel verbs (check, close, miss, lose, book, buy) and a done/not-yet list for a traveller Anna — passport, camera battery, suitcase, flight time (pp. 42–43). "Have you ever…?" questions are written to given answers, and learners draft e-mail news from a done-something prompt (p. 43). The second half contrasts Present Perfect with Past Simple *with ago*: sentence-to-photograph matching (a painting of a man who "has cut off his ear", a gondola ride, the Champions League; p. 44), long choose-the-correct-form life stories (a 25-year marriage, the Eiffel Tower, the Hermitage and dancing with "Kossaks" [sic] in Gorky Park; p. 45), linking phrases, transformations of the "It's ages since I saw Mary" type, and a closing pair of tasks inferring from two travellers' suitcases which countries Erica and Gerhard have visited (pp. 46–48).

**Unit 6 — What a waste! (printed pp. 49–54).** First conditionals and *unless*, through rubbish and recycling. True/false prediction statements open the unit ("If we throw rubbish in the sea, fish will die"; p. 49); learners complete *unless* sentences, reuse ideas for sixteen household items, and work pollution vocabulary (bags, cans, appliances, scraps, products; p. 50). A wordsquare hides the environment set (pollution, landfill, plastic…; p. 51), an "How environmentally friendly are you?" questionnaire is scored against classmates (p. 52), five public signs are interpreted as conditionals (p. 53), and weather adjectives (strong/heavy/light/bitter) and eco-art vocabulary close the unit (p. 54).

**Review of Units Five and Six (printed pp. 55–58).** Scored Revision + Test: a letter to Nefeli with ten verbs to put in the correct form (a Limnos holiday, a Paris trip), letter phrases (as you know, that's all for now, in fact, as for), London sightseeing expressions, and correct-word choices (pollution/litter; unless/if; junk/pollution). Total /40 (p. 58).

**Unit 7 — Magnetism and the world we live in (printed pp. 59–66).** Past Continuous against Past Simple, plus *used to* — the heading on p. 59 spells it "Past Continious" [sic]. Learners circle/underline the two past forms in short texts (p. 59), match *used to* dialogue halves (Damien in Lamia; not knowing about magnetism; p. 60), answer-match seven questions on the "Aurora Boreallis" [sic] / Northern Lights and magnetic poles (p. 61), and write an e-mail about what happened and what they were doing at the time. Static electricity from combing hair leads a situations list (p. 62); word-building sorts verbs that take the noun suffix *-ment* (pp. 63, and again in the appendix section), and the unit ends with compass/fridge-magnet vocabulary choices, *way* expressions (find your way, no way, in a way…) and verb + preposition matching (pp. 64–66).

**Unit 8 — Getting Around (printed pp. 67–74).** Question tags and relative clauses (*who, which, where, when, how*) on transport. Sentence halves are matched (the boy *whose* father is a train conductor; irregular buses; p. 67), travel idioms are fitted to sketches and to questions about sideways biking, skateboards and waterbikes (p. 68), and learners explain the word *Maglev* from the unit's magnetism (magnetic levitation; p. 69). Collocations (public transport, backseat driver…), a transport-clue matching (pedals, tracks, wings, tow vehicle; p. 71) and two workbook readings follow: a road-law scenario — Henrietta doing 60 mph in a 40 mph zone, no seat belt, blue flashing lights — with questions on the law, what she should do and her punishment (p. 72), and a Fodor's-based walking tour of central Athens (Technopolis in Gazi, the Kerameikos Cemetery, Ermou, the Museum of Islamic Art) whose route is drawn on a map (p. 72). Printed p. 73 is a picture-only page, and road signs are interpreted on p. 74. Comparatives/superlatives are revised inside the unit, per the Contents.

**Review of Units Seven and Eight (printed pp. 75–78).** Scored Revision + Test: a past-tense cloze (Joanna meets Gerasimos), compound-noun matching (captain's log, magnetic fields, light bulbs), a one-preposition-fits-all set (cargo, intervals, energy), and magnet-verb choices (attract, sponsor, regard, report, repels, consist). Total /40 (p. 78).

**Unit 9 — 'Keeping up appearances' (printed pp. 79–87).** Second conditional and *I wish* + Past, through clothes, status and image. Before/after photographs are titled from the Student's Book sayings page, and learners write a 30-word article on what they would change about themselves if they had the money (pp. 79–80). Vocabulary is layered: nouns, collocations, character adjectives (aggressive, responsible, immature, confident, shy…), body parts and clothing idioms ("wear his heart on his sleeve", "talk through your hat", "be in someone's shoes"; pp. 80–82). Grammar completes second-conditional sentence pairs (no clothes for Irene's party; a brother too young for a nose ring; p. 83) and revises the year's tenses, with true/false fashion-history statements (the zip invented in 1893; Levi Strauss; p. 84). Workbook-only highlights: a **mediation** task — summarise in English, as briefly as possible, a Greek leaflet on silk in Byzantium (a luxury sold by weight, first imported from China, then, in 553 under Justinian I, produced after monks brought the secret; p. 85) — and a reading on the dangers of copying models, built around a 14-year-old aspiring Brazilian model who died of anorexia nervosa, turned into a short article (p. 86). A shop dialogue (T-shirt, jeans, changing room, sizes) closes the unit (p. 87).

**Unit 10 — A Material World (printed pp. 88–94).** The passive unit. Learners locate pictured Greek products on a map of Greece (p. 88) and complete a "History of Caoutchouc" cloze — natural rubber, from the Indian word "cahuchu", "weeping wood", renamed for rubbing out pencil marks (p. 88). Materials vocabulary follows (a nine-word hidden grid: spices, porcelain, rubber, string…; countries producing aluminium, wood, rubber, wool; p. 89), then passive forms proper: *made of / made from / used to / used for / produced by* statements about products (p. 90), invention facts (a first fridge "invented by Einstein"; mobile phones made from hemp; p. 91), a what-can-be-dyed/woven/baked table (p. 92), a Stonehenge text with missing sentences to insert — Stonehenge as a "Neolithic Lourdes" where the sick came to be cured, compared to the Oracle at Delphi (p. 93) — and an inventions table to complete (1840, Kirkpatrick Macmillan; the camera, Joseph Niepce; Karl Benz; pp. 93–94).

**Review of Units Nine and Ten (printed pp. 95–98).** Scored Revision + Test: *made of/from, produced in, used to* preposition completion, Unit 10 collocations (the first steam engine, Hero of Alexandria, first century AD; silk-making introduced by Justinian), word matching (plain skirt, spiked hair, round-neck shirt) and clothing idioms in sentences ("dressed to kill", "pull up your socks", "a load of rubbish"). Total /40 (p. 98).

**Appendix — "It's Your Choice" (printed pp. 99–129).** Thirty-one pages, one block per unit (U1 pp. 99–100; U2 pp. 101–105; U3 pp. 106–108; U4 pp. 109–110; U5 pp. 111–114; U6 pp. 115–116; U7 pp. 117–119; U8 pp. 120–122; U9 pp. 123–126; U10 pp. 127–129). It is a second pass, not new teaching: the main units' own texts and tasks return in choice form — the Bushman text as a five-gap multiple-choice cloze (p. 99), the Pocahontas story as a tense-gap fill (p. 103, where her name is spelled "Pochahontas" [sic] in the instruction line), the gadget quiz and shop dialogues reordered (pp. 107–108), Greek body idioms translated (p. 109: e.g. "Σφίγγω τα δόντια" to be rendered in English), the Kalamata letter with missing sentences to place (p. 113), the Maglev train identified from a description (p. 122), Greek-glossed travel definitions (p. 123), the second-conditional tasks repeated almost verbatim (p. 126), and the Caoutchouc history again as a gap-fill, plus *-port* word family work (deport, airport, seaport, exports, imports, passport; pp. 127–129). Because the tasks repeat, this section doubles as the book's only built-in self-check material — but it still carries no printed answers.

**Back matter (printed pp. 130–134).** Printed p. 130 is a one-page **Irregular Verbs** table in two column pairs (Infinitive / Past Simple / Past Participle): *be – was/were – been*, *begin – began – begun*, running at least to *hide – hid – hidden* in the second column pair. Printed p. 131, "SOURCES AND RELEVANT INTERNET SITES", lists only four sources in total (see Honest negatives). Printed pp. 132–133 are blank; printed p. 134 is the standard legal/distribution notice stating the book is printed by ITYE–Diophantos under Law 3966/2011 and distributed free to public schools. PDF p. 142 repeats the cover spread.

**Grammar spine as it arrives (summary):** Present Simple vs Present Continuous and infinitive of purpose (U1) → Past Simple, all question forms (U2) → comparatives/superlatives, relative clauses, present/past review (U3) → modals: *will/won't, have to, should* (U4) → Present Perfect vs Past Simple with *ago* (U5) → first conditional and *unless* (U6) → Past Continuous vs Past Simple, *used to*, tense/modal review (U7) → question tags, relative clauses, comparative revision (U8) → second conditional, *I wish* + Past, tense revision (U9) → passive voice in three passes: *made of / used for*, question form, with agent (U10) — with a scored Revision + Test after every second unit and a full choice-format rerun in "It's Your Choice".

### Honest negatives

- **The Beginners stream word is not printed in this book.** Αρχάριοι appears nowhere on the cover, spine, title or imprint pages of this file (and Προχωρημένοι nowhere either); the stream is proven by book code, production slug, author and unit list, as set out in the identity block. A reader holding only this workbook could not tell its stream from its own pages' wording alone.
- **No publication year is printed** on the cover, title page or imprint pages; only the reissue note and in-file production dates (2013 front/back signatures, 2016 front matter) are present. Any catalogue year for this book comes from outside the book itself.
- **There is no answer key.** The five Revision + Test blocks are scored (each totalling /40) and "It's Your Choice" is multiple-choice, but no answers, mark scheme or self-assessment checklist are printed anywhere in the 142 PDF pages.
- **There is effectively no listening strand in the workbook itself:** despite the Contents listing listening skills (it reprints the Student's Book map), only one activity is labelled "Listening" (printed p. 33) and it is a written word-form gap-fill with no script or audio reference in the book. Speaking is limited to pair games and guessing activities (e.g. pp. 4, 24, 68).
- **The workbook cannot be used alone:** tasks throughout depend on the Student's Book for their input texts and pictures (e.g. printed pp. 2, 8, 48, 79, 107 explicitly cite Student's Book pages), so several workbook activities are unanswerable from this book by itself.
- **Internal inconsistency as printed:** the Bushman lives in the "Kalahari desert" in the main reading (printed p. 2) but in the "southern Sahara desert" in the "It's Your Choice" version of the same text (printed p. 99). Both are reproduced here as found, not reconciled.
- **Print errors stand as printed** and are not silently corrected above: "Past Continious" (printed p. 59), "Aurora Boreallis" (printed p. 61), "Pochahontas" in the appendix instruction line (printed p. 103, against "Pocahontas" in the main unit), "Colloseum" and "Kossaks" (printed p. 45). The errors inside the printed p. 6 letter are deliberate — correcting them is the exercise.
- **The sources page is minimal:** printed p. 131 credits only four texts out of the whole book; the many other readings (tribal descriptions, Agnes, gadget advertisements, the Stonehenge-adjacent material, the anorexia article's workbook text) carry no source there beyond those four entries.
- **Dated content is part of the book as printed:** gadget prices and offers (€565 laptop, €97 CD player, walkman/iPod references, printed pp. 23–29), a 2007 blog as the source of the anorexia reading (printed p. 131), and the claim in a workbook text that a first fridge was invented by Einstein (printed p. 91, presented as a fact-completion item). These reflect the book's era, not the present day.
- **A few pages are blank or picture-only:** PDF p. 5 and printed pp. 132–133 are blank, and printed p. 73 carries pictures and its page number only; their neighbours were used to describe the surrounding activities.
## Grade 8 — Glossaries (Advanced and Beginners)

Two separate printable glossaries, one for each Grade 8 *Think Teen!* stream. Both are "Digital School" (Ψηφιακό Σχολείο) productions of the Greek Ministry, issued as printable-form (Εκτυπώσιμη Μορφή) companions, and both were read whole for this section. They share an identical credits page and production team but differ sharply in size, structure and — most visibly — in whether they give Greek equivalents.

### Identity block — Advanced glossary

- **Real title as printed (cover, PDF p. 1, an image page read from the render):** ΑΓΓΛΙΚΑ — «Β΄ Γυμνασίου - Προχωρημένοι / Γλωσσάρι», with the English title "Think Teen 2nd Grade - Advanced / Glossary". The cover carries the Hellenic Republic / Ministry header, the Ψηφιακό Σχολείο (Digital School) banner, a large "Β ΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΟΥ" panel, and a thumbnail of the Advanced Student's Book (the purple, jigsaw-photo cover).
- **Stream verdict:** ADVANCED — confirmed from this file itself. Unlike the Beginners Student's Book, whose cover prints no stream word, this glossary prints its stream in both languages on its own cover (Προχωρημένοι / Advanced). Its contents also match the Advanced course: one continuous lesson numbering, Lessons 1–24, plus a Workbook part (see below).
- **Producer / publisher:** Developed inside the ministry project «Ψηφιακή Εκπαιδευτική Πλατφόρμα, Διαδραστικά Βιβλία και Αποθετήριο Μαθησιακών Αντικειμένων» (Digital Educational Platform, Interactive Books and Learning-Object Repository), of the Operational Programme "Education and Lifelong Learning" of the Ministry of Education and Religions (ΥΠΑΙΘ), co-funded by the European Union (European Social Fund) and the Greek state under ESPA, and implemented by the Institute of Computer Technology and Publications «Diophantos» (ITYE). Distributed via ebooks.edu.gr.
- **Credits (PDF p. 2):** An eleven-person development team (Ομάδα ανάπτυξης), almost all listed as English teachers — Eleni Argyriou, Katelis Vigklas, Georgia Gyftoula, Katerina Makri (e-learning specialist), Susan Moutsouroufi, Antigoni Bratsoli, Sofia Mysirlaki (computing teacher), Katerina Nikolaki, Chrysanthi Sotiriou, Mary Frentzou, Vasilis Chartzoulakis. Digitisation by Ioannis Bitros; coordinator Vasiliki Mitsikopoulou, Associate Professor at ΕΚΠΑ (the University of Athens). These are the glossary's compilers; the *Think Teen!* Student's Book authors are not named anywhere in this file.
- **Version / year as printed:** «Έκδοση/Ημερομηνία 1.0 / Απρίλιος 2013» — Version 1.0, April 2013 (PDF p. 2). Licence printed on the same page: Creative Commons 3.0 / CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. No other year is printed in the file.
- **ISBN / book code:** None. No ISBN and no book code are printed anywhere in this glossary — not on the cover (checked on the render) and not in the credits. The companion Advanced Student's Book is code 0-21-0112 (with a Set ISBN), but those identifiers come from the Student's Book, not from this file.
- **Extent:** 135 PDF pages: PDF p. 1 cover, PDF p. 2 credits/licence page, PDF pp. 3–135 glossary tables (133 content pages).
- **Page offset:** **None — there are no printed folios.** No page number appears on any page (headers carry only the section heading, e.g. "Workbook - Unit 8 – Lesson 24"). All references in this section are therefore to PDF pages directly.

### Identity block — Beginners glossary

- **Real title as printed (cover, PDF p. 1, an image page read from the render):** ΑΓΓΛΙΚΑ — «Β΄ Γυμνασίου - Αρχάριοι / Γλωσσάρι», with the English title "Think Teen 2nd Grade - Beginners / Glossary". Same Digital School wrapper as the Advanced twin; the thumbnail book cover is the Beginners Student's Book (the orange Rubik's-cube cover), on which the name "Patrick McGavigan" is legible in small print.
- **Stream verdict:** BEGINNERS — confirmed from this file itself. The glossary cover prints the stream word the Beginners Student's Book itself omits (Αρχάριοι / Beginners), and the contents match the Beginners course exactly in shape: ten units whose lessons restart at 1–3 inside each unit — the numbering scheme of Patrick McGavigan's single-author Beginners book (companion Student's Book code 0-21-0206, again from the Student's Book, not printed here).
- **Producer / publisher:** The same ministry Digital School project, ESPA/EU co-funding and ITYE Diophantos implementation as the Advanced glossary (identical wording, PDF p. 2). Distributed via ebooks.edu.gr.
- **Credits (PDF p. 2):** The credits page is identical to the Advanced glossary's — the same eleven-person development team, the same digitisation credit (Ioannis Bitros) and the same coordinator (Vasiliki Mitsikopoulou, ΕΚΠΑ). One production team evidently made the whole glossary series. The Beginners book's author, Patrick McGavigan, is not named in the credits; his name reaches this file only through the thumbnail cover image on PDF p. 1.

- **ISBN / book code:** None printed anywhere in the file (cover checked on the render; credits page checked in the text layer).
- **Extent:** 79 PDF pages: PDF p. 1 cover, PDF p. 2 credits/licence page, PDF pp. 3–79 glossary tables (77 content pages).
- **Page offset:** **None — there are no printed folios**, as in the Advanced file. All references are to PDF pages directly.

### How the two glossaries are organised (own words)

Each book is one long set of tables in course order. There is no single A–Z list, no contents page and no index: the reader finds a word by going to the unit and lesson where the course book teaches it. Inside each lesson section the headwords run alphabetically, and every section restarts its own alphabet. The table has the same six columns in both books: **Word** (the headword in bold, followed by a part-of-speech tag in brackets — (n), (v), (adj), (adv), (phr) and a few others such as (prep), (conj), (id) for idiom), **Definition** (a short definition in simple English), **Example** (one invented example sentence), **Synonym**, **Antonym** and **Word Family** (derived forms). Rows alternate shaded and unshaded. Many Synonym / Antonym / Word Family cells are simply left blank — the columns promise more than most rows deliver. There is **no phonetic transcription anywhere in either book**, and no entry gives a page reference back into the Student's Book: the lesson heading is the only locator.

The **Advanced glossary** follows its Student's Book's continuous numbering and then keeps going. Its first part (PDF pp. 3–79) covers the Student's Book: Units 1–8, Lessons 1–24, with extra **Introduction** sections for Units 1, 2, 5, 7 and 8 and **Self Assessment** sections for Units 1, 2, 6, 7 and 8. Its second part (PDF pp. 80–135) is a complete second glossary for the **Workbook**, headed "Workbook - Unit N – Lesson M", running through the workbook's Lessons 1–24 in the same table format. Definitions are in English only: a search of the whole content text finds **no Greek at all** in this book. Counting part-of-speech-tagged bold headwords gives about 1,290 entries for the Student's Book part and about 900 for the Workbook part — **approximately 2,200 entries in total** (approximate: a machine count of tagged headwords, cross-checked against table-row counts; a handful of entries are untagged or wrap oddly).

The **Beginners glossary** covers its Student's Book only — there is no Workbook part and no Self Assessment section. It runs Units 1–10, each with Lessons 1–3 numbered inside the unit, plus an **Introduction** section for Unit 5 and Unit 6 only. Its one big kindness to the learner is Greek: the Definition column appends a Greek equivalent, in Greek script, at the end of most English definitions (short samples: *amaze* — συναρπάζω; *government* — κυβέρνηση; *tool* — εργαλείο). The Greek is not a separate column and not every entry has it, but most do. The same count gives **approximately 1,100 entries in total** (approximate, same method as above) — about half the Advanced book's haul, matching the Beginners course's smaller vocabulary load.

**Differences between the two, in short:** (1) Greek equivalents — present for most entries in Beginners, entirely absent in Advanced. (2) Coverage — Advanced glosses the Workbook as well as the Student's Book; Beginners glosses the Student's Book only. (3) Numbering — Advanced uses the continuous Lessons 1–24 of its course; Beginners restarts at Lesson 1–3 in each of its ten units. (4) Extra sections — Advanced adds unit Introductions and Self Assessment word sets; Beginners has Introductions for two units only and nothing else. (5) Size — about 2,200 entries on 133 content pages against about 1,100 on 77. What is identical: the publisher, the credits page, the version (1.0, April 2013), the licence, the six-column table, the alphabetical-within-lesson order, and the absence of folios, phonetics and cross-references.

Two filing cautions from the read. First, the Advanced glossary's own unit grouping for the middle lessons does **not** match its Student's Book: the glossary heads Lesson 9 as "Unit 4 – Lesson 9" (PDF pp. 34–37), leaving its Unit 3 with Lessons 7–8 only, whereas the Student's Book places Lesson 9 inside Unit 3; the Workbook part shows the same shift (Lesson 7 under Workbook Unit 2, Lessons 8–9 under Workbook Unit 3). Anyone citing by the glossary's headings should quote the heading as printed, not "correct" it. Second, words are re-entered when they recur: the Advanced book enters *globe* in both the Unit 1 Introduction (PDF p. 3) and the Unit 7 Introduction (PDF p. 62), and the Beginners book gives *plant* twice on one page as separate verb and noun entries — so entry counts count entries, not unique words.

### Honest negatives

- **Neither glossary prints an ISBN or a book code anywhere.** The link to the companion Student's Books (Advanced code 0-21-0112; Beginners code 0-21-0206) rests on the printed cover titles, the thumbnail covers and the ministry catalogue titles, not on any identifier inside the glossary files.
- **Neither glossary names the author(s) of the course book it serves.** The Advanced Student's Book's four authors appear nowhere in its glossary; the Beginners author, Patrick McGavigan, appears only as small print on the thumbnail cover image. The only people credited are the glossaries' own development team.
- **No printed folios, no contents, no index, no phonetics, no cross-references** in either book: a learner cannot look a word up alphabetically across the whole course, cannot hear or read how it sounds, and is never pointed to the page of the Student's Book where the word is taught — only to its lesson.
- **Entry counts are approximate**, produced by counting part-of-speech-tagged bold headwords and cross-checking against table rows (Advanced ≈ 2,200: ≈ 1,290 Student's Book + ≈ 900 Workbook; Beginners ≈ 1,100). They count entries, not unique words — recurring words are entered again, and a word used as two parts of speech gets two entries.
- **The Greek difference cuts both ways:** the Beginners book's Greek equivalents stop at the definition — examples, synonyms, antonyms and word-family items are never translated — and a minority of Beginners entries carry no Greek at all; the Advanced book gives no Greek support of any kind in its content pages.
- **Small production flaws survive in both files:** e.g. in the Beginners book the *can (n)* row (PDF p. 47) carries a stray "cheaply" in its Word Family column (it belongs to *cheap* below), and in the Advanced book the *phonograph (n)* Word Family cell (PDF p. 135) reads "photography, phonographic photographert" (sic). Definitions and examples occasionally show the same haste. None of this changes what the books are, but the tables are not error-free.
- **The example sentences are generic dictionary-style sentences written for the glossary**, not extracts from *Think Teen!* — with rare exceptions (the Eldredge quotation in the Advanced book) they do not quote the course books, so the glossaries evidence the course's vocabulary list, not its texts.

### Identity block

(No year is asserted beyond what is printed/stamped.)
- **Production-stem note:** the in-file signature stamps name the production file "21-0165", not the book's own code 21-0208. The cover/back-cover code 0-21-0208 governs — it matches the ministry source file (21-0208-01) in the library record — and 21-0165 is recorded here only as an internal production-stem discrepancy inside the PDF.
- **Extent:** 174 PDF pages; printed pages 1–166 plus unnumbered front matter and covers.
- **Page offset:** **printed page = PDF page − 7** throughout the numbered body and appendices (e.g. printed p. 1 = PDF p. 8; printed p. 63 = PDF p. 70; printed p. 160 = PDF p. 167). PDF p. 1 is the front cover; PDF pp. 2–4 are title/imprint pages; PDF p. 5 is blank; PDF pp. 6–7 are the Contents; PDF pp. 171–172 (printed pp. 164–165 positions) are blank; PDF p. 173 is the legal/distribution notice at the printed p. 166 position; PDF p. 174 is the back cover.
- **Structure:** 10 units, 30 lessons (three per unit), each unit closing with a two-page Self-evaluation scored out of 20 points plus a can-do checklist. Back matter is only two appendices: Appendix 1 "It's your choice" (extra tasks and split/partner texts, printed pp. 121–159) and Appendix 2 Maps (pp. 160–163). There is **no** Grammar Reference, word list or irregular-verb appendix in this book.

### Unit-by-unit summary (own words; printed page references)

**Unit 1 — What a Wonderful World! (printed pp. 1–12).** A consolidation unit on holidays and famous places. *Lesson 1, "The Right Holiday" (p. 2):* learners rank pictured places (a palace with guards, a flooding-threatened old city, a statue under repair, waterfalls), match traveller statements to them, then jigsaw-match six holiday-seekers' accounts — quiet fishing village near Chania, mountaineering ambitions, weather as the deciding factor — to six destination descriptions; phrases with *time* and binomial phrases with *and* (*peace and quiet, safe and sound, sick and tired*) are harvested from those accounts, and Present/Past Simple-and-Continuous forms are contrasted inside them rather than presented fresh. *Lesson 2, "The Seven Wonders" (p. 6):* the unit song is the famous "wonderful world" lyric with gaps (trees of green, red roses, skies of blue), then a listening lecture works through the seven ancient wonders — Great Pyramid at Giza, Colossus of Rhodes, Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, Hanging Gardens of Babylon, Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, Lighthouse of Alexandria, Statue of Zeus at Olympia — with a date/reason table to complete; a class survey on what makes a place exciting feeds a percentage report. *Lesson 3, "A Postcard Home" (p. 10):* a model postcard from Eva (sun, an old temple, George's fall and hospital visit, a taverna meal) teaches attitude adjectives and linking words (*because, as, although, but, so*); learners complete and then write their own postcard. Self-evaluation pp. 11–12.

**Unit 2 — Teen Idols (printed pp. 13–24).** Fame, opened by a short text on Roman gladiators as the idols of their day. *Lesson 1, "So, you want to be famous?" (p. 14):* star facts and a quiz (birth dates, Eurovision, a poor young man on a famous ship) carry the book's central contrast, Past Simple against Present Perfect, including the *since* + Past Simple pattern and paraphrase work ("saying things in another way"); a statement attributed to the *Titanic* actor ("first film in 1990 at 16", stepfather's advice) has to be identified and fact-checked online. *Lesson 2 (p. 18):* listening for feelings and attitude (adjectives such as *sociable, shy, confident, ambitious*), an interview with a fictional idol, Willie Robinson, to complete from audio, a fact-file planner modelled on Daniel Radcliffe (birth date, height, pets, favourite food as categories to match), a "Have you ever…?" star-interview role-play and a class popularity survey. *Lesson 3, "Produce your show" (p. 22):* a three-stage project — pitch a school-show production team, audition talent as producers, then edit a "Fame and Fortune" school-newspaper sheet; the writing strand (p. 21) is a biography with circle-the-correct-tense choices and an opinion letter on TV talent shows organised by linking phrases. Self-evaluation pp. 23–24.

**Unit 3 — Thrills and Spills! (printed pp. 25–36).** Theme parks as applied physics. *Lesson 1, "Newton's Laws" (p. 26):* ride types are matched to feelings (scared to death, sick, excited), then four short "laws of motion" texts — action/reaction, inertia, force/mass/acceleration, plus a joke fourth "law" about student effort that learners must spot as not Newton's — are matched to plain-English versions and diagrams and applied to roller-coaster design; park leaflets follow (Southport's Pleasureland and its Traumatizer coaster, a Sea Life centre whose octopus has three hearts, a Hello Fun Park), read as a jigsaw against shorter versions in Appendix 1. *Lesson 2, "The bravest student" (p. 30):* a character quiz, compound nouns built from word pairs, and the gerund system — verbs and expressions of liking, hating and avoiding followed by *-ing* (*can't help, avoid, fancy, mind, enjoy*) — drawn out of a dialogue about the Big Wheel and the Vertical Drop; a funfair map practises suggestions (*How about…? / Why don't we…?*). *Lesson 3, "Amusement Park" (p. 34):* present-tense revision through a group project to design, price, present and vote on a new theme park. Self-evaluation pp. 35–36.

**Unit 4 — Click On-Line! (printed pp. 37–48).** Gadgets, internet and media, built around duration-up-to-now. *Lesson 1, "Gadgets" (p. 38):* telephone-history pictures to order, seven short dialogues on internet use, and a journalist's article on internet use in Ireland whose statistics (roughly 30% using the web for information, 35% for e-mail, about 20% for chat rooms, 5% for e-banking and commerce, school-age access tripled in twelve months) must be matched to the right pie chart; the *since* (point of time) / *for* (period) rule is drawn from the article. *Lesson 2, "Speak your mind" (p. 42):* attitude expressions, then the formal Present Perfect Simple vs Continuous contrast (finished result against activity still in progress, p. 43), a "what have they been doing?" evidence game, a Bulgarian media-habits bar chart, and instruction-writing: an aunt who cannot send e-mail is answered by re-sequencing a software leaflet's setup steps in simple language. *Lesson 3, "Media habits" (p. 46):* a research project — interview 100 people in groups, feed results into a spreadsheet, present a pie chart on how young people spend Saturday evenings. The Contents credits this lesson with Comparatives, but no comparative presentation appears in its pages (see Honest negatives). Self-evaluation pp. 47–48.

**Unit 5 — The Myths We Live By (printed pp. 49–60).** The conditional unit. *Lesson 1, "An ancient fortune teller" (p. 50):* myth figures who embody a condition (the Sphinx's riddle, Medusa's gaze, Pandora's box, Icarus's wings, the Delphic oracle) introduce the **1st Conditional** with its rule built by the learners (Present Simple in the *if*-clause, *will* in the main clause, for possible situations); the same characters then supply **2nd Conditional** sentences to analyse (p. 52), and full short readings follow on Thor and his goats Gap Tooth and Tooth Grinder, Perseus sent for Medusa's head to free his mother Danae, and Midas, whose golden touch turns even food, drink and his own daughter to gold — greed as the moral; gods of many civilisations (Geb, Lono, Cybele, Citlalicue and others) widen the frame. *Lesson 2, "If I were…" (p. 54):* word formation (*-ic, -ment*, negative prefixes *im-/in-*), prepositional phrases (*from hand to mouth, from bad to worse*), a radio interview about heroes, six village problems to solve in the 2nd Conditional, school-problem advice ("If I were you, I would…"), and a fact-or-myth writing lead-in: Kapodistrias, first Greek head of state, murdered at Nafplion, said to have guarded potato sacks so people would steal and plant them. *Lesson 3, "An attractive tourist destination" (p. 58):* both conditionals extended through a tourism leaflet for Epidaurus (theatre, sanctuary of Asclepius, routes via the Corinth Canal, Nafplion and ferries from Piraeus) and a group leaflet competition for the learners' own area. Self-evaluation pp. 59–60.

**Unit 6 — Keeping Traditions and Customs Alive! (printed pp. 61–72).** Festivals of Britain and the wider world. *Lesson 1, "Halloween and St. Valentine's Day" (p. 62):* a split reading — half the pair reads the Halloween text in the lesson (31 October, All Hallows Eve, Celtic spirits, dressing up, pumpkins, trick or treat), the other half reads the St Valentine text in Appendix 1 (p. 144) and they teach each other; set phrases with *on*, noun formation, and the book's verb-syntax presentation (p. 65): verbs sorted by pattern — no object, object, object + *to*-infinitive, two objects, *to*-infinitive alone — with *believe/think/feel + that* in the Contents row. *Lesson 2, "The 5th of November" (p. 66):* a Guy Fawkes text deliberately seeded with **five factual errors** (the date given as 15 November, the year 1705, King Henry I, Parliament placed in Manchester, twenty-five days of torture) that learners must catch against the recording; the correct frame — James, the Gunpowder Plot, bonfires, effigies, Parkin cake, "a penny for the Guy" — comes through the same text's uncorrupted parts. *Lesson 3, "World celebrations" (p. 70):* teenagers worldwide comment on Christmas (materialism against family and food), and a project surveys what Easter means locally and writes it up as "The Meaning of Easter in Modern Greece". Question forms are revised. Self-evaluation pp. 71–72.

**Unit 7 — Shades of Meaning! (printed pp. 73–84).** Colour in clothes, homes, food and feeling. *Lesson 1, "Colours in our lives!" (p. 74):* definitions of colour to judge, Wordsworth's rainbow poem (1802) as a feelings text, a reading on colour in clothes and environment (colour as a signal of mood, wealth, status and belonging), and three short texts — kitchens and energy colours, food colourants that make butter yellower and peas greener than nature, and make-up already elaborate in Egypt around 3000 BC; phrases with *go*. *Lesson 2, "Colour's my world!" (p. 78):* the modal presentation is deliberately narrow — *must, should, shouldn't, might, could* + bare infinitive, sorted by job (advice, strong obligation, possibility) and practised entirely on what colours to wear for occasions from a job interview to a baptism; colour idioms follow. *Lesson 3, "Visualising colour" (p. 82):* a guided visualisation walk, a colour-preference personality test, a project to redesign the classroom's colours for the headmaster, and a culture corner on Trooping the Colour and the "greenback". Self-evaluation pp. 83–84.

**Unit 8 — Food for Thought! (printed pp. 85–96).** Food, culture and the passive. *Lesson 1, "Food, places, cultures!" (p. 86):* what counts as food is cultural (alligator, kangaroo, horse, turtle and dog meat acceptable somewhere, taboo elsewhere; Greek examples named in Greek), then a process text on olive oil — grinding to paste, pressing on stacked disks, water run down the sides — whose passive sentences prepare the grammar, and which praises the oil's monounsaturated fat and lower heart-disease risk. *Lesson 2, "One man's meat…" (p. 90):* the **Passive Voice is formed here, and only here in the Gymnasio single-stream book**: a riddle text about a product first found in the Andes and called a "ground apple" in France (the potato) is mined for passive equivalents of active statements, the formation rule is completed (form of *be* + past participle; the doer need not be named), Greek and English passives are compared, a timeline listening ties foods to historical moments, and food idioms (*food for thought, spill the beans, as cool as a cucumber*) and restaurant-review writing (a London French restaurant review checked against its details for planted inaccuracies) close the lesson. *Lesson 3, "Food Pyramid" (p. 94):* tense review through listening on anorexia and bulimia, food "stressors and supporters", and a Mediterranean-diet menu project for a visiting London athlete friend. Self-evaluation pp. 95–96.

**Unit 9 — What's the Weather Like? (printed pp. 97–108).** Energy and environment — the reported-speech unit, though it arrives by stealth. *Lesson 1, "Energy around us!" (p. 98):* energy sources in a picture (solar, wind, steam, gas, biomass and others) with advantages and disadvantages, then three children's accounts in an international project — Jiang An Li in Beijing (coal-fired electricity, bicycles against polluted streets, hydro-power from the Three Gorges dam on the Yangtze), Brynja in Iceland (four hours of winter daylight, water heated underground by lava, outdoor swimming, electric buses), and Lalita in India (horse cart, wood fire, kerosene lamp, Bombay nearly 1,000 km away). The accounts are quietly full of reporting verbs — *mum says that…, she said that the government should…, he told me that…, my mum asked me if…, Dad has told us that one day he would…* — but no grammar box names the pattern in this lesson. *Lesson 2, "Alternative sources of energy!" (p. 102):* a science teacher's talk is completed in reported form ("She said that…"), and only here (p. 103) is the rule stated: report a past statement and the verb moves **one tense back** — worked on a conditional ("If we cover 1% of the Sahara Desert with solar panels, we can generate enough electricity for the whole world!" → *she said that if we covered… we could generate…*) and on *will → would* for oil running out; a mediation task reports a 2008 speech by the President of the Hellenic Republic on the Greek forest fires to an international green group. Greenhouse-gas ideas, appliance electricity costs, CFCs, forms of lighting and the Kyoto/Bali logos fill the rest. *Lesson 3, "Electricity bills" (p. 106):* a poster project built on a real household bill — unit name, cost per unit, class-average bill, who uses what, and how to cut it. Contents also lists comparison/modals/passive revision for this lesson. Self-evaluation pp. 107–108.

**Unit 10 — Natural Phenomena (printed pp. 109–120).** Disasters, and the book's grammatical ceiling. *Lesson 1, "Such things happen all the time!" (p. 110):* **perfect modals** — *must have / can't have / might have / could have / should have* + past participle (and *must have been* + *-ing* for continuous past) — for deduction, probability and criticism about the past, formed on p. 111 and immediately used on two readings: a short Atlantis text ("Around 350 BC Plato described Atlantis…") whose city of rings, tunnels and gold statues vanished in a day and a night, and "An Unwelcome Neighbour", on Vesuvius waking at noon on 24 August AD 79 and killing 2,000 people who *can't have* prepared and *should have* been evacuated; captioned photographs (the 26/12/04 Indonesian tsunami, New Orleans before Katrina on 28 August 2005, the Bromo crater) are commented on in the same forms. *Lesson 2, "Tragedies!" (p. 114):* UNESCO-sourced warning-sign texts for hurricanes, tsunamis (the sea drawing back before the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004) and earthquakes; disaster stress — its signs, causes and remedies, applied to the Peloponnese fires of summer 2007; a listening shipwreck reconstructed from rescue workers' comments, a report written from it plus a Greek newspaper extract about pollution in the Santorini caldera, and a Titanic survivor interview role-play. *Lesson 3, "Catastrophes" (p. 118):* Aesop's animal stereotypes completed as similes (*as busy as a bee, as blind as a bat, as stubborn as a mule*), stereotyping of people discussed, and a closing project reporting three Greek natural disasters — causes, what *should have* been done, precautions now in place, damage and cost. Self-evaluation pp. 119–120.

**Appendices (printed pp. 121–166).** Appendix 1, "It's your choice" (pp. 121–159): one section per unit of extra and partner-split material — the missing holiday accounts for Unit 1, Asian teen idols for Unit 2, roller-coaster energy texts and theme-park readings for Unit 3, Greek mobile-phone use for Unit 4, Delphi and Finn McCool material and an "If I had a hammer" song task for Unit 5, the partner St Valentine text and wedding/Halloween texts for Unit 6, colour-in-history texts for Unit 7, food games and a sugar text for Unit 8, the Unit 9 children's energy accounts repeated in full, and shortened Atlantis/Vesuvius texts for Unit 10. Appendix 2, Maps (pp. 160–163): World Map (p. 160), an uncaptioned map (p. 161), England (p. 162) and Europe (p. 163). Printed pp. 164–165 are blank; p. 166 is the legal notice (books printed by ITYE–Diophantos under Law 3966/2011 and distributed free to public schools).

**Grammar spine as it arrives (summary):** Present/Past Simple-and-Continuous revision in use (U1) → Past Simple vs Present Perfect (U2) → gerunds after love/hate/avoid-type verbs, present-tense revision (U3) → Present Perfect Continuous and Simple-vs-Continuous, *since/for* (U4) → **Conditionals Type 1 → Type 2, both presented in a single lesson (pp. 50–52), extended in U5 L3** → verb patterns/complementation and question-form revision (U6) → present modals *must/should/shouldn't/might/could* (U7) → **Passive voice formed once, present-and-past simple forms in context (pp. 90–91)** (U8) → **Reported speech: statements only, one-tense-back rule, including a reported conditional (p. 103)** (U9) → **perfect modals *must have / can't have / might have / could have / should have* (pp. 110–111)** (U10).

### Honest negatives

- **No publication year is printed** on the cover, title pages or imprint pages; only the Revised Edition stamp and in-file production dates (2018 on most signatures, 2022 on two Units 1–2 pages, 2023 on the covers and many later signatures) are present. Any catalogue year for this book comes from outside the book itself.
- **The Contents over-promises twice.** (1) Unit 4, Lesson 3 is credited with "Comparatives", but no comparative or superlative presentation, rule or practice set appears in the lesson or anywhere else in the body (the only hit for the word family is "comparatively recently" inside a Unit 7 reading). (2) Unit 9, Lesson 1 is credited with "Reported Speech", but the lesson contains no grammar presentation — reporting verbs occur inside its readings, and the one-tense-back rule is not stated until Lesson 2, printed p. 103.
- **Reported speech is statements-only.** There are no reported questions, orders or requests, no *say/tell* contrast work and no time/place word-change table anywhere in the book — a narrower treatment than the Grade 8 Advanced book's.
- **No third conditional, and no mixed conditional, appears anywhere in the book** (checked across the full text): *would have* occurs only inside the reported-speech lesson and in perfect-modal sentences, never in an *if*-clause construction.
- **No reference back matter:** unlike the Grade 8 Advanced book, this book has no Grammar Reference, no word lists and no irregular-verb table. Self-evaluations are in-unit only, with no printed answer key in the student's book.
- **Listening content cannot be verified from the PDF alone:** many core texts exist only as audio (the Seven Wonders lecture, the Willie Robinson interview, the Guy Fawkes recording against which the five errors are checked, the food-history timeline, the electrician's talk, the shipwreck report), and several tasks point to a separate "Resource Material" recording script that is not part of this file. Where the script is not printed, this draft describes the task and its printed frame, not the audio's content.
- **Internal factual inconsistency as printed:** the hurricane reading (printed p. 114, repeated in Appendix 1) dates Hurricane Katrina to "August 2007", while the book's own photograph caption on printed p. 113 dates it "August 28, 2005". The five Guy Fawkes "errors" on p. 67 are, by contrast, a deliberate exercise, stated as such on the page.
- **The production stem inside the file (21-0165) differs from the book's printed code (21-0208)**; the printed code and ISBN are the ones verified on the covers and used in this draft.
- Dated content is part of the book as printed: dial-up-era e-mail setup instructions and "Soft Outlook", spreadsheet-and-pie-chart projects, Wikipedia as the named fact-check route, a 2008 presidential speech, and disaster material anchored to 2004–2007 events.

### Series-final verdicts — Gymnasio English (Grades 7–9)

- **The series changes shape at Grade 9.** Grades 7–8 run two streams of *Think Teen!* (Advanced and Beginners, different authorship teams); Grade 9 is a single, undifferentiated *Think Teen!* by a single author, Patrick Mc Gavigan, with a different writing contractor (Linguaphone / Michail Levis S.A.). Whatever level a learner reached in the Grade 8 Advanced stream, this book — not a higher one — is the common ceiling for all.
- **Ceiling — conditionals:** Types 1 and 2 only, both introduced inside one lesson of Unit 5 and reused thereafter. There is no Type 0 as a named form, no Type 3 and no mixed conditional anywhere in the Gymnasio single-stream book. A learner finishing Gymnasio here can hypothesise about the present/future but has never been taught to hypothesise about the past with a conditional.
- **Ceiling — passive:** formed once, in Unit 8, from contextual present/past simple examples, with the *by*-agent never given the systematic treatment the Grade 8 Advanced book gives it, and no Present Perfect or Future passive presentation. The Grade 9 book's passive is a consolidation at or below the Grade 8 Advanced level, not an advance on it.
- **Ceiling — reported speech:** statements only, taught through one rule (one tense back) in Unit 9, including the elegant special case of a reported conditional. Reported questions and reported orders/requests — both present in the Grade 8 Advanced book — do not appear. On this strand the series' final book is narrower than its middle book.
- **The one genuine advance is the perfect modals.** Unit 10's *must have / can't have / might have / could have / should have* (+ past participle, and the continuous *must have been …-ing*) is new grammar that neither Grade 8 stream book presents, and it is taught thoroughly — deduction, probability, regret/criticism — through Atlantis, Pompeii, the tsunami and Katrina. This, with Present Perfect Continuous (Unit 4) and verb-pattern complementation (Unit 6), is where Grade 9 actually raises the ceiling.
- **Overall verdict:** the Gymnasio course ends as a consolidation year with one new peak. Its spine re-runs the Grade 8 Advanced big three (conditionals, passive, reported speech) in simpler form for the merged cohort, and its only upward steps are Present Perfect Continuous and the perfect modals. For LiqLearns, material drawn from this book can safely be cited up to: conditionals Types 1–2, simple passive, reported statements with backshift, perfect modals for past deduction — and for nothing beyond those limits.
## Grade 9 — Teacher's Book

### Identity block

- **Real title as printed:** *Think Teen!* — "3rd Grade of Junior High School / TEACHER'S BOOK" on the cover wrap (PDF p. 1), the title page (PDF p. 2) and the imprint title page (PDF p. 4). Γ΄ Γυμνασίου is the third year of Greek junior high school, i.e. Grade 9. There is **no stream word** anywhere on the cover, title or imprint pages: unlike Grades 7–8, Grade 9 *Think Teen!* is a single-stream set, and this is its (only) Teacher's Book. The record title "Agglika C' Gymnasiou (Grade 9) – Vivlio Ekpaideutikou" matches this book.
- **Author:** Patrick Mc Gavigan — sole named author (ΣΥΓΓΡΑΦΕΙΣ) on the cover, the credits page (PDF p. 3) and the imprint page (PDF p. 4). The credits page also names three teacher reviewers/evaluators, illustrator Θεόδωρος Πιακής, philological editor Γεώργιος Τζανετάτος, the Pedagogical Institute member responsible for the subject, Ιωσήφ Ε. Χρυσοχόος, and prepress Αφοί Ν. Παππά & Σία Α.Ε.Β.Ε.; the credits box records the book as an EU-co-funded project (Γ΄ ΚΠΣ / ΕΠΕΑΕΚ ΙΙ, 75% European Social Fund / 25% national funds).
- **Writing contractor (ανάδοχος συγγραφής):** Μιχαήλ Λεβής Α.Ε. — **Linguaphone** (imprint page, PDF p. 4).
- **Publisher:** The PDF wears the ITYE Diophantos distribution: cover wrap (PDF pp. 1 and 190) — Υπουργείο Παιδείας, Έρευνας και Θρησκευμάτων (Ministry of Education, Research and Religious Affairs) / Ινστιτούτο Εκπαιδευτικής Πολιτικής (Institute of Educational Policy), published by Ινστιτούτο Τεχνολογίας Υπολογιστών και Εκδόσεων «ΔΙΟΦΑΝΤΟΣ» (ITYE Diophantos). The book's own imprint page (PDF p. 4) carries the earlier institutional names: Υπουργείο Εθνικής Παιδείας και Θρησκευμάτων (Ministry of National Education and Religious Affairs) / Παιδαγωγικό Ινστιτούτο (Pedagogical Institute), with the original publisher Οργανισμός Εκδόσεως Διδακτικών Βιβλίων (Organisation for the Publication of Teaching Books), Αθήνα (Athens).
