### What the guide adds (own words; printed page references)

**Method introduction (printed p. 1 only).** A single-page Editor's Foreword — there is no multi-page teaching manual in this book. It states that the course follows the Pedagogical Institute's fundamental concepts and cross-curricular approach and aims to take learners' existing language awareness to a more advanced competence "roughly corresponding to B1" in the Council of Europe framework within one school year; because the timetable allows only 2 hours of tuition per week, it adopts a holistic approach rather than drilling isolated language patterns, prioritising authentic comprehension alongside thorough production skills. It explains the course architecture the rest of the guide serves: each Student's Book unit opens with a summary box of content and aims, each unit has three lessons plus a self-evaluation, and there is a revision test after every second unit. It states plainly what this Teacher's Book contains — the answers to the lesson tasks, the self-evaluations, the Workbook activities, the revision tests and the differentiated "It's your choice" activities — and then **defers the whole philosophy**: the philosophical orientation of *Think Teen* "can be studied in the Teacher's Book of the 2nd Grade of Junior High School" (i.e. the Grade 8 book). Unit 4's opening repeats the practical consequence: the teacher is deliberately given more material than can be used, to select from according to time, class and facilities (p. 41).

**Per-unit teaching notes — Student's Book, Workbook, self-evaluation and "It's Your Choice" (printed pp. 2–176).** Every unit follows the same four-part pattern: task-by-task procedure notes for the Student's Book lessons (keyed throughout to Student's Book page numbers, with answers and suggested answers printed inline at the point of use, plus background briefings, board-work, alternative projects and websites); the answers to the unit's self-evaluation; a Workbook section that is almost entirely answer keys; and two short differentiated sections, "It's Your Choice" for the Student's Book and for the Workbook — the tiered-task material the Introduction promises. In order: **Unit 1 — What a wonderful world!** (pp. 2–12: Lesson 1 Finding the Right Holiday, matching travellers to Santorini, Everest, Crete and Egypt; the "What a Wonderful World" song with its missing words supplied; a Seven Wonders of the Ancient World lecture, table and full listening text; Lesson 3 A Postcard Home, working on linkers — but, although, because, so, and — with Past Simple/Past Continuous and gerund practice referred to the Workbook, and an alternative UNESCO World Heritage poster project); **Unit 2 — Teen idols** (pp. 13–26: gladiators as the Roman original of stardom, celebrity true/false statements used to teach Present Perfect against Past Simple, a Daniel Radcliffe fact-file, a letter-writing lesson on linking words and explaining by example, and a closing section on how parents can deal with teenagers' idols); **Unit 3 — Thrills and Spills!** (pp. 27–40: fun-fair physics — a full text on Newton's three laws of motion and on potential and kinetic energy with answers, register and "fun" idioms, the gerund, a recorded Fun Park message printed in full, and a Create-a-Theme-Park project); **Unit 4 — Click on-Line** (pp. 41–62: the longest unit — a "Goals" page on teacher discretion, the history of communication from smoke signals to Bell's telephone of 1876, blogs and mass media, internet use, the reading "The Bug Spreads" on chain messages/viruses, Present Perfect Simple against Continuous, a fully scripted telephone conversation about a son's computer use, a Bulgaria media-use mini-project, step-by-step e-mail account set-up, and a closing project); **Unit 5 — The myths we live by** (pp. 63–86: what a myth is and why Greek gods have human weaknesses, the First Conditional (p. 66) and the Second Conditional with its rule stated in full and an "If I were you, I'd…" advice-giving extension (p. 71), Perseus, a Culture Corner on Finn McCool, fortune-telling, tapescripts at pp. 75 and 77, a leaflet project, and a Workbook word-square of myth-derived expressions — Achilles heel, Herculean effort, Pandora's box, the Midas touch and others (p. 82)); **Unit 6 — Keeping traditions and customs alive** (pp. 87–104: social and family values, St Valentine and Emperor Claudius, suffix spelling and noun formation, the unit's stated grammar aim — that verbs have different syntactic patterns and not all verbs take an object (p. 91), Guy Fawkes and Bonfire Night, a recording script of Hogmanay in Scotland, the San Fermín bull-running and St Patrick's Day in New York (p. 97), Greek Easter and wedding-description writing, and Christmas-tree vocabulary); **Unit 7 — Shades of meaning!** (pp. 105–126: colour and metaphor — the two senses of "shade", colour in the home, shopping and cosmetics, the full lyrics of the "Colour My World" song (p. 111), colour idioms — see red, white elephant, green with envy, black sheep (p. 113) — modal verbs and question forms (pp. 113–114), the Holi festival in India with its listening text, and a colour-and-personality article); **Unit 8 — Food for thought!** (pp. 127–144: Arcimboldo's *Summer* of 1573 as the cover briefing, food cultures and taboos, the Passive Voice built inductively from a text about the potato — pattern "Subject + be + Past Participle" (p. 132) — short histories of sugar and spices, restaurant-review writing, and a listening script adapted from the BBC in which an endocrinologist discusses food "stressors" and "supporters" and anorexia and bulimia, percentages supplied (pp. 137–138)); **Unit 9 — What's the weather like?** (pp. 145–160: energy sources and fossil fuels, the Halkida tidal current, greenhouse gases and cutting electricity use — with the electrician's listening text printed in full, 0.43 kg of CO₂ per kilowatt-hour saved (p. 153) — reported speech taught with and without backshift (pp. 150–152), and a mediation mini-project); **Unit 10 — Natural Phenomena** (pp. 161–176: natural against man-made disasters, modal verbs of deduction in the present (pp. 162–163) and the past — should have, could have, must have, can't have (pp. 163–164, 175) — Pompeii in AD 79, the 2004 Banda Aceh tsunami and the 2007 Greek forest fires named in the picture set (p. 163), and the *Sea Diamond* sinking at Santorini in 2007, with two listening scripts, the second adapted from BBC news: nearly 1,600 tourists, the ship sinking some 15 hours after hitting the rocks (pp. 168–169)).

**Transcripts — the audio layer the Student's Book lacks.** There is no separate tapescript appendix. Scripts are printed **inline, at the point of use, under varying headings** — "Recording script" (pp. 16–17, 47, 52, 97), "Tapescript" (pp. 75, 77), "Listening text" (pp. 6, 33, 115, 153), "Listening script" (pp. 94, 133, 137, 168) — and song lyrics are likewise printed where the song is taught (the Unit 1 song's missing words, p. 5; "Indigo Girl" referenced in the Unit 5 Workbook, p. 82; the full Unit 7 song, p. 111). Coverage is **selective, not complete**: many listening tasks in this guide give answers only, with no script printed (see Honest negatives).

**Revision Tests — answer keys only (printed pp. 177–180).** The closing section headed "REVISION TESTS" does **not** reprint any test paper. It gives the keys, eight activities per test, to the five revision tests that sit in the Student's Book after every second unit: Units 1 & 2 (p. 177), Units 3 & 4 (pp. 177–178), Units 5 & 6 (pp. 178–179), Units 7 & 8 (p. 179) and Units 9 & 10 (pp. 179–180). The keys mix closed answers, "Open answer(s)" markers and "Suggested answers" for the productive items (e.g. Units 1 & 2, Activity 5, p. 177: five model Present Perfect sentences about a new taverna, a new school canteen and a father's new car). No marks, scores or rating scales are given for any test. Printed p. 181 is blank and printed p. 182 is the Greek legal page, closing the book.

### Honest negatives

- **No publication year is printed** anywhere on the cover, title, credits or imprint pages — only the 25 November 2008 production stamps on every sheet and the PDF's 2012/2017 file dates. Any catalogue year for this book comes from outside the book itself.
- **The method introduction is one page, and it is not self-contained.** The Foreword (p. 1) states the level, timetable and architecture and then sends the reader to the Grade 8 (2nd Grade of Junior High School) Teacher's Book for the course's philosophical orientation. Only Unit 4 adds a further method note (the teacher-discretion "Goals" page, p. 41); Units 1–3 and 5–10 open straight into lesson notes, most without even a goals/objectives box.
- **There are no test papers in this book.** The "Revision Tests" section (pp. 177–180) is answer keys only — the five tests themselves live in the Student's Book — and the keys carry no marks, totals or rating scales, with several activities keyed only as "Open answer(s)".
- **Transcripts are selective and scattered.** Scripts appear inline under at least four different headings (Recording script / Tapescript / Listening text / Listening script) with no gathered tapescript appendix and no index of them; a number of listening tasks are keyed with answers only and no script, so those recordings cannot be recovered from this file. There is no audio in the PDF.
- **There is no gathered answer key.** All Student's Book, self-evaluation, Workbook and "It's Your Choice" answers exist only inline inside each unit's notes, in that order; nothing is collected at the back except the revision-test keys.
- **Original errors and inconsistencies, recorded as printed:** the Unit 3 Workbook section is headed "Workbook – UNIT 2" (printed p. 35); "It's Your Choice – Workook" is misspelled in Units 5 and 6 (pp. 86, 104); the running footer shortens Unit 6's title to "Keeping traditions and custome alive" throughout; the Hogmanay script prints "Old Lang's Ayne" for *Auld Lang Syne* (p. 97); and Unit 4's e-mail lesson is built around setting up an account in "Soft Outlook" (p. 56). Unit and lesson numbering inside the notes is also uneven — not every unit's three lessons are explicitly headed Lesson 1/2/3.
- **The guide does not reprint the Student's Book or the Workbook.** Reading texts and task wording are generally not reproduced (listening scripts, the Newton's-laws text and song lyrics excepted); the notes are unusable without the Student's Book — and, for the Workbook sections, the Workbook — open beside them at the cited page.
- **Blank pages:** production sheet 4 (PDF p. 5), the blank roman sheet ii (PDF p. 7) and printed p. 181 (PDF p. 188) carry only printer's crop/registration marks.
- **Dated content is part of the book as printed:** dial-up and ADSL connections, chain e-mails and "Soft Outlook" (Unit 4), and the websites cited throughout are those of the book's 2008 production.
- This guide is the **single-stream** Grade 9 book; it contains nothing stream-specific, and nothing for Grades 7 or 8 beyond the one cross-reference to the Grade 8 Teacher's Book for the course philosophy.

### The Workbook — how it maps onto the Student's Book

The workbook follows the Student's Book unit-for-unit: the same ten units in the same order with the same titles — 1 "What a wonderful world!", 2 "Teen idols", 3 "Thrills and Spills!", 4 "Click on-Line", 5 "The myths we live by", 6 "Keeping traditions and customs alive", 7 "Shades of meaning!", 8 "Food for thought", 9 "What's the weather like?", 10 "Natural phenomena" — and the same grammar and vocabulary spine in the same order (see the spine summary below). Pagination is independent of the Student's Book (workbook Unit 5 opens on printed p. 46, Student's Book Unit 5 on p. 49 there), and the workbook does **not** reproduce the Student's Book's three-lesson subdivision: inside each unit the work is a single continuous run of numbered Activities (Activity 1 to roughly Activity 15–20, restarting at 1 in each unit), with no Lesson headings anywhere in the book.

Three structural features define what the workbook adds:

- **It is largely self-contained — the opposite pattern from the Grade 7 and Grade 8 workbooks.** Most tasks work on texts and material printed in the workbook itself. There is no listening strand at all (no task anywhere in the book asks the learner to listen), no pronunciation strand, and only one explicit cross-reference to the Student's Book in the whole book (Unit 7, Activity 6, sending the learner to "Reading 2, p.77, in your Student's Book" for phrases with *go*), plus a handful of tasks that reuse Student's Book unit material without naming the book (e.g. Unit 3, Activity 2, which draws its word pairs from "TASK 4, p. 28 in the student's book"). A learner can do the great majority of this workbook with the workbook alone open.
- **Scored Review blocks after every two units (printed pp. 21–24, 42–45, 64–67, 86–89, 107–110).** Each block alternates pages headed "Revision" and "Test"; individual activities carry a printed "marks /5", and the final Test page of the block carries a printed "Total marks / 40" (verified on printed pp. 24, 67, 89 and 110). These are the only scores printed in the book; there is no answer key.
- **Appendix I: "It's your choice" (printed pp. 111–144).** A second full pass over all ten units, in the same unit order, which re-presents the main units' core texts and tasks in an alternative form — the same letters, cloze texts and grammar points re-set with changed or more guided task demands (for example, the Unit 1 letter that the main unit practises with mixed tenses reappears with a Past-Simple-only gap-fill; the Unit 5 myths text and the Unit 10 Atlantis cloze are each set twice, once in the main unit and once in the appendix). It is choice/extension material keyed to the units, not new units and not an answer key. The contents page lists it as "Appendix I: It's your choice p.111"; no Appendix II exists in the workbook (the Student's Book's Appendix 2, Maps, has no workbook counterpart).

**Practice added, in general terms:** tense and form drills set inside short new texts (letters, news-style reports, adverts); multiple-choice cloze readings; sentence transformation and rewriting (so…that, passive, reported speech, conditionals); word-formation, collocation, compound-noun and phrasal/prepositional-phrase work; "similar but different" word-choice exercises; short guided writing (a reply letter, an invitation e-mail of 40–50 words, a competition letter of about 100 words, a magazine letter on fast food); one mediation task (a Greek Art Therapy text to be rendered as a short English description); and puzzles (word squares, quizzes, simile matching). Extended composition is rare and short throughout.

**Grammar spine as practised (summary, identical in order to the Student's Book):** Present/Past Simple and Continuous (Unit 1) → Present Perfect vs Past Simple (Unit 2) → likes/loves/hates + gerund, gerund verbs, present-tense revision (Unit 3) → Present Perfect Simple vs Continuous, comparatives (Unit 4) → First and Second Conditionals (Unit 5) → verb syntax (*believe/think/feel* + *that*), question-form revision (Unit 6) → modal verbs — *must / should / shouldn't / might / could / can* (Unit 7) → Passive Voice (Unit 8) → Reported Speech, conditionals in reported speech (Unit 9) → past modals — *must have / might have / could have / should have* (Unit 10). The workbook's contribution is drill volume and the workbook-only texts below, not new grammar.

### Workbook — unit-by-unit summary (own words; printed page references)

**Unit 1 — What a wonderful world! (printed pp. 1–10).** The unit opens with a report task placing Greek holiday names (Mykonos, Meteora, the Acropolis, the Faragi Gorge and others) on a map of Greece, and a true/false "Culture Shock" set on greeting customs in Australia, Greece and Japan. The tense work is carried by two workbook-only letters: a letter from James asking Maria about Crete and the Minoan civilisation, with the correct Present/Past form to be underlined in each pair, a reply to be completed from it, and a second letter (to Irene, about an adventure holiday) for tense gap-filling. Linking words (*because / as / although / but*), adjective formation with suffixes (*-al, -y, -ful, -ive…*), and "similar but different" word choice follow. The main workbook-only reading is a deliberately hostile multiple-choice cloze travel piece about "Bruug, Switzerland" — a dull town of expensive holey cheeses where, the text claims, two out of three married couples met at a watch exhibition — followed by a *so + adjective + that* rewriting task and a notices-to-places matching task in which three notices belong in a travel agent's.

**Unit 2 — Teen idols (printed pp. 11–20).** Grammar first: verb-form completion on star facts (with factually incorrect statements to be spotted), then the workbook-only reading "Stars in Their Eyes" — three British teenagers on their idols (a Newcastle boy on David Beckham, said to have felt proud when he captained England in 2003; a Liverpool girl on Christina Aguilera; a Manchester girl who has gone off Britney Spears for Westlife) — worked as a sentence-restoration task using pronoun clues, and mined for the *by far / by heart / by chance / by luck* phrase set. Present Perfect vs Past Simple is drilled on dated facts (Neil Armstrong in 1969 among them) and on picture-based "what has happened" matching. The unit ends with an internet research task: find an address and information for named period stars (Mischa Barton, Nicole Richie, Eminem among them).

**Review of Units One and Two (printed pp. 21–24).** Five short texts to be matched to holiday destinations for five people, a time-phrases completion (the *for the time being / just in time / from time to time* set), statements about changes in the learner's own town or life, sentence rewriting with a given word, and a Madonna verb-form circle task ("a star for more than 25 years", a pre-fame job as a waitress in a New York fast-food restaurant). Activities are marked /5; the block total is printed as /40 (p. 24).

**Unit 3 — Thrills and Spills! (printed pp. 25–32).** The physics of the fairground, in workbook-only texts: a roller-coaster cloze built on the word set *kinetic energy, friction, potential energy, track, ascent*; a second cloze reusing Student's Book word pairs on amusement rides (coaster cars with no engine or brakes); compound-noun building; a signs task (choose what each notice means, A/B/C); pair-matching vocabulary (baby-sitter, gift shop, protective clothing type sets); a light-hearted "Fun Quiz" on what you do not take to a theme park; and a multiple-choice reading on inertia and seat belts — a person in motion stays in motion unless an unbalanced force acts, and the seat belt supplies it. The writing task is a competition entry: a letter of about 100 words to win a family weekend at "Camelot", meals and theme-park entry included, the break to be taken before October 29th.

**Unit 4 — Click on-Line (printed pp. 33–41).** The Present Perfect Simple/Continuous contrast is carried by a workbook-only news text, "Alert over schoolgirls' Bebo use": a Kent girls' school head, Linda Wybar, writing to parents after 700 pupils signed up to the Bebo networking site, some posting photographs and in one case a home address, with Bebo UK responding that safeguards are in place. Media and statistics vocabulary, noun-plus-preposition phrases, verb-plus-noun collocations and "similar but different" choices (*discoveries / inventions* and the like) follow, with a "what has she been doing?" picture task on a girl's room. The closing comprehension text argues that the telephone — invented, it states, by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876 — has influenced behaviour more than newspapers, cinema or television, because phone lines brought the internet; a jumbled five-panel history of telephone design (1877 Edison handset material through 1990s videophones) is to be put in order.

**Review of Units Three and Four (printed pp. 42–45).** Dialogue-response matching (bullet train, Big Dipper), a true/false text arguing fun-park rides are safer than football or basketball, a mobile-phones verb-form cloze ("so important to our lives today that it is difficult for many…"), and "what has each person been doing?" descriptions from evidence (sunburn, an injured leg and the like). Marked /5 per activity as before.

**Unit 5 — The myths we live by (printed pp. 46–55).** Conditionals are introduced by function before form: First Conditional statements are matched to warning, threatening, promising, predicting and talking about a strong possibility; Second Conditional statements to advice, daydreaming and unlikely events. Myth content is then worked hard: verb-plus-noun collocations, naming Greek gods and figures from clues (the god of light and the sun and others), a word square of ten mythical characters matched to set phrases (Achilles' heel among them), "If I were…" identifications (raising and calming storms, flying), full-sentence answers to hypothetical situations, and a workbook-only comprehension text arguing that myths are not fixed truths but ways of explaining existence — pain, suffering, life and death — with Shiva, who both creates and destroys and lives on Mount Kailasa with Parvati, as the non-Greek example, and Greek parallels to be named. The unit closes with the Labours of Hercules to be named under cartoons.

**Unit 6 — Keeping traditions and customs alive (printed pp. 56–63).** The opening multiple-choice cloze is the workbook-only "The Carnival in Rio" text: a four-day pre-Easter celebration, seven weeks before Easter, whose name is explained as *carne vale*, "farewell to meat", running from the Friday night through Mardi Gras ("Fat Tuesday"), with samba schools parading a single annually changed theme from dusk to daybreak. Learners then write a 40–50-word e-mail inviting an English-speaking friend to their own pre-Easter carnival, interpret short phone-message texts ("What does it say?"), match Greek celebration dates to feasts (28th October, 25th March, 25th December among them), work the *from year to year / from time to time / from dusk to…* phrase set, hunt ten festival words in a word square, and sort deliberately misplaced festival vocabulary (*effigy* and friends) back into the right sentences.

**Review of Units Five and Six (printed pp. 64–67).** Sentence-ending choice, word choice in myth sentences (Heracles "half God", Thor's temper), a *custom / traditions / celebrations / beliefs / festivals* completion, and word-pair matching (*fancy dress, annual…*). Activities /5; block total /40 (p. 67).

**Unit 7 — Shades of meaning! (printed pp. 68–76).** Colour in language. Unit vocabulary is first sorted into nouns, adjectives and verbs; flag symbolism follows — what Iceland's flag colours might stand for, then a description of what the Greek flag's colours symbolise. Phrases with *go* (*on the go, have a go, all the go…*) are taken from the Student's Book reading (the book's one explicit Student's Book page reference) and used in dialogues. The main workbook-only reading is "The Psychology of Colour", a boxed set of colour idioms explained in prose — purple prose, green with envy as the balance point between the warm and cool ends of the spectrum, seeing red and the "fight or flight" response inherited from ancestors, and yellow-bellied for a coward. A mediation task asks for a short English description of Art Therapy from a Greek source text (cave painting as early expression, therapy centres worldwide and one on Skopelos). The unit ends with colour-idiom sentence matching and modal choice (*can/might, might/could*).

**Unit 8 — Food for thought (printed pp. 77–85).** A food word square opens the unit. The main workbook-only reading, "Brand-name rip-off foods", argues in strong terms that processed, advertised, coupon-carrying brand foods deliver the least nutrition for the money and con the buyer; learners choose its best caption from three near-identical options. The Passive is then built in stages: identify it among actives and progressives, rewrite food-preparation steps (*You peel orange → The orange is peeled*), complete a Coffee text with passive forms, and rewrite sentences in the passive. Three workbook-only dish descriptions — rice toasted in butter or oil before broth is added ladle by ladle; biscuits soaked in coffee, rum and sugar and layered with cheese-and-custard; a rice dessert of Asian origin finished in the oven — are to be matched to Tiramisu, Rice pudding and Risotto. Newspaper headlines are expanded into full (passive) sentences, world dishes are matched to countries (Doro Wat, jerk fish among them), the writing task is a magazine letter on fast food in Greece today from printed notes (quick, tasty, cheap, places to hang out), and a true/false food quiz closes the unit (pyramid workers paid in bread, honey as the food that cannot go bad, Greece's olive varieties among its claims, all as printed).

**Review of Units Seven and Eight (printed pp. 86–89).** Verb completion on interior design, colour-idiom responses (*like a black sheep, a white elephant, once in a blue moon, green with envy, she saw red*), a preposition completion on making olive oil ("the olives are ground…"), and verb-to-noun matching. Activities /5; block total /40 (p. 89).

**Unit 9 — What's the weather like? (printed pp. 90–98).** Weather and energy vocabulary is matched to sketches (drought, volcanic eruption and others) and verbs to nouns (convert, spin — a water pump, electricity, a wheel). Words with two meanings are separated out (*wave, spend* and others), the *light* family is completed (moonlight, daylight, candlelight, sunlight, fluorescent light), and Reported Speech is practised inside an energy-saving dialogue ("She says that…"). The substantial workbook-only reading is a top-ten list of actions to reduce climate-change impact — insulate your house, switch to a renewable supplier, monitor your use, install energy-saving bulbs, turn appliances off, cut unnecessary flights and the rest — with actions to be matched to their descriptions; the descriptions as printed state that energy-saving bulbs last up to 12 times longer than normal bulbs and emit 70% less carbon dioxide, and that on average 30% of a house's heat escapes through its walls.

**Unit 10 — Natural phenomena (printed pp. 99–106).** Picture-led disaster work opens the unit: name the catastrophe pictured, list five kinds of damage it can do, decide what caused three pictured events and suggest how the people in them could recover from the shock. Transformation rewriting practises past modals (*must have / can't have* type inferences, e.g. about a captain near rocks), prepositional phrases place Vesuvius and others (*on the outskirts, off shore, at a low height…*), verb-plus-preposition matching covers the tsunami set (*tied up, slow down, set off, draw back, find out, prepare for* — reworked in a sentences task about seismologists and a receding sea), and a word-formation choice text works *predictions/predictors, indicators/indication, occurring/occurrence* around an earthquake passage. The Atlantis cloze — a beautiful city of precious-metal-covered walls, hot and cold fountains and a canal to the ocean, with farmers on its outskirts — practises the past-modal/open cloze forms, and the unit ends with animal similes (*as stubborn as a mule, as quiet as a mouse, as blind as a bat*) and a same-spelling-different-meaning set (*sign, capital, field, matter, cycle…*).

**Review of Units Nine and Ten (printed pp. 107–110).** Sentence-meaning choice (underground water and steam), place-phrase completion (across the river, over the dam, on an island…), a noun-choice cloze on Plato's Atlantis (works of art, marble buildings), and time-expression completion. Activities /5; block total /40 (p. 110).

**Appendix I — It's your choice (printed pp. 111–144).** Ten unit sections in the main units' order, each re-setting that unit's core material: the Unit 1 letters again (tense identification, then a Past-Simple version), the time-phrases again with sentence support, the Unit 2 idol texts again for phrasal verbs and the *by…* phrases defined, the Unit 3 compound nouns and the Camelot competition again, the Unit 4 Bebo text again (full text reprinted) with noun-plus-preposition and mass-media comprehension work, the Unit 5 conditionals and myths text again, Unit 6 festival vocabulary with Greek-to-English matching (τελετή, ομοίωμα and others) and Christmas sentence completion, the Unit 7 colour article again as true/false, Unit 8 passive identification and food compounds, Unit 9 Greek-equivalent matching, two-meaning words and reported-speech rewriting with a worked example, and Unit 10 transformations, the tsunami prepositional phrases and the Atlantis cloze again, closing with animal-name simile completion. Blank printed p. 145 and the Law 3966/2011 legal/distribution notice on printed p. 146 follow.

### The Glossary — organisation, scope and format (own words)

**Organisation.** The glossary is organised exactly as the Student's Book is: by unit (Units 1–10, in course order), and inside each unit by the Student's Book's own subdivisions — an **Introduction** set where the unit has one, then **Lesson 1, Lesson 2 and Lesson 3**, and finally a **Self-Evaluation** set. Page ranges (printed): Unit 1, pp. 1–4; Unit 2, pp. 5–7; Unit 3, pp. 8–11; Unit 4, pp. 12–14; Unit 5, pp. 15–18; Unit 6, pp. 19–22; Unit 7, pp. 23–26; Unit 8, pp. 27–30; Unit 9, pp. 31–33; Unit 10, pp. 34–36. Inside each lesson set the words are alphabetical by headword. There is no separate A–Z index for the whole book, no introduction or instructions page, and no contents page: after the cover and credits pages the word lists begin immediately (printed p. 1). The running head on every page is "Think Teen! Γ' Γυμνασίου" with the unit number.

**Scope.** The glossary covers the vocabulary of all ten Student's Book units, including the phrase-level items the course teaches as vocabulary — binomial phrases (*hustle and bustle* type pairs are entered through their parts and as phrases), phrasal items (*hang out*), and the Self-Evaluation phrase sets (in Unit 1, the *time* phrases: *behind the times, for the time being, time and again*). A page carries roughly 15–17 entries, giving on the order of 570 headwords across the 36 printed pages (estimate from the page density; no total is printed in the book). Nouns are the largest class, then verbs and adjectives; adverbs and phrases are few.

**Format.** Every page is the same six-column table: **Word | Definition | Example | Synonym | Antonym | Derived forms**. The headword carries a part-of-speech tag — (n), (v), (adj), (adv), (phr) — and the Definition column gives a short definition in simple English **followed by the Greek equivalent** (e.g. the definition of *flood* ends with the Greek πλημμύρα; *guard* with φρουρός). Each entry has one example sentence in English showing the word in use. The Synonym, Antonym and Derived forms columns are filled only where the compilers had something to give — many entries leave one or more of them blank — and derived forms are given as bare related words (e.g. under *affirmative*: *affirmatively*; under *suitable*: *suitably, suitability, suitableness*). **There is no phonetic transcription anywhere in the glossary** — no IPA, no respelling, no stress marks (verified by searching the whole text layer: no IPA characters occur). There are no pictures, no exercises and no Greek-to-English reverse section: it is an English-headword study list for Greek-speaking learners, designed to be printed (its own subtitle is "Printable Form").

Worked shape of a typical entry, in paraphrase: a noun such as *waterfall* is defined in English as a stream falling from a higher place, glossed in Greek as καταρράκτης, exemplified by a sentence about Niagara Falls, and given *fall / falls / torrent* in the synonym column, with the antonym and derived-forms cells empty. A fuller entry, such as *suitable*, fills nearly every column: English definition plus Greek, an example about buying a gift for a new house, three synonyms, and three derived forms.

### Honest negatives

- **Workbook: no publication year is printed** on the cover, title pages or imprint pages; only the reissue note and in-file production stamps (2014–2016, varying by section) are present. Any catalogue year for this book comes from outside the book itself. **Glossary:** the only date is the credits-page "Version 1.0 / April 2013"; there is no ISBN, no book code and no printed-book imprint, because it is a printable web glossary.
- **The workbook has no listening tasks, no pronunciation work, no tapescripts and no answer key** — a real contrast with the Grade 7 and Grade 8 workbooks in this set, which do carry listening (Grade 8) and pronunciation strands. The only feedback device is the printed marks scheme (/5 per activity, /40 per Review block) in the five Review blocks.
- **The workbook barely points at the Student's Book** — one explicit page reference in 144 printed pages (Unit 7, Activity 6, to Student's Book p. 77). Claims that this workbook "cannot be used without the Student's Book" would be wrong for Grade 9; the reverse caution applies to Grades 7–8, not here.
- **The appendix is not new material.** "It's your choice" (printed pp. 111–144) re-sets the main units' own texts and tasks — the Bebo text, the Atlantis cloze, the Camelot competition and others each appear twice in the book. Page counts of "texts in the workbook" must not double-count them.
- **The glossary has no phonetics of any kind** (no IPA characters occur anywhere in its text layer), **no illustrations, no exercises, no whole-book alphabetical index and no Greek-to-English section**; its Synonym, Antonym and Derived forms columns are frequently empty for a given entry. Its headword total is not printed; the ~570 figure given above is a density estimate, not a count performed entry by entry.
- **The glossary's Greek is inside the Definition column**, not a separate translation column; a reader looking only at column heads could miss that every definition is bilingual.
- Spelling and factual details are reported as printed, not corrected: the workbook prints "David Beckam" (Unit 2 text), "Turley" for Turkey in a Unit 8 matching list, and a duplicated option ("someone" twice) in the Bruug cloze; the telephone text credits Bell alone with the 1876 invention; the Rio Carnival text's sentence about "the end of beginning of Spring" is garbled as printed. Dated content is period content: Bebo and MySpace are the social networks of Units 4, the Unit 2 idols and the Review's Madonna text are 2000s-era, and web addresses, prices and statistics in the texts are as printed, not verified as live.
- A few workbook pages are blank or picture-only in the text layer (PDF pp. 5 and 7, blank apart from production stamps; the unit divider pages, printed pp. 1, 11, 25, 33, 46, 56, 68, 77, 90, 99, carry only the unit title; picture tasks throughout). Those pages are described from the rendered pages, not from extracted text. The glossary's PDF p. 1 (cover) has no text layer at all and was read from the rendered page.

### What this book is — and what it is not

This is **not a conventional graded coursebook**. There is no unit-by-unit grammar syllabus in the Contents, no vocabulary lists, no workbook section, no answer key and **no CEFR level printed anywhere in the book** (checked by search and by reading: no B1/B2/C1 or equivalent statement appears). The Greek introductory note (Εισαγωγικό σημείωμα, printed p. 7 / PDF p. 8) presents it in its own terms as *proposed teaching material* for English in the General Lykeio: eight thematic units of comprehension and production of spoken and written language, built on the communicative abilities pupils already have, designed for authentic communication situations, critical and creative processing of information, individual and group work, and optional use of new technologies — with teachers explicitly advised to supplement or adapt it to their class's level, needs and interests, and told that lack of technology must not block its use.

In practice the level is upper-secondary / post-intermediate in demand, judged from the texts themselves, not from any printed label:

- The reading load is long, authentic and unsimplified in feel: a full newspaper feature on Tilos and refugees (Unit 2, three printed pages), a Guardian report of a terrorist attack (Unit 3), a two-page Van Gogh biography (Unit 4), adapted Guardian and ASPCA articles (Unit 5), a four-part Independent feature read as a jigsaw (Unit 6), adapted plot summaries and genuine extracts from *Pride and Prejudice* (Unit 7), and a ten-paragraph BBC Future article plus a Guardian counter-article (Unit 8).
- Language work is **embedded in the units, not sequenced as a course**: past tenses are noticed and drilled inside Unit 3, the passive is noticed inside Unit 5, word formation and prefixes inside Unit 6, and the book's one systematic grammar block — conditionals in full, including mixed conditionals, *if*-alternatives and inversion — sits inside Unit 8. A learner who needs grammar taught from zero in order will not find that here.
- The skills spine is consistent across units: group/pair discussion first, reading or viewing, a structured response (very often the "5-4-3-2-1" table), vocabulary/grammar noticing, then a spoken product (presentation, debate, action plan) and/or a guided piece of writing with an explicit plan, linking-word bank and checklist. Two full essay scaffolds are given (opinion essay, Unit 5; for-and-against essay, Unit 8).
- Greek is used openly as a working language of the classroom: Unit 3 asks pupils to render the gist of Cavafy's Greek poem "Thermopylae" in English for a foreign friend, and the front and back matter, the introductory note and the legal page are in Greek.

### Unit-by-unit summary (own words; printed page references)

**Front matter (printed pp. 5–8).** Contents (p. 5): the eight units at pp. 9, 13, 23, 35, 49, 65, 79 and 93. Image credits (p. 6): free-use images from Pixabay and Wikimedia Commons, other sources credited in place, online texts last retrieved 04.09.2018. Introductory note in Greek (p. 7, summarised above). Printed p. 8 is blank.

**Unit 1 — Group Work (printed pp. 9–12).** A four-page ice-breaker unit with no reading text and no language syllabus. Pupils pair with someone they barely know, exchange basic biographical information, a favourite summer memory and two free-time enthusiasms, keep notes, then report their partner to the class (p. 10). A teacher-dealt card (same number, colour, fruit, writer or hobby) sorts the class into groups, and each group invents a name and fills in a three-box "group's boat" — name, members' first names, and the characteristics of the ideal English lesson — to draw, display or stick on the wall (p. 11). Printed p. 9 is the pictorial opener and printed p. 12 is a full-page picture (a tree whose foliage is made of coloured gears, checked on the render); there is nothing else in the unit.

**Unit 2 — A refugee's "dreamland" (printed pp. 13–22).** Opens with two videos — a National Geographic short film on Syrian refugees and a BBC News report on a Greek island that welcomes them (p. 14) — then the unit's long reading text (pp. 15–18), a Telegraph feature on Tilos in the Aegean: a depopulated island of about 500 residents and some 15,000 goats that took in about a dozen Syrian families (around 70 people), housed them in a purpose-built camp in the port of Livadia rather than a large detention-style camp, found the adults work in hotels, restaurants, shops and the bakery, put the children into Greek and English lessons and then local schools, and planned a cheese factory using the goats' milk to give both locals and refugees work. Voices in the text include the mayor, Maria Kamma, who presents Tilos as a model that could be scaled up in proportion to population; an NGO team leader; a long-settled British resident; and refugees themselves, including a Syrian father who contrasts Tilos with a previous camp on Rhodes and an eight-year-old girl already speaking confident Greek. Comprehension work (pp. 19–20) is true/false, short answers and multiple choice on those points. The product work is outward-looking: groups build an action plan, using a "Read Think Write" timeline tool, for integrating refugees in their own town or village — numbers, possible businesses, the school's role, benefits to the community — and present it (p. 20); then, imagining their own family fleeing Syria, they choose an escape route on a BBC interactive and narrate the journey with a Tour Builder map and pictures (p. 21). Printed p. 22 is a closing picture page. No grammar or vocabulary section is given in this unit.

**Unit 3 — On Duty (printed pp. 23–34).** The careers-and-heroism unit, and the book's past-tense unit. It opens with group discussion of how pupils will choose a career (money, status, skills), whether they would take a dangerous job, and what sort of people risk their lives for others, supported by a full photo page of occupations (printed p. 25, checked on the render: artist's brushes, farm machinery, film crew, business, classroom, schoolchildren, laboratory, fire engine, firefighters in protective suits, welding). Pupils first invent a story from a headline, then read the real Guardian report (pp. 26–27) of the March 2018 attacks in Carcassonne and Trèbes, southern France: an attacker who had been under surveillance killed people in a car hijacking, shot at off-duty riot police out jogging, then took hostages in a Super U supermarket, where Lt Col Arnaud Beltrame voluntarily exchanged himself for a hostage, left his phone line open so forces outside could hear, and died of his injuries after the assault that killed the gunman. A "5-4-3-2-1" response table follows (p. 28: five key words, four feeling words, three impressive facts, two questions, one connection). Pupils then discuss President Macron's tribute to Beltrame, mediate Cavafy's "Thermopylae" into English as a treatment of duty, and build vocabulary with an online dictionary and a class word wall (pp. 29–30). The language block (pp. 31–33) works entirely from the report: pupils sort example sentences on a timeline to notice the contrast between completed past events, background activity in progress, and earlier past events, then complete a second news version of the same incident with the verbs in the correct past forms. The unit closes with research into officers and ordinary people who died or sacrificed themselves saving others, group reporting, and a choice of writing — a narrative essay, a police report, or a film-scene script — supported by a table of eight kinds of narrative ending (circular, reflection, surprise, moral, emotion, question, cliffhanger, dialogue, funny — nine rows as printed) (pp. 33–34).

**Unit 4 — Vincent van Gogh (printed pp. 35–48).** An art unit built around three sources: a song, a biography and the painter's own letters. Pupils brainstorm famous painters, then work with Don McLean's song about Van Gogh ("Starry, starry night" / "Vincent"): match underlined phrases to paintings, order the stanzas while watching the video, and then do a close listening repair task on a deliberately corrupted lyric sheet — filling blanks, correcting wrong words and striking out extra words (pp. 36–38). Discussion and short factual writing from the song follow (p. 39), then web research on the Van Gogh Museum / Google Art Project sites: each pupil chooses four or five paintings and records title, type, dimensions, year and viewing notes (p. 39), and matches six paintings to museum viewing notes — among them a café still life with a glass of absinthe, *The Potato Eaters*, *The Harvest* (1888), an almond-blossom sprig in a glass with a Japanese-print influence, an unfinished view of the Seine near Paris, and a farmhouse in a cornfield near Arles (p. 40). The biography (pp. 41–42, in the citation section below) tells the life in two dense pages: Zundert childhood as a pastor's son, work for an art dealer in The Hague from age 16, the lifelong correspondence with and financial support of his brother Theo, taking up painting in earnest in 1880 on Theo's suggestion, lessons from Anton Mauve, Paris in 1886 and the encounter with Impressionism and pointillism (the book classifies him as a post-Impressionist, using colour and line to express emotion rather than to describe accurately), the move to Arles, the disastrous Gauguin stay and the ear incident, the Saint-Rémy asylum where he painted about 150 works including *The Starry Night*, only one painting sold in his lifetime, the move to Dr Gachet at Auvers, his death at 37 two days after shooting himself, Theo's death six months later, and his posthumous fame and record prices. Pupils order the life events, judge true/false statements, answer character/style questions, watch a "Van Gogh – In His Own Words" video, compare self-portraits and caption them, and invent a dialogue between Van Gogh and Dr Gachet (pp. 43–45). The letters strand (pp. 46–47) gives two extracts from one 1876 letter to Theo written from Isleworth — a sunset walk, news of family, longing to see him — and a reflective passage on illness, discouragement and recovery in nature, ending in a meditation on a human life as being born, working, loving, growing and disappearing; pupils discuss his feelings for his family, underline the images, paint from them, and discuss his attitude to life. The unit ends with a collage, a school-newspaper article entitled "My Vincent Van Gogh" with prizes for the three best, browsing his letters online, and a field-study visit to an art gallery (p. 48).

**Unit 5 — Animal Rights (printed pp. 49–64).** The ethics-and-argument unit, and the book's passive-voice and opinion-essay unit. Discussion opens on whether animals are property and whether killing or using them for food, labour, entertainment or experiments can ever be justified (p. 50). The main reading (p. 51) is an adapted Guardian article on animal testing: UK research funders ordered scientists to design studies properly after finding that under-powered, poorly designed drug experiments — too few animals to detect an effect, or more than necessary — wasted animals' lives and produced meaningless results; new guidelines require statistically robust work, on pain of losing funding, and the scientists quoted argue for using no more animals than necessary, and no fewer. Comprehension is layered: gist questions, true/false/not-mentioned, multiple choice on purpose, audience and reference, and a vocabulary match (robust, insight, scrutiny, funding, culminate, pinpoint and others) extended into concept cubes for a word wall (pp. 52–54). Grammar is noticed from the article itself (p. 55): pupils compare sentences about results being wasted, guidelines being welcomed and procedures being started, and state how a passive differs from an active and when it is chosen. A second text, the ASPCA on American factory farms (p. 56) — industrial scale, the overwhelming majority of US farm animals raised in factory conditions, billions of chickens for meat and hundreds of millions for eggs, birds excluded from federal protection — must then be explained and summarised **without** passive sentences, to show what the passive is doing. Listening/viewing follows: a BBC radio talk to title and identify (script not printed), and a TED talk on de-extinction, completed as a ten-item gap-fill about an extinct North American bird, its genome and reviving a species (pp. 57–58; the talk's wording is not printed in full). Speaking work covers reasons against keeping animals in captivity as a mind map, choosing an endangered animal to sponsor, comparing animals in contrasting living conditions in photographs, short presentations on saving endangered species, and a formal for/against debate on animal testing (pp. 58–60). Writing is fully scaffolded (pp. 61–63): an opinion essay of 120–150 words for the school magazine on whether animal-tested cosmetics should be banned, with a five-paragraph plan (introduction, two viewpoint paragraphs, opposing viewpoint, conclusion restating the opinion), a large linking-word bank organised by function (stating an opinion, listing, reasons, examples, results, contrast, summing up) and a tips checklist; then a second 120–150-word opinion essay on protecting endangered species, writing about pollution, hunting and the pupil's own ideas. Printed p. 64 is a closing picture page (a fawn in grass, checked on the render).

**Unit 6 — Fast Fashion (printed pp. 65–78).** The environment-of-clothing unit, organised as prediction → jigsaw reading → checking. It opens with a no-right-answer survey of the pupil's own habits (what they do with a plastic bottle, whether they recycle, how many T-shirts they own, whether price, Fair Trade or fabric drives a purchase, favourite fabric) and a ten-statement true/false prediction set about fast fashion, plus a KWL chart on "the environmental impact of my closet", both left open to be checked after the reading (pp. 66–68). The reading (pp. 69–71) is a four-part Independent article handled as a true jigsaw: pupils each read one part, meet in "expert groups" for that part, then return to teach it to their "jigsaw group". In own words, the four parts argue: (1) cheap, rapid newness is environmentally costly — speed and low price mean corners are cut, toxic dyeing pollutes clean water, and campaign pressure has pushed brands to remove hazardous chemicals from supply chains; (2) the fibres themselves are a problem both ways — polyester sheds non-biodegradable microfibres in washing that pass into waterways and up the food chain to fish eaten by humans, while cotton needs heavy water and pesticide use, is mostly genetically modified, and is linked in a cited documentary to a US farmer's death and birth defects in India, with organic cotton still under one per cent of the world crop; (3) waste is built in — wardrobes are saturated, retailers must manufacture newness, rising incomes and lost mending skills make repair seem pointless, supermarket fashion and sales make clothes feel disposable, and most unwanted clothing in Britain is thrown away rather than donated or recycled despite charity shops and in-store schemes; (4) consumer choices are genuinely complicated — natural is not automatically better than synthetic once spinning, dyeing, finishing and transport are counted, recycled content is presented as best of all (with a brand making fleece from plastic bottles and moving to organic or recycled T-shirt fabrics as the example), and the closing advice is to keep clothes in use longer and buy less. Pupils then match headings to parts, re-do the opening true/false set and compare with their predictions, and complete the KWL chart (p. 72). Vocabulary work is heavy and text-tied: a twenty-item definition match drawn from the article (biodegrade, array, saturated, woven, aquatic, excrete, exacerbate, disposable and others, p. 73), a prefix chart to be filled from the article and from the pupils' own words (anti-, bi-, de-, dis-, inter-, mis-, non-, over-, re-, semi-, sub-, super-, trans-, un-, under- and more, with *re-* exemplified by "remove", p. 74), and word-formation gap-fills (p. 75). The unit ends in action: a list of further reading links (WWF, The Economist, The Guardian, Greenpeace, Fairtrade and a life-cycle study of a sustainable T-shirt), a "talking image" poster or interactive image tracing a T-shirt's life-cycle stage by stage, and poster-making to spread the message (pp. 75–77). Printed p. 78 is a closing picture page. No separate grammar presentation is given; the language focus is lexis and word-building.

**Unit 7 — Pride and Prejudice (printed pp. 79–92).** A literature unit on Jane Austen's novel, using summaries and short genuine extracts rather than the full novel. An opening panel (p. 80) introduces it as a romantic novel about love in late-18th-century England, originally titled *First Impressions*, about marrying for love rather than money under social pressure, its comedy lying in manners, education, marriage and money in the Regency period. Pupils discuss reputation, first impressions and what makes a person significant, then read a plot summary (p. 81): the Bennet household in Hertfordshire — overbearing mother, five daughters (beautiful Jane, clever Elizabeth, bookish Mary, immature Kitty, wild Lydia) whose security depends on marriage because the house will pass to a distant cousin — is stirred by the arrival of the rich Mr Bingley, who brings his sister and his wealthy, proud friend Mr Darcy; the summary frames the book as the romance of the spirited, poverty-stricken and prejudiced Elizabeth and the pompous, proud aristocrat Darcy, and as Elizabeth's emotional development from hasty judgement to distinguishing the superficial from the essential. An adapted summary of the opening chapters in seven lettered sections (pp. 82–83) then works the detail: the stir at Longbourn and Mrs Bennet's matchmaking, the Meryton ball where Jane dances twice with Bingley and Darcy refuses Elizabeth in her hearing, Bingley's inherited fortune and his steady, contrasting friendship with Darcy, the sisters' exchange of visits, Darcy's growing attraction as he listens to Elizabeth's conversations, and Miss Bingley's jealous manoeuvres to hold his attention and mock Elizabeth's family. Analysis tasks (pp. 84–85) ask for examples of irony, Austen's criticism of her society set against today's in a chart, a character map justifying her characterisation, why marriage to a well-off man mattered for women then against women's position now (as a poster), why *First Impressions* was an apt first title, paragraph titles, and — from Oxford and Collins definitions, two senses each for *pride* and for *prejudice* — which character shows which, evidenced from the text. Discussion turns to why a novel published in 1813 is still popular, which of its values are universal, and whether Elizabeth would count as a remarkable woman today (p. 86). Three extracts are then read closely with questions (pp. 87–89): the famous opening line, with its themes, its definition of individuals and of women's status, and an invitation to rewrite it from another perspective; Darcy's slight at the Meryton ball together with Elizabeth's composed refusal of his first proposal; Elizabeth's self-accusation after reading his letter — vanity, not love, as her folly, and never having known herself until that moment; and Darcy's confession that he had been a selfish being all his life, spoilt as an only son, taught good principles but not to correct his temper, and properly humbled by Elizabeth. Questions press on whether each has recognised and owned their fault, how upbringing shaped behaviour, and whether self-awareness alone determines future happiness (pp. 89–90). The unit closes personally: encountering and overcoming prejudice in pupils' own relationships, class consciousness and social structure in Greece compared with the novel, the family's role in educating children in Austen against today, and a debate on whether family or friends and peers mostly shape children's personality (p. 91). Printed p. 92 is a closing picture page. No grammar work is set in this unit; the language work is literary vocabulary and the two title concepts.

**Unit 8 — Social Media (printed pp. 93–112).** The longest unit (twenty printed pages) and the book's grammar-and-essay capstone. Pre-reading discussion covers social-media vocabulary, whether social media is needed, and life without it (p. 94). The main reading (pp. 94–96) is an adapted BBC Future article in ten numbered paragraphs arguing, in own words, that social media is harming sleep and mental health together: teenagers build up very large daily screen time and even adults spend more time on screens than asleep; depression and social-media use appear to feed each other in a circle that also involves anxiety, isolation and deprivation; use in the last half-hour before bed is, in a large study of young adults, the strongest predictor of poor sleep regardless of total daily use, plausibly through blue light suppressing melatonin, rising anxiety, or simple displacement of sleep time; lack of sleep is in turn linked to heart disease, diabetes, obesity, poor school performance, slower driving reactions, risk behaviour and substance use; adolescents are hit hardest because of the biological and social changes of that stage; comparing one's own life with others' posts in bed worsens mood and wakefulness; and the recommended response is moderation — ring-fenced screen-free times and set places at home where devices may or may not be used. Comprehension is exam-like in density: purpose, paragraph-title matching for all ten paragraphs, paragraph-location questions, and ten multiple-choice items on audience, theme, reference and the writer's conclusion (pp. 96–97), followed by another "5-4-3-2-1" response table (p. 98). A counter-text (p. 99), a Guardian article arguing that teenagers' social networking may actually be good for them — generational panic over new media from 1930s radio to the Walkman, the heaviest texters also seeing friends most in person, older teenagers easing off as their freedom grows, careful privacy management and deleting traces, and weak evidence that short-form writing is eroding literacy — is compared with the first text for difference and preference. Then comes the book's only systematic grammar block, all on **conditionals** (pp. 100–105): completing and personalising conditional sentences; a type table (0–3) to complete; tense drills mixing types; noticing a sentence in which a present condition carries a modal result and saying how it differs; mixed conditionals (a type-2 condition with a type-3 result and vice versa); alternatives to *if* (*as long as, provided/providing that, on condition that, what if, unless, in the event of / in case of*) with a choose-the-right-item exercise; formal inverted conditionals introduced (with *Should you…, Were I you…, Had I known…*) and rewritten with *if*; ten sentences to rewrite using inversion; and ten prompts from which pupils build and justify conditional sentences of more than one possible type. Listening/viewing returns (pp. 106–107): a BBC radio talk on recording one's love life on social media (topic, title, reasons, impact — script not printed), discussion of social media's impact on personality, time, conversation skills, communities and relationships, and Sherry Turkle's TED talk "Alone Together", with a ten-item gap-fill and discussion of her two closing claims — being "alone together" and sacrificing conversation for mere connection. Discussion widens through a Mark Zuckerberg quotation on sharing making the world more transparent (brainstorming transparency, and what "power" means, in a mind map), a survey of pupils' own accounts and habits, class discussion of how far social media has changed life and how to prevent its negative effects, and a debate on whether social networking technology is making people more antisocial (pp. 108–109). Writing closes the book (pp. 110–112): a for-and-against essay of **200–240 words** on whether social networking has improved the quality of relationships, scaffolded by topic analysis, a given positive/negative points table (connecting worldwide set against sleep deprivation, to be completed), a four-paragraph plan, the book's largest linking-word bank (introducing the topic and advantages/disadvantages, presenting arguments for and against, listing, justifying, examples, results, contrast, concluding), an exercise sorting fourteen further linking phrases into those categories, a guide to introductory and concluding paragraphs, a formal-style checklist (sophisticated vocabulary, long complex sentences, impersonal constructions, passive voice, inversion, non-contracted forms, no colloquial words) and a writing-tips checklist. Printed pp. 113–115 (PDF pp. 114–116) are blank; the legal notice follows (PDF p. 117), then the repeated cover spread (PDF p. 118).
